1.3.src: World Bank, World Development Indicators — Employment in agriculture (% of total employment) (modeled ILO estimate), Egypt, Arab Rep.
1.3.note: ILO modeled estimate (ILOEST) rather than a direct survey observation; the 2025 figure is a model nowcast, and the World Bank country page displays it rounded to an integer. Next level not proposed: Level 4 requires the share to fall below 15% of total employment. It does not: the T1 published value is 18 for 2025, and the closest national survey evidence (CAPMAS LFS 2024, 18.7%) is higher still. No admissible source in the retrieved pages shows Egypt's agricultural employment share under 15%; even the unrounded aggregator series (17.5%, T5, not admissible for a statistic) would remain above the cut. The indicator name 'Employment in agriculture (%)' omits the denominator; the quoted series is explicitly '% of total employment', which is the standard reading and is what is recorded here. The series covers ISIC-A (agriculture, hunting, forestry and fishing), i.e. slightly broader than crop-and-livestock agriculture alone, so the figure is a mild upper bound on agriculture-only employment share. It is also a modeled ILO nowcast for 2025, not an observed CAPMAS survey result. National corroboration sits on the same side: the CAPMAS 2024 Labor Force Survey, as reported by Egypt's State Information Service (T3), states 'Agriculture and fishing remained the largest employment sectors, engaging 5.594 million workers, representing 18.7 percent of the workforce.' A T5 aggregator (statisticsoftheworld.com) shows the unrounded WDI value as 17.5% for 2025, but T5 cannot carry a statistic, so the rounded T1 value of 18 is recorded. An independent T1 series (World Bank WDI SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS (ILO modeled estimate)) reports 17.52 for 2025, which differs from the value recorded here.
1.3.tier_detail: ILO modelled estimate (ILOEST) rather than a direct survey observation; the 2025 figure is a model nowcast, and the World Bank country page displays it rounded to an integer

1.2.src: World Bank, World Development Indicators — Cereal yield (kg per hectare) - Egypt, Arab Rep. (AG.YLD.CREL.KG)
1.2.note: FAO-compiled from national questionnaire returns; WDI notes complete cross-country consistency is not possible. Next level not proposed: Not required: level 5 is the top of the ladder and the value 7,402 kg/ha exceeds the highest cut point of 6000. The only caveat worth recording is that the most recent Egypt observation is 2023, one year behind the 2024 observation available for many other economies in the same table. The WDI series AG.YLD.CREL.KG is exactly the named construct: cereal yield in kilograms per hectare of harvested land, covering wheat, rice, maize, barley, oats, rye, millet, sorghum, buckwheat and mixed grains harvested for dry grain (per the WDI metadata glossary page retrieved as Source 2). The figure is national for Egypt, Arab Rep., which is the unit the indicator names. Corroborated by an independent T1 series (World Bank WDI AG.YLD.CREL.KG): 7402.2 for 2023.
1.2.tier_detail: FAO-compiled from national questionnaire returns; WDI notes complete cross-country consistency is not possible

1.1.src: World Bank, World Development Indicators — Agriculture, forestry, and fishing, value added per worker (constant 2015 US$) (NV.AGR.EMPL.KD)
1.1.note: Numerator from national accounts; denominator is ILO modeled employment estimate (ILOSTAT modeled series), so the ratio is partly modeled. Value is in constant 2015 US$, not current USD. Next level not proposed: Level 5 was not proposed because the published value, 8,942.42, does not exceed the 10000 cut point. Nothing in the retrieved pages shows Egypt above 10000 on this series in any year — the constant-2015 US$ series peaks at the 2025 value quoted, and the older constant-2010 US$ vintage tops out at 7,680 (2019). No alternative published per-worker figure for Egypt in current USD or on a narrower agriculture-only scope was found in the supplied pages that would cross 10000. The indicator name reads "Agriculture value added per worker (USD)". The quoted figure is WDI NV.AGR.EMPL.KD, whose published title is "Agriculture, forestry, and fishing, value added per worker (constant 2015 US$)" — sector scope is ISIC Rev.4 divisions 01-03 (agriculture PLUS forestry AND fishing, per the metadata glossary), and the price basis is constant 2015 US$ rather than current USD. Both differences sit on the unratified side of the census's open question: if the row is later defined as narrow crop-and-livestock agriculture, or as current USD, this figure would need replacing. No narrower agriculture-only or current-USD per-worker figure for Egypt appears in the retrieved pages. Related Egypt context from the same publisher: agriculture, forestry and fishing value added was 52,746.55 million constant 2015 US$ in 2025 and 16.6% of GDP, with 18% of total employment in agriculture (modeled ILO estimate). Corroborated by an independent T1 series (World Bank WDI NV.AGR.EMPL.KD): 8942.42 for 2025.
1.1.tier_detail: Numerator from national accounts; denominator is ILO modelled employment estimate (ILOSTAT modelled series), so the ratio is partly modelled. Value is in constant 2015 US$, not current USD.

1.4.src: World Bank, World Development Indicators — Food production index (2014-2016 = 100) - Egypt, Arab Rep.
1.4.note: FAO-compiled index; latest available reference year is 2022 (series ends 1961-2022). Next level not proposed: Level 4 would require the published index to exceed 115. Egypt's 2022 value of 109.1 falls 5.9 index points short, and the series peak in the quoted evidence (109.200 in 2021, per the corroborating record) never reaches 115, so no published year of this series supports the next rung. The quoted figure is exactly the WDI/FAO indicator AG.PRD.FOOD.XD, 'Food production index (2014-2016 = 100)', for Egypt, Arab Rep. Unit and base period match the indicator name precisely. Corroborated by an independent T1 series (World Bank WDI AG.PRD.FOOD.XD): 109.07 for 2022.
1.4.tier_detail: FAO-compiled index; latest available reference year is 2022 (series ends 1961-2022)

1.7.value: DATA GAP — 1) Egypt Findex 2025 microdata data-dictionary page (Source 1) — reviewed the full 199-variable list for a credit/agriculture cross-item; found borrowing variables (borrowed, fin22a, fin22e) and 'receive_agriculture', but the page is a variable index with no values. 2) Egypt Findex 2025 study description (Source 3) and Egypt Findex 2021 study description (Source 5) — methodology and coverage only, no indicator values; noted 2021 Egypt coverage excludes frontier governorates. 3) Findex download-data landing page (Source 2) — points to Excel/Databank files not supplied; confirms rural/urban disaggregation exists but the rural cut is rural ADULTS, not farmers. 4) Findex 2021 microdata codebook (Source 4) — confirms 'borrowed' and 'urbanicity_f2f' definitions, reinforcing that the population is adults 15+, not farmers; no Egypt values. 5) Multi-country fin22a variable page (Source 6) — has the only numbers on offer (10.2% Yes), but pooled across 141 economies and explicitly not a population statistic; rejected under the no-cross-border and construct rules. 6) FAO Egypt Agricultural Census 2009-2010 catalog page (Source 7) — the one source with a genuine farmer/holding denominator, but its listed scope omits credit and the page publishes no tabulations. 7) IFPRI 'An Agricultural Policy Review of Egypt' (Source 8) — only cover, contents and introduction retrieved; mentions the Principal Bank for Development and Agricultural Credit in the acronym list but no credit-access share appears in the retrieved text. 8) RFILC summary of IFAD's Egypt rural finance note (Source 9) — T5 aggregator page, qualitative only ('limited access to credit'), no statistic and not admissible for one. Dead ends: no CAPMAS, Central Bank of Egypt financial-inclusion, or IFAD full-text page was supplied, so the plausible homes for a farmer-level credit figure could not be checked.
1.7.note: Next level not proposed: Not applicable in the usual sense because no level is proposed: the evidence does not establish even the lowest rung, since it contains no Egypt-specific farmer credit figure at all — not a value below 10, not a value above it. The indicator names a share of FARMERS with credit ACCESS. The nearest thing in the supplied pages is Global Findex variable fin22a, 'Borrowed from a formal bank or similar financial institution', whose category table on the multi-country microdata page shows 10457 'Yes' cases (10.2%) — but that percentage is an unweighted case count pooled over 'Albania, Algeria, Argentina...and 137 more' economies, explicitly flagged on that page as not interpretable as a population summary statistic, and it is not Egypt. Even the Egypt-specific Findex file measures individual adults aged 15+ (with a rural/urban split via 'urbanicity'), i.e. a population that includes non-farmers, and measures past-12-month BORROWING rather than ACCESS to credit. Carrying either figure into this cell would substitute a general-population borrowing rate for a farmer credit-access rate.

1.6.value: DATA GAP — Reviewed all ten supplied pages in order. (1) IFAD 'Egypt: Smallholder contract farming for high-value and organic agricultural exports' — only front matter and table of contents captured; no market-access percentage in the retrieved text. (2) FAO NENA small-scale agriculture Egypt page — blocked by Cloudflare verification, no content. (3) IFAD COSOP 2025-2030 — smallholder workforce (18.5%) and landholding (95%) shares only; market access discussed qualitatively as 'inclusive access to finance and markets' objective. (4) IFAD 2017 country strategy and programme evaluation — smallholder definition (<3 feddans) and qualitative effectiveness findings, no market-access rate. (5) IFAD scaling-up note — project-level outputs (36,000 families, marketing associations, collection centers), not a national share. (6) IFAD11 Impact Assessment Report — global corporate market-access beneficiary counts, not Egypt-specific. (7) World Bank EBA 2019 Egypt country profile — regulatory scores (overall 47.06), different construct, all farmers. (8)+(9)+(10) IFPRI/CGIAR/AgEcon/RePEc versions of Tabe-Ojong & Abay (2023) — the construct is participation in value chains and contract farming among smallholders in seven Upper Egypt governorates; abstract and policy-note text give qualitative findings and correlates but no participation percentage in the retrieved text, and in any case it is neither 'access' nor national. Dead ends: no FAOSTAT/CAPMAS/World Bank indicator on smallholder formal-market access was among the supplied pages. Conclusion: found=false with a ratification hold on construct mismatch and unquotable value.
1.6.note: Best available evidence is a sub-national research sample (seven governorates, Upper Egypt), not a national statistic; no headline percentage present in the retrieved text. Next level not proposed: No level above 0 was proposed because no source in the retrieved set states, for Egypt, any national percentage of smallholders selling into or having access to formal markets; the only Egypt-specific quantitative work is sub-national and measures contract-farming/value-chain participation, and even that percentage does not appear in the retrieved page text. The indicator names smallholder ACCESS to FORMAL MARKETS, nationally. The available Egypt evidence measures (a) participation in high-value crop value chains and contract farming among irrigated smallholders in seven Upper Egypt governorates (IFPRI/CGIAR, 2023), which is a participation/uptake measure of one specific formal marketing channel rather than access, and is not national in coverage; and (b) context figures that are not market-access measures at all — IFAD's 2025-2030 COSOP states smallholder farmers 'constitute 18.5 per cent of the national workforce and operate 95 per cent of agricultural landholdings', and the World Bank EBA 2019 country profile gives an overall Enabling the Business of Agriculture score of 47.06 for Egypt (a regulatory-environment index covering all farmers, not smallholder market access). Each of these sits on the wrong side of the open definitional question flagged in the indicator census: participation/regulatory-environment versus access, and regional/whole-sector versus national smallholder.

1.8.value: DATA GAP — Worked through all nine supplied pages in tier order. (1) World Bank 'Bringing the Concept of CSA to Life' feature page and (5) its Documents & Reports record: global/33-country synthesis, Egypt not named, no country adoption percentages on either page. (4) CCAFS CSA Country Profiles index: enumerated the profile list for LAC, Africa, Asia, Europe — Egypt is not among the profiled or in-development countries, closing the most likely source of a country CSA adoption statistic. (3) FAO SHARP+ project page GCP/EGY/039/CAN: Egypt-specific and on-construct in subject matter, but the only number is a forward-looking target of over 8,000 farmers across 3,000 hectares — a project output target, not an adoption rate; recorded in construct_note rather than as a value. (7) and (8) USDA FAS Grain and Feed Annual EG2025-0009 and EG2026-0002: searched the wheat production sections for any raised-bed adoption share; both describe ARC 'encouraging farmers' to adopt raised beds and quantify only the practice's effects (25 percent less water, 15 percent fewer seeds), never uptake. (2) CAPMAS cropped-area bulletin 2014/15: gives total and crop areas (wheat 3.47 million feddan) but no climate-smart or raised-bed breakdown, so it supplies a possible denominator with no numerator. (6) ScienceDirect raised-beds-in-Egypt article: page returned a CAPTCHA challenge, no text retrieved, so nothing quotable. (9) World Grain: T5 news, and in any case reports only agronomic potential (30 percent yield gain, 75 percent water-use efficiency), not adoption prevalence; T5 cannot carry a statistic. Dead ends noted: no CAPMAS or MALR survey of CSA/conservation-agriculture adoption, and no FAOSTAT-style adoption series, appears in the retrieved set. Concluded found=false with a ratification hold.
1.8.note: Next level not proposed: Even the lowest rung is withheld because no source in the supplied set reports any denominator-based adoption share for Egyptian farmers. What level 1 would require — a published figure for the named construct that happens to fall below 20 — does not exist in these pages; and what level 2 would require (a verified figure above 20 percent) is not approached by any evidence here, the only quantities being an 8,000-farmer project target and a 3,000-hectare project footprint. The indicator names the share of FARMERS adopting climate-smart practices. The closest Egypt evidence in the supplied pages is (a) FAO project GCP/EGY/039/CAN, which states an ex-ante target that 'over 8,000 farmers will adopt climate-smart agriculture and biodiversity-friendly practices across 3,000 hectares' — a project beneficiary target, not a national share, and not an observed outcome; and (b) USDA FAS Grain and Feed Annual reports (EG2025-0009, EG2026-0002), which describe government encouragement of raised-bed wheat cultivation and its water/seed savings but give no adoption figure at all — neither a share of farmers nor a share of wheat area. Egypt's total wheat area is published by CAPMAS (3.47 million feddan in 2014/15) and by USDA (1.5 million ha harvested in MY2026/27), but no numerator for raised-bed area appears in any retrieved page, so even the wrong-side-of-the-question 'share of wheat area under one practice' variant cannot be quote-verified here. The World Bank/CIAT CSA Country Profile series (Source 4 listing, Source 1/5 synthesis) does not include Egypt among its ~33 profiled countries, so that dataset yields no Egypt adoption figure either.

1.5.value: DATA GAP — Started with the FAO Egypt country page for food loss and waste (Source 1) - returns a 404 error page, no data. Checked the FAO SDG Indicators Data Portal pages for 12.3.1 (Sources 2 and 4) - these carry only global and regional food-loss percentages (13.3 percent world 2023; sub-Saharan Africa 23.0 percent; commodity-group splits) and no Egypt country value in the page text; the country datasets are behind a download link not retrieved. Checked the FAO Technical Platform food-loss measurement and FLW database user-guide pages (Sources 3 and 5) - methodology and filter documentation only, no Egypt figure in text. Found Egypt-specific numbers only in the FAO Egypt factsheet on openknowledge.fao.org (Source 6): wheat 10-20 percent in shona storage, grapes 25-35 percent preliminary, tomatoes more than half spoilt/quality-damaged. Cross-checked with the peer-reviewed grape supply-chain study abstract (Source 9), which gives node-level PHL percentages for Egypt. The COMCEC/NRI report (Source 8) has a 'Cereals in Egypt' case study in its table of contents, but the retrieved text stops at the contents pages and contains no Egyptian loss percentage, so no figure could be quoted from it. The Food Systems Dashboard page (Source 10) returned a security-checkpoint stub with no data. Conclusion: no single national all-crop post-harvest loss rate for Egypt is present in any supplied page.
1.5.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. Commodity-specific and partly described by the source as 'preliminary' estimates; the wheat figure covers one stage (traditional shona storage) rather than the whole chain, and no weighting to a national all-crop rate is published. The indicator name asserts an all-crop NATIONAL post-harvest loss rate for Egypt. Nothing in the retrieved pages publishes such a national figure. What exists is (a) FAO commodity-level estimates for Egypt (wheat 10-20 percent in traditional shona storage; grapes 25-35 percent 'preliminary'; tomatoes 'more than half' spoilt or quality-damaged) and (b) a peer-reviewed grapes-only supply-chain study with node averages of 10.06/5.82/6.53/7.06 percent. These are partial, commodity- and stage-specific measures, some of which mix quantity loss with quality/economic loss (the tomato and grape statements explicitly include 'quality loss and damage'), which sits on the wrong side of the census's open question. The FAO SDG 12.3.1a portal pages retrieved give only global and regional food-loss percentages (world 13.3 percent in 2023; sub-Saharan Africa 23.0 percent) with no Egypt value, and those are not this country's figure.

8.1.src: World Bank Open Data (World Development Indicators) — Prevalence of undernourishment (% of population), Egypt, Arab Rep. (source: FAO)
8.1.note: World Bank display rounds the FAO estimate to whole percent (shown as 9 for 2023); FAO PoU is a modeled three-year-average estimate derived from food balance sheets and household survey parameters, not a direct measurement. Next level not proposed: Level 4 would require the undernourishment prevalence to be below 7.5 percent. The published 2023 figure is 9 (9.4 in the unrounded restatement of the same WDI series), which is above 7.5 on both roundings, so the third cut is not passed. The trend in the retrieved data runs the wrong way for the higher rung as well: the series rises from 4.8 percent in 2001 to 9.4 percent in 2023, so there is no recent year at the current vintage that clears 7.5. The World Bank series SN.ITK.DEFC.ZS, sourced from FAO/FAOSTAT Suite of Food Security Indicators, is exactly the prevalence of undernourishment (% of population) for Egypt, Arab Rep. Context on precision: a T5 aggregator (statisticsoftheworld.com) restating the same WDI series gives 9.4% for 2023; the WHO NLiS Egypt profile carries an older vintage of the same construct, 4.5% for 2016-2018, which is superseded by the 2023 FAO/WDI figure. Only the T1 rounded figure of 9 is recorded here. An independent T1 series (World Bank WDI SN.ITK.DEFC.ZS) reports 9.4 for 2023, which differs from the value recorded here.
8.1.tier_detail: World Bank display rounds the FAO estimate to whole percent (shown as 9 for 2023); FAO PoU is a modelled three-year-average estimate derived from food balance sheets and household survey parameters, not a direct measurement

2.4.src: World Bank Open Data — Individuals using the Internet (% of population) - Egypt, Arab Rep. (source: ITU World Telecommunication/ICT Indicators Database)
2.4.note: World Bank country table displays the value rounded to whole percent; underlying ITU series value is reported elsewhere as 74.65. Next level not proposed: Level 5 would require a published figure above 80% of the population using the Internet. The most recent T1 observation is 75 (2024), five points short of the 80 cut; no source in the retrieved pages publishes an Egyptian figure at or above 80 for any year, and the series trend on the same page shows the value essentially flat since 2020 (72-75), so the 80 threshold is not met. World Bank indicator IT.NET.USER.ZS, defined as 'Internet users are individuals who have used the Internet (from any location) in the last 3 months', sourced from ITU — identical to the named construct 'Individuals using the Internet (%)'. National-population figure, which is what the indicator names (no rural/urban restriction applies). Corroborated by an independent T1 series (World Bank WDI IT.NET.USER.ZS): 74.65 for 2024.
2.4.tier_detail: World Bank country table displays the value rounded to whole percent; underlying ITU series value is reported elsewhere as 74.65

2.1.value: DATA GAP — 1) ITU DataHub home (datahub.itu.int) — indicator portal only; popular indicators shown for the United States by geolocation; no Egypt values, no rural coverage indicator value. 2) ITU-D Statistics landing page — confirms ITU publishes 'Population covered by a mobile-cellular and a mobile-broadband network, total and by urban/rural area', but only as world/region/development-group time series downloads; no country-level Egypt rural figure on the page. 3) ITU DataHub UMC dashboard — focus economy fixed to United States; contains no coverage-by-technology row and no Egypt data. 4) ITU DataHub About page — methodology only; notes the March questionnaire collects 'mobile population coverage (total, 3G, 4G and above)', confirming the national-total framing of the collected series but giving no values. 5) ITU World Telecommunication/ICT Indicators Database page — states the database was discontinued in 2024 and redirects to DataHub; no data. 6) MCIT Egypt Indicators index (T3) — lists ICT Indicators in Brief and Quarterly Bulletins; no coverage figure on the index page itself. 7) MCIT 'ICT Indicators in Brief', September 2023 (T3) — searched for rural coverage; found only mobile subscriptions/penetration, mobile internet users, ADSL regional distribution, and 'Number of Local Exchanges in Rural Areas' (fixed exchanges, wrong construct). 8) GSMA Coverage Maps page and GSMA State of Mobile Internet Connectivity 2025 'Network Coverage and Infrastructure' (T4) — global 96% covered / 4% gap and country figures for DRC, Afghanistan, Pakistan, Papua New Guinea, Tanzania, Zambia only; Egypt not mentioned, and T4 is inadmissible for this prerequisite row regardless. 9) GSMA Mobile Connectivity Index (T5) — lists Egypt and lists '3G Population Coverage'/'4G Population Coverage' as indicators, but the retrieved page carries no values and T5 may not carry a statistic. Dead end: no admissible, quotable Egypt rural mobile broadband coverage figure in the supplied corpus. To close this cell an auditor should pull the ITU DataHub country page for Egypt for indicator 'Population covered by at least a 3G/4G mobile network, rural (%)' if ITU disseminates the rural split at country level, or Egypt's NTRA/MCIT coverage obligation reporting.
2.1.note: Next level not proposed: Withholding rather than proposing a level: the specific missing item is a published rural-disaggregated mobile broadband (3G/4G) population-coverage percentage for Egypt from a T1–T3 publisher, quotable verbatim. Neither the ITU DataHub pages retrieved (which show only United States defaults and aggregate download links) nor Egypt's MCIT bulletins (which publish mobile subscriptions/penetration, and rural counts only for fixed local exchanges) supply it. The indicator names RURAL mobile broadband coverage. The figure ordinarily used to populate this row for Egypt is the ITU 'population covered by at least a 3G mobile network' series, which is a NATIONAL total, not a rural share — recording it here would answer a different construct and would score level 5 mechanically off a non-rural number. ITU does publish a rural/urban split of 'Population covered by a mobile-cellular and a mobile-broadband network, total and by urban/rural area', but the retrieved ITU pages only advertise that series at global/regional aggregate level ('Download time series of ICT data for the world, by geographic regions, by urban/rural area and by level of development') and expose no Egypt country value. No Egypt rural percentage, and no Egypt national percentage either, appears anywhere in the supplied pages, so no context figure can be quoted.

8.5.value: DATA GAP — 1) FAO Gender and Land Rights Database country page — returned a 404 'Page not found', so no GLRD Egypt ownership indicator was obtainable. 2) FAOSTAT 'Structural data from agricultural censuses' catalog pages (two variants) — describe that 'sex of agricultural holders' is a disseminated indicator but carry no Egypt values. 3) FAO country summary of the Egypt Agricultural Census 1999/2000 — carries 'HOLDERS BY SEX' counts (female 236 632 of 4 537 319 civil persons) but no percentage. 4) FAO summary of the Egypt Agricultural Census 1990 — holders by sex counts (female 285 753 of 3 470 813), again no percentage. 5) FAO microdata catalog entry for Egypt Agricultural Census 2009-2010 — metadata only; the retrieved text lists scope topics (holdings characteristics, cultivated area, irrigation, employment, machinery, livestock) and contains no sex-of-holder result, so no 2010-round figure could be quoted. 6) CAPMAS Economic Census 2022/2023 metadata page — questionnaire and results listings only, no women-landholder statistic in the retrieved text. 7) FAO/PIM 'Gender and Land Statistics' technical note — defines the ownership indicators (Indicators 2-5) but the retrieved text stops before any Egypt row. 8) AUC Social Research Center page — the only retrieved page publishing an explicit percentage for the construct, which is what is recorded. 9) Land Portal Egypt country narrative (T5) — historical land-governance context only, no sex-disaggregated ownership statistic. Dead ends: no World Bank/WDI 'female share of agricultural holders' page and no SDG 5.a.1 (ownership/secure tenure rights over agricultural land, by sex) value for Egypt appeared in the supplied pages.
8.5.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. Figure published on a university research-center web page citing an unpublished background paper; no reference year is stated on the page and the figure is roughly two decades old. No percentage from the 2009/2010 agricultural census surfaced in the retrieved pages. The indicator's name says women who OWN land, but its own parenthetical unit is '% holders', and every figure available for Egypt in the retrieved pages counts female agricultural HOLDERS/landholders (operators of a holding, who may rent rather than own) rather than registered landowners. The quoted 5.72% is a share of landholders, not of documented owners. Corroborating holder counts from FAO's T1 census summaries: the 1999/2000 Agricultural Census reports 'Total (Civil persons) 4 537 319', 'Male 4 300 687', 'Female 236 632'; the 1990 census reports holders 'Total 3 470 813', male '3 185 060', female '285 753'. Both are counts, not published percentages, so they are used only as corroboration and not as the recorded value. Separately, the same AUC page reports women hold 6.1% of the cultivated area in Lower Egypt and 4.1% in border governorates — an area-based, not holder-based, measure. No sex-disaggregated statistic on legal land OWNERSHIP (e.g. FAO Gender and Land Rights Database Indicator 2, 'Distribution of agricultural landowners by sex') was retrievable for Egypt: the GLRD country page returned a 404 error, and the FAO/PIM technical note in the retrieved pages lists the indicators but its Egypt tables were not in the supplied text.

2.5.value: DATA GAP — 1. Opened the two ITU DataHub ICT-prices dashboard URLs filtered to Egypt (?e=EGY and ?e=EGY&u=PPP$) — both returned navigation chrome plus, in the second, the dashboard title and the list of selectable indicators ('Data-only mobile broadband basket 5 GB, as a % of GNI pc'; 'Mobile broadband data and voice low-consumption basket total (70 min, 50 SMS, 1 GB), as a % of monthly GNI per capita'; the 5 GB high-consumption basket). No numeric series values for Egypt in either page's text. 2. Checked the ITU DataHub indicator catalog page — confirms 'Current ICT price baskets' and 'Other ICT price baskets' exist under Affordability, but is a catalog with no country values. 3. Checked both copies of 'Measuring digital development: The affordability of ICT services 2024' (D-IND-ICT_PRICES.01-2025-PDF-E.pdf and 2500663E.pdf) — retrieved text covers only cover, foreword and the start of the contents; the country annex tables that would carry Egypt's value are not in the supplied extract. 4. Checked the ITU ICT prices landing page — it announces 2025 results for ~200 economies and links the 2008-2025 country-level Excel download, but publishes no country figures on the page itself. 5. Checked the ITU Statistics IPB dashboard page and the DataHub homepage — homepage figures shown are geolocated to USA, i.e. another country, and are therefore inadmissible here. Dead end: no page in this retrieval set carries an Egypt number, so found=false with a ratification hold.
2.5.note: Retrieved pages are dynamic dashboards whose data payload did not render in the captured text; no country value available for quote verification. Next level not proposed: Level withheld rather than set at 1: the evidence does not show that Egypt's basket price exceeds 10 per cent of GNI pc any more than it shows it falls below 1 per cent. The specific missing element is the Egypt row of the ITU ICT price basket dataset (country-level data 2008-2025 spreadsheet, or the rendered DataHub dashboard value), which would supply the figure and its basket definition. The retrieved ITU dashboard page confirms that ITU publishes, for Egypt among 196 economies, at least two distinct series that could each answer to the name 'Mobile broadband price (% GNI pc)': 'Data-only mobile broadband basket 5 GB, as a % of GNI pc' and 'Mobile broadband data and voice low-consumption basket total (70 min, 50 SMS, 1 GB), as a % of monthly GNI per capita', plus a high-consumption (140 min, 20 SMS, 5 GB) variant. The indicator name as written fixes neither the allowance (1 GB / 2 GB / 5 GB), nor the basket type (data-only vs voice+data), nor whether the denominator is monthly or annual GNI pc — and the ITU pages show the denominator wording differs between series (one says '% of GNI pc', the other explicitly '% of monthly GNI per capita'). Until the definition is ratified, even a correctly retrieved ITU value could be assigned to the wrong side of that question. No national-level Egypt figure of any of these variants appears in the supplied pages, so nothing is offered here as context either.

2.9.src: World Bank Open Data — Access to electricity, rural (% of rural population), indicator EG.ELC.ACCS.RU.ZS (SDG 7.1.1 Electrification Dataset)
2.9.note: Modeled/estimated series: World Bank Global Electrification Database compiles nationally representative household surveys and censuses, with modeling used to fill missing years; value is capped at 100.0 (universal-access assumption once surveys show full coverage). Next level not proposed: Not applicable — level 5 is the top band and the published value (100.0) exceeds the highest cut point of 80. The one caveat worth recording is that the figure is a modeled/assumed universal-access value rather than a fresh survey measurement for 2024, and it measures household connection only, not supply reliability or hours of service, which the indicator as named does not require. The quoted figure is from the World Bank indicator page for EG.ELC.ACCS.RU.ZS, defined as 'the percentage of rural population with access to electricity' — the rural-specific series, not the national series. For context, the national figure (EG.ELC.ACCS.ZS, Source 4) is also 100.0 for 2024, but the value recorded here is taken from the rural indicator page. Corroborated by an independent T1 series (World Bank WDI EG.ELC.ACCS.RU.ZS): 100 for 2024.
2.9.tier_detail: Modelled/estimated series: World Bank Global Electrification Database compiles nationally representative household surveys and censuses, with modelling used to fill missing years; value is capped at 100.0 (universal-access assumption once surveys show full coverage)

3.1.value: DATA GAP — Started with the UN DESA E-Government Knowledgebase country profile for Egypt (Source 1), which carries the headline 2024 EGDI 0.6699, rank 95 of 193, plus the full 2003-2024 historical series and the three sub-indices. Cross-checked the UN Data Center 193-country ranking table (Sources 2, 4, 6), which lists 'Egypt HEGDI H3 95 0.6699' — consistent. Checked Survey 2024 report pages (Sources 7, 10) and Chapter 3 (Source 8) for a narrative Egypt figure; they give only global and regional averages (global 0.6382, Africa 0.4247), no Egypt-specific number, so they were not used as the quoted source. Source 9 (statbase.org) reproduces the same series but is a T5 aggregator and was rejected in favour of the T1 primary. Quoted the historical-series row from the UN country profile because it contains the value at full published precision.
3.1.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. The quoted row is the UN EGDI historical series for Egypt; the 2024 column value is 0.66994, which the same page also displays rounded as 'E-Government Development Index 0.6699, Rank 95 of 193'. The UN Data Center table (Source 2/4) independently lists 'Egypt HEGDI H3 95 0.6699'. This is the national composite EGDI (OSI 0.70016, TII 0.69456, HCI 0.61503), exactly the named construct.

2.11.value: DATA GAP — 1) MCIT (T3) news on device policy — found only NTRA Telephony payment channels for IMEI registration fees; no financing or subsidy of device purchase. 2) SIS (T3) items on imported-mobile taxation — both URLs returned 404 'Page not found', so no evidence extractable. 3) GSMA handset-affordability corpus (T4): the 2024 GSMAi analysis, the 2022 Making internet-enabled phones more affordable report, the Handset Affordability Coalition page and the Nov 2024 policy brief — all generic to LMICs, with country coverage in the 2025 Africa deep-dive limited to DRC, Kenya, Nigeria, Rwanda, Senegal, South Africa, Togo and Zambia; Egypt absent. 4) GSMA MENA taxation review page (T4) — lists Egypt but describes taxes/fees, not device subsidies. 5) Business Today (T5) — customs-fee instalment via ValU, April 2026; existence fact only, and it finances customs dues, not devices. Dead ends: no Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation, Agricultural Bank of Egypt or Haya Karima document offering farmer device loans or subsidised handsets/tablets was in the retrieved set; no Vodafone/Orange/Etisalat/WE Egypt handset-instalment page was retrieved, so the census's disputed 'commercial telco instalment' class could not be tested for Egypt on this evidence.
2.11.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. Absence established against the retrieved page set only; Arabic-language MCIT/NTRA/Ministry of Agriculture material and operator commercial pages were not among the supplied sources. The indicator names device financing/subsidy schemes. The Egyptian evidence retrieved covers payment facilitation for statutory fees on devices (NTRA registration/IMEI fees via the Telephony app, T3 MCIT; and a customs-fee instalment plan via ValU reported at T5 by Business Today). Financing a customs or registration fee is on the wrong side of the construct: it does not lower or spread the acquisition cost of a handset or any other agricultural device, and it carries no subsidy element and no targeting of farmers or rural users. On the unresolved census question — whether commercial telco handset instalments count — the question does not even arise here, because no Egyptian operator handset-instalment offer appears in the retrieved pages; the only instalment product documented is for a government levy. GSMA's handset-affordability corpus in the set is generic to LMICs, and its country deep-dive (Accelerating Smartphone Adoption in Africa, Nov 2025) covers DRC, Kenya, Nigeria, Rwanda, Senegal, South Africa, Togo and Zambia — Egypt is not among them.

2.7.value: DATA GAP — 1) Checked ITU DataHub UMC dashboard for Egypt (T1) — has 'Mobile phone ownership 97.4% (2024)' but national and handset-agnostic; no smartphone or rural split. 2) Checked ITU 'Households with Internet access at home' page for Egypt, which offers a Rural/Urban Location disaggregation — the retrieved text shows the selector but no numeric values, and the construct is household internet access, not smartphone ownership. 3) Checked CAPMAS microdata catalog pages: Egypt Family Health Survey 2021 household questionnaire (urban/rural identifier only, no device tabulations) and the BEIMIS 2011 data dictionary (variables r_u_code, comp_have, laptop etc. — computer/laptop possession, no smartphone variable and no published tabulation) plus the BEIMIS 2007 catalog landing page (document list only). 4) Checked MCIT 'ICT Indicators in Brief' September 2023 and January 2020 (T3) — national mobile subscriptions/penetration and internet penetration only; the only rural-flavoured item is 'Number of Local Exchanges in Rural Areas', which is infrastructure, not ownership. 5) Checked World Bank 'Access is Not Enough' (T2) — pooled 71-country LMIC estimates and MENA-region gender gaps; no Egypt row, no rural split. 6) A Facebook post (T5) quoting rural smartphone ownership across surveyed countries returned no retrievable text and is in any case ineligible for a statistic. Dead end: no admissible page in this set states rural smartphone ownership for Egypt.
2.7.note: Next level not proposed: Level withheld rather than set at 1: the evidence does not show that rural smartphone ownership is below 20% either. There is simply no rural-disaggregated, smartphone-specific measurement in the retrieved sources, so no cut point — the lowest included — can be tested. Closest available evidence: ITU DataHub Universal and Meaningful Connectivity dashboard for Egypt reports 'Mobile phone ownership / Individuals who own a mobile cellular telephone % 97.4% ... 2024'. That is (a) NATIONAL, not rural, and (b) any mobile cellular telephone, not a smartphone — two separate construct mismatches. ITU also lists 'Households with Internet access at home' with a Rural/Urban disaggregation for Egypt, but the retrieved page shows only the disaggregation selector and no numeric value, and household internet access is not smartphone ownership. The World Bank note 'Access is Not Enough' reports cross-country sample smartphone ownership (58% of its 71-country LMIC sample; 60% of adults in LMICs) but publishes no Egypt-specific and no rural figure. On the unratified definitional question: even the best-fitting candidates here sit on the wrong side twice over — they are device-agnostic and geographically undifferentiated, so the household-vs-individual question does not yet arise for Egypt.

3.3.value: DATA GAP — 1) FAO 'Situation analysis of farmer registries in the Near East and North Africa (NENA)' — the most directly on-point source; page returned only a Cloudflare bot-verification interstitial, no text, so nothing quotable. 2) FAO NENA news item on farmer registries in the region (T1) — substantive, but the country cases are Morocco (Registre Agricole National), Lebanon (~48,000 registered) and Jordan (120,000 individuals / 70,000 holdings); Egypt is not mentioned at all, so it is not evidence for this country. 3) FAO Microdata catalog, Egypt Agricultural Census 2009-2010 (two pages) — a decennial complete enumeration whose statistical unit is 'the agricultural holding'; a census is a periodic statistical operation, not a maintained registry, and the last one is 2010. 4) CAPMAS microdata catalog, 'Agricultural Property and Rein 2017' — a land/holding property dataset, again not a farmer registry, and only a press release and PDF are exposed. 5) MALR Economic Affairs Sector site (agri.gov.eg/register) — the 'Register' page is a user account sign-up for the statistics portal, with menus for crop maps, agricultural censuses and databases; no farmer registry service is listed. 6) FAO/CIHEAM/CIRAD small-scale family farming study, Egypt (T2) — table of contents covers holdings typologies and tenure but no registry. 7) State Information Service (T3) — the only government artifact describing a national farmer-level data system, quoted here. 8) Al-Ahram Weekly (T5) — used only to corroborate the existence and mechanics of the scheme (owner-not-tenant rule, heirs rule); its figures are excluded as T5 statistics.
3.3.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. Government communiqué rather than a programme document or legal instrument; the unit of record is ambiguous (cardholder vs. landholding), and no official enumeration of registrants was found in an admissible-tier source. The indicator names a register of FARMERS (individuals). The only Egyptian instrument found is a subsidy smart-card scheme whose database is built from landholding records — the card is issued against agricultural landholding numbers, and Al-Ahram (T5) reports that the card must go to the owner rather than the tenant and that heirs of one plot must nominate a single cardholder. That means the unit of record is effectively the holding, not the farmer, and cultivating tenants can be excluded. The evidence therefore sits on the holding-registry side of the open definitional question flagged in the indicator census. No FAO farmer-registry assessment covering Egypt was retrievable: the FAO NENA regional dialogue page names Morocco, Jordan and Lebanon only, and the FAO situation-analysis page was blocked by a bot check.

3.6.value: DATA GAP — Order of examination: (1) World Bank MENA Climate and Hydrometeorological Services Atlas — correct document type and confirmed to contain an Egypt country profile per its contents list ('Egypt .... 108'), but only front matter was in the retrieved text, so no station-density, archive or data-policy sentence could be copied verbatim; (2) WMO GBON compliance app 'About' page — explains methodology (target station numbers, 80%/80% reporting rule) but is the methodology page, not the Egypt Member page, so no Egypt compliance figure; (3) WMO GBON implementation/compliance and GBON station visualisation pages — global framework and tool descriptions, no country data; (4) WMO 'Required action by Members' page — procedural, no Egypt content; (5) WMO SOFF page and un-soff.org Operations page — SOFF prioritises LDCs/SIDS; no mention of Egypt in either retrieved text; (6) ClimGen Egypt climate observations (CRU/UEA) — Egypt-specific but a derived gridded climate-normals product, i.e. a different construct from national data infrastructure. Dead ends: no Egyptian Meteorological Authority page, no national data-access portal or open-data license document, and no Country Hydromet Diagnostic for Egypt was among the supplied sources.
3.6.note: Only front matter of the key source (World Bank MENA hydromet atlas) was retrieved; the Egypt country profile body text was not in the supplied page extract. Next level not proposed: Not applicable — no level proposed. The specific missing evidence that would settle the rung: (a) the Egypt section (pp. 108-113) of the World Bank MENA hydromet atlas, (b) the WMO GBON compliance app Member page for Egypt showing surface/upper-air station targets and gaps, (c) the Egyptian Meteorological Authority's own data-catalog or data-request page. The indicator names data INFRASTRUCTURE — observation networks, archives, APIs/data access. The only Egypt-specific item in the supplied pages is a table-of-contents entry showing that the World Bank MENA hydromet atlas contains an Egypt country profile (pp. 108-113); that establishes a national hydromet service was profiled but states nothing about station counts, archive holdings or data-access channels. The ClimGen page gives Egypt national-average 1961-1990 CRU precipitation normals (annual 3.6 mm/month), but this is a third-party academic gridded product derived from global station archives, not a measure of Egypt's own observation network, archive or data-access infrastructure — it sits on the wrong side of the census question. The WMO GBON compliance app and SOFF pages describe the global compliance framework only; no Egypt station target, gap or compliance figure appears in the retrieved text. No evidence at all on farmer advisory products was retrieved here, so the overlap with indicator 8.17 flagged in the census could not be tested either.

3.5.value: DATA GAP — 1) CAPMAS Central Data Catalog root (censusinfo.capmas.gov.eg/.../catalog) — 629 studies, checked the FILTER BY DATA ACCESS control, which offers only 'Licensed data files' and 'Data not available'. 2) CAPMAS Agriculture collection page — 47 studies, no open-format indication. 3) Two individual agriculture study pages (catalog/321 production movement 2017; catalog/788 Fish Production 2022) — downloads are PDF reports only, no CSV/microdata file. 4) catalog/788/accesspolicy — confidentiality clause, citation requirement, copyright CAPMAS; no open license (no CC/ODbL) named. 5) Agriculture-Quarter collection 'about' page — descriptive only. 6) MALR Economic Affairs Sector databases index (agri.gov.eg/databases) and the crop-production database (agri.gov.eg/databases/42) — Arabic HTML query interface, year range 2010–2019, no export, license or API. 7) Open Data Watch ODIN 2024 Egypt profile — agriculture-and-land-use openness 40/100; used as context only, not as the recorded value (T5 domain tiering, and it measures statistical-category openness rather than the existence of an AI-ready open agricultural data asset). Dead ends: no Egyptian national open-data portal page (e.g. a data.gov.eg-style CKAN instance) and no agricultural data-sharing policy or interoperability framework document was among the retrieved sources, so I could not test those; if such artifacts exist they were not reachable in this retrieval set.
3.5.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. Nearest-adjacent artifact cited as absence evidence, not as a measure of the construct; catalog pages retrieved without login, so behind-login holdings could not be inspected. The named construct is a conjunction — open AND machine-readable AND AI-ready agricultural data. The quoted CAPMAS page is offered as evidence that the right place was searched: it is Egypt's national statistical microdata catalog and it does hold an Agriculture collection (47 studies), but its data-access filters offer only 'Licensed data files' and 'Data not available', the study pages (e.g. Annual Bulletin of Fish Production 2022, catalog/788) expose only a PDF 'Other Materials' download, and the access-policy page states 'The site does not publish individual data about individuals'. That fails 'open' and fails 'machine-readable/AI-ready'. The MALR Economic Affairs Sector 'قواعد البيانات' pages (agri.gov.eg/databases, /databases/42) are a queryable crop-production interface with year pickers ending at 2019 and no export format, license or API. For context only, and not recorded as the value: Open Data Watch's ODIN 2024 country profile scores Egypt's 'Agriculture and land use' category 70 coverage / 40 openness (overall 55) — an openness measure of statistical categories, published on a page tiered T5 here, and not a statement about an AI-ready agricultural data instrument. This cell therefore sits on the strict side of the census's open question: had the row been read loosely as 'government publishes agricultural statistics digitally', Egypt would rate Operating; read against the name as written, the instrument is Absent.

3.7.value: DATA GAP — 1) CAPMAS T1 microdata catalog (central catalog, 629 studies; cultivated area 2016; irrigation and water resources 2016; land reclamation 2017-2018; agricultural income estimates) — searched for any EO/remote-sensing-derived agricultural statistical product; the agricultural collection is survey/administrative bulletins with no EO input documented: dead end for T1 evidence of integration. 2) ESA DUE project page (T3) — the Egypt entry retrieved is TIGER Lake Manzalah water-quality monitoring, status Completed; water quality, not agriculture, so a different construct and not usable for this cell. 3) Peer-reviewed literature (T2): IJRS 2025 crop-type and cultivation-stage mapping in El-Behera Governorate, acknowledging NARSS financial support — establishes national-agency EO crop-mapping capability but at governorate scale in a research setting; MDPI Geosciences 2017 Nile Delta paper is archaeological remote sensing, not agriculture. 4) Daily News Egypt (T5) — the only retrieved item describing NARSS and the Ministry of Agriculture jointly presenting national-season crop maps; used solely as an existence fact for the rung. No official NARSS, MALR or Egyptian Cabinet document was among the supplied pages, so the strength of institutional integration could not be verified beyond this.
3.7.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. Operational claim rests on a single T5 news report (existence fact only); no NARSS or MALR primary document, budget line or service description was retrieved, and the news item describes the work in project language ('the project's principal researcher'), leaving routine institutionalisation unverified. The indicator name 'Satellite/EO data integration' fixes neither the object nor the bar. The retrieved evidence establishes production of EO-derived crop maps by the national space agency in coordination with the agriculture ministry — i.e. EO products reaching the agricultural administration. It does NOT establish 'integration' in the stronger sense of EO layers embedded in a national agricultural information system, statistical production, or a formal institutional data-sharing arrangement: the CAPMAS agricultural bulletins in the T1 microdata catalog (cultivated area, land reclamation, irrigation) show no EO-derived input. Judged against the name as written, the evidence sits on the 'produces national crop maps' side of the open question, not on the 'institutional arrangements / systems integration' side.

3.11.value: DATA GAP — 1) Checked the national policy layer first: ai.gov.eg Open Data Policy (2025) — read scope, guiding principles, institutional framework (EDGA, Interagency Data Release Board, Open Data Officers) and the table of contents listing Annex I 'Metadata Standards for Open Data'; entirely sector-neutral, agriculture never mentioned in the retrieved text. 2) Checked the sector owner: agri.gov.eg/databases (MoALR Economic Affairs Sector) — lists crop, livestock, poultry, fisheries, food-balance and trade databases; no standards, API, schema or interoperability documentation on the page. 3) Checked the statistical system: CAPMAS paper at unstats.un.org — confirms CAPMAS's legal mandate for interagency coordination and standard-setting is 'not yet fully materialized', with duplications and inconsistencies across producers, which is the opposite of an operating interoperability regime; the CAPMAS SDG 6.4.1 deck (fao.org) documents delays and national-vs-international methodology divergence for agricultural water data. 4) Checked FAO's agricultural-data work in Egypt: three GSARS II news items (2023-2024) covering dissemination training including 'open data standards and principles' and Nesstar microdata documentation — these are training events for 11-17 officials, not adopted national standards, and give no coverage figures usable as scale. 5) Checked the regional legal review: FAO 'Regulatory framework for agricultural data in the Near East and North Africa region' (2023) — its contents explicitly flag insufficient legal frameworks for agricultural data and variety of data formats and interfaces as unresolved regional gaps. 6) Checked agriculture-specific semantic work: AGRIS lists ARC/MoALR as an active data provider participating in the AGRIS Open Data Set (a bibliographic metadata network, not a national agri-data interoperability standard), and Nile University's AgriSem project (T5) is research-stage. Dead ends: no Egyptian e-government interoperability framework document, no national agricultural data-sharing decree, and no Egyptian AGROVOC/ontology adoption instrument were among the retrieved pages, so any figure or claim about those would be unverifiable here.
3.11.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. The quoted instrument is Egypt's horizontal, cross-government Open Data Policy (2025), not an agricultural data interoperability standard. It is cited only as the nearest adjacent instrument examined — evidence that the right domain was searched — not as a measure of the named construct. On the census's open question: if cross-government open-data/DPI instruments were allowed to count, Egypt would rate Adopted on the strength of this policy (it sets metadata standards, licensing models and an institutional framework via the Egyptian Data Governance Authority) and possibly Announced on the forthcoming Data Governance Law. Judged against the indicator's name as written — AGRICULTURAL data interoperability standards — nothing agriculture-specific was found: the FAO NENA regional review (openknowledge.fao.org, 2023) devotes sections to 'Insufficient legal frameworks concerning agricultural data', 'Variety of data formats and interfaces' and 'Deficiencies in current data regulations with respect to agricultural data', and recommends harmonizing regulatory frameworks in the region rather than reporting an existing Egyptian one; the MoALR Economic Affairs Sector database pages list sectoral datasets with no published standard or exchange specification; and the AgriSem semantic-interoperability work (Nile University, T5) is a bilateral research project, not a national instrument.

3.8.value: DATA GAP — 1) FAO Soils Portal legacy maps page — confirmed Egypt is among countries with archived/scanned FAO paper soil maps, but noted these are JPEG and not geo-referenced (weak side of the definition question). 2) FAO GLOSIS / Global Soil Partnership 'Soil information and data' page — checked the list of regional and national soil information systems; Egypt not listed. 3) FAO SoilSTAT pages — one returned a 404; the other describes SoilSTAT as still being designed, no Egypt-specific content. 4) FAO Near East land resources information systems proceedings: the NARSS paper (y4357e05) describing production of digital soil and terrain data of Egypt with FAO and the European Soil Bureau; the EALIP welcome address (y4357e16) reporting GIS-based soil degradation data since 1996 and nationwide 1:100 000 maps; and the Egypt country report (y4357e07), which carries the quoted statement on the GIS-based soil database — this was chosen as the citation. 5) EUDASM/JRC entry 'Soil Map of Egypt' (Hammad 1975) — confirms a legacy national soil map exists; page is a catalog record only. 6) ScienceDirect article on digital soil mapping in Egypt — blocked by captcha, text unavailable, so not used. Dead ends: no Egyptian government (MALR, NARSS, ARC) page, no current national soil information system portal, and no evaluation or performance report on any Egyptian soil database was retrieved among the supplied pages.
3.8.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. Primary evidence is 2001-vintage (FAO workshop country report); no post-2010 official documentation of the national soil database's current status was retrieved. The indicator census asks whether a digitized legacy paper map satisfies the row or whether an operating digital soil information service is required. The Egyptian evidence sits on BOTH sides but strongest on the weaker side: the clearest artifacts are legacy products (Soil Map of Egypt, Hammad 1975, in EUDASM; ~scanned, non-georeferenced FAO legacy paper maps listing Egypt). The stronger, database-side evidence — EALIP's GIS-based national soil database with nationwide 1:100 000 salinity/sodicity/water-table maps — is documented only as of 1997-2001. If the ratified definition requires an operating, current digital soil information service, this cell would drop toward Announced/Absent, because Egypt does not appear among the regional and national soil information systems listed on FAO's GLOSIS page (CamSIS, MaSIS, SISLAC).

4.1.value: DATA GAP — Started with the World Bank GovTech pages supplied (GTMI main page, GTMI 2025 update, 2025 GTMI survey guidance note, GovTech data page, 2025 GTMI Brief): all describe the index and its 'laws and regulations' enabler component but none of the retrieved text contains any Egypt-specific data protection value or statement, so none could be quoted for this cell. Checked the World Bank Digital Business Indicators 'Data Privacy and Security' brief: it describes the indicator and links to an Excel download, but the retrieved page text carries no Egypt figure. Then went to the primary legal artifact: the full English text of Law No. 151 of 2020 on ILO NATLEX (Source 7), corroborated by identical text on acc.com (Source 9) and a law-firm translation (Source 10, T5, not used for the quote). The NATLEX record landing page (Source 8) returned only a Cloudflare bot-verification screen and carried no usable text. Quoted the NATLEX-hosted law text. Dead ends: no Egyptian Official Gazette page, no MCIT page on the Executive Regulations, and no Personal Data Protection Center page were among the retrieved sources, which is why the Operating rung could not be tested and why quality and scale fields are left empty.
4.1.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. Unofficial English translation of the Arabic text; the crawler labelled the natlex.ilo.org domain T5, but the document quoted is the national legal instrument itself, reproduced in the ILO's NATLEX national legislation database, hence tiered T3 as a government legal artifact. The indicator names a data protection/privacy law; the quoted artifact is Egypt's economy-wide personal data protection statute (Law 151/2020). It is general-purpose, not agriculture-specific, and by its Article 3 excludes data held by national security authorities, the Central Bank, and data processed for official statistical purposes.

3.4.value: DATA GAP — Started with the World Bank Modernization of Egyptian Property Registration Project PID (P177720, T1) — confirms a national land administration modernisation operation and a new-urban-communities focus, but the retrieved text carries no coverage or performance statistic. Checked the World Bank 'Assessment of Land Governance in Egypt' PDF — retrieved text is only the acronym list and acknowledgements, no substantive findings quotable. Checked the 2007 IFC SmartLessons brief on property registration reform (fee reform, deeds per month) — that is a pre-digital fee reform, not digital registration, so not used as the anchor. Discarded the Bosnia and Herzegovina Real Estate Registration Project PID as another country. Then went to Egyptian government artifacts: Ministry of Justice sector page (digital transformation and mechanisation mandate), MCIT press release of 30 Jan 2012 (mechanisation programme scale figures, link to the agricultural sijil ayni geographic databases), Cabinet news 24902 (nationwide elimination of handwriting, branch counts, first phase of the agricultural sijil ayni), and Cabinet news 82685 of 17 July 2025 (paperless G2G registration launched in 16 new-city registry offices under Law 27/2018 as amended by Law 177/2022). A T5 newspaper text of the draft unified national property-ID law was read for context only and not cited for any statistic. Dead end: no source in the set gives a figure for the share of agricultural plots or holdings digitally registered, and no independent evaluation or audit of registry performance was retrieved.
3.4.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. Operating and coverage statements come from government/implementer press releases (Cabinet, MCIT); no independent audit or evaluation of registry performance was retrieved, and no published coverage figures exist for the agricultural cadastre specifically. The indicator name reads generically as 'Digital land/plot registration', and the operating evidence is for Egypt's economy-wide real-estate registration and notarisation system (Shahr Aqari / sijil ayni), which is dominated by urban and new-urban-community property: the July 2025 G2G paperless launch covers 16 registry offices in new cities (Alamein, New Administrative Capital, 6th of October, etc.), and the 2021 World Bank project (P177720) frames the objective as scaling up registration 'in selected new urban communities'. The specifically agricultural register — al-sijil al-'ayni al-zira'i — appears in the same government sources only as a geographic database linked to the notarisation system (MCIT 2012) and as 'first phase' development (Cabinet). So the evidence sits on the all-property/urban side of the unresolved definitional question; if this row is later ratified to mean digital registration of agricultural holdings or usufruct specifically, the rung would need to be re-scored downward, as no operating national agricultural digital cadastre with published coverage was found in these pages.

4.3.value: DATA GAP — 1) MCIT press release 'ICT Sector Achievements in 2025' (mcit.gov.eg, T3) — the only government/official page retrieved; it names the Government AI Readiness Index but reports only a 60-place rise since 2019, no score, no current rank. 2) Oxford Insights 'Government AI Readiness Report 2025' PDF (oxfordinsights.com) — retrieved text stops after acknowledgements, contents and introduction; the 'Full rankings' section (p.59) and the MENA regional report (p.38), which would carry Egypt's score, are not in the supplied text. 3) Oxford Insights '2024 Government AI Readiness Index' PDF — same problem: table of contents and findings only; 'Full rankings' (p.41) not in supplied text; Egypt is not named anywhere in the retrieved portion. 4) Statista 'Government AI readiness index by category Egypt 2024' — paywalled, rank and overall score both masked ('*****'), and T5 in any case. 5) KAI LAB blog (T5) — gives Egypt 2024 overall 55.63, rank 65, plus pillar scores; blog, not admissible for a statistic. 6) Ahram Online (three URLs, same article, T5) — gives Egypt 2025 overall 57.5, rank 51/195, and all six pillar scores, sourced to an MCIT statement; news, not admissible for a statistic. Dead end: no T1/T2/T3/T4 page in this set reproduces the score, so the cell is held rather than scored off T5 numbers.
4.3.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. Admissible-tier evidence is a government press release reporting a rank movement, not a score; the score itself is available only through secondary news/blog reporting of an MCIT statement. The named construct is the Oxford Insights Government AI Readiness Index for Egypt. On the census's open question: the 2025 (8th) edition, per the Oxford Insights report retrieved here, rebuilt the framework around 69 indicators in six pillars (Policy Capacity, Governance, AI Infrastructure, Public Sector Adoption, Development and Diffusion, Resilience), and secondary reporting of the MCIT statement does quote an overall 2025 figure of 57.5 (rank 51/195), so an overall score appears to exist for 2025 rather than having been dropped — but that figure sits on the wrong side of the tier line here (T5 news only). Context figures that could NOT be admitted: 2025 overall 57.5 with pillar scores 100 Policy Capacity, 62.5 Governance, 46.06 AI Infrastructure, 60.07 Public Sector Adoption, 45.41 Development and Diffusion, 62.81 Resilience (Ahram Online, T5); 2024 overall 55.63, rank 65/188, with pillars Government 68.98, Technology Sector 42.13 (KAI LAB blog, T5); Statista's 2024 Egypt figure is paywalled and masked.

4.2.value: DATA GAP — Started with the ITU GCI publication landing pages (itu.int/pub and itu.int/epublications) - both carry front matter, acknowledgements, foreword and disclaimers only; neither retrieved page contains any country score table, so Egypt's 2024 figure could not be quoted from ITU. Checked the ITU-D GCI programme page (two variants) - describes the five pillars, the tier-based 5th edition and links to the GCI 2024 report, but carries no per-country data. Checked the ITU news item 'Egypt Ranked Ninth at Global Cybersecurity Index' - this is the 2014 first edition (rank 27th of 193 per that page's own text) and is a decade out of date, so not used as the value. Checked the Belgian CCB mirror of the GCI 2024 PDF - the retrieved extract stops at the foreword and contains no country tables. Checked Egypt's NTRA (tra.gov.eg) page - title asserts Tier 1 but the retrieved body was 'undefined', so not quotable. Settled on the MCIT (Egyptian ICT ministry) Cyber Security page, a T3 government artifact, which states the Tier 1 / perfect score GCI 2024 result verbatim. Recorded as a statement rather than a number because ITU GCI 2024 publishes tiers and 0-100 pillar scores, not a 0-1 overall index score of the kind the register's cut points assume.
4.2.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. Government self-report of an ITU classification; the ITU GCI 2024 report page carrying Egypt's own country profile/score was not among the retrieved sources, so the figure could not be quote-verified from ITU itself. A second government source (NTRA, tra.gov.eg) carries the same Tier 1 claim in its page title but the retrieved body text was empty. The indicator is named 'Cybersecurity framework (ITU GCI)'. The evidence is the GCI 2024 result for Egypt. Note the census question flagged for this row: ITU's GCI 2024 moved to a tier-based model and does not publish a single overall 0-1 index score per country; scores in that edition are expressed out of 100 (and the register's Egypt entry of '100' is on that 0-100 scale, not the 0-1 scale implied by the cut points, while Nigeria's 0.824 is on a 0-1 scale). The two register entries are therefore indeed incommensurable. The evidence here sits on the 0-100 / tier side of that question. Normalised (100/100 = 1.0), Egypt still clears the top cut point of 0.8, so the ambiguity does not change the level for this country, but it does mean the recorded 'value' is a tier/statement rather than an ITU-published 0-1 overall score.

4.4.value: DATA GAP — 1) ITU e-Agriculture Strategies page (T1) — checked the list of countries with dedicated e-agriculture strategies; Egypt not listed. 2) FAO openknowledge NENA 'Digital Agriculture Strategy' leaflet (T2) — generic guidance and roadmap for the region, no Egypt country strategy named. 3) Egypt MoALR official site, Welcome Message (T3) — nearest adjacent instrument: Agricultural Development Strategy aligned with NDP 2030 including a digital transformation programme; no dedicated digital-ag strategy document or link found on the site's Laws and regulations / Publications navigation as rendered. 4) ICARDA 'Current Situation of Digital Agriculture in Egypt' (2023, T2, limited access) — abstract describes tool categories and government apps under development, no national digital agriculture strategy mentioned. 5) FAO e-Agriculture news item on Egypt (2019, T1) — project-level digital extension model, not a strategy. 6) World Bank programmatic support to MALR (2021, T1) — only a table-of-contents section 5.5 'Digital Technologies' was in the retrieved text; no strategy statement quotable. 7) SIS story on Food Security and Agricultural Innovation Strategy — 404, dead end. 8) UNESCWA Arab National Development Planning Portal — blocked by Cloudflare bot check, dead end. Domain was searchable; the named instrument was not found in it, hence Absent rather than a data gap.
4.4.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. Ministry website is labelled "Beta Version"; no strategy document text or adoption instrument is published on the page. The indicator names a national DIGITAL AGRICULTURE strategy. The best Egypt-specific evidence retrieved is a broader Agricultural Development Strategy (aligned to NDP 2030) that merely 'is including number of programmes, & a digital transformation programme in the agricultural sector' — i.e. a digital-ag component embedded in a general sector strategy, not a dedicated digital-agriculture strategy document. This sits on the 'embedded component' side of the unresolved definitional question flagged in the indicator census. Under the name as written (a dedicated national digital agriculture strategy) the instrument is absent; under the broader reading that credits embedded components, Egypt would instead sit at 'Adopted'. Ratifiers should note the score would change with the definition. The ITU e-agriculture strategies page, which names the countries that have adopted dedicated e-agriculture strategies (Afghanistan, Bhutan, Fiji, Papua New Guinea, The Philippines, Sri Lanka), does not include Egypt.

4.5.value: DATA GAP — Started with the sector-specific sources: FAO GSARS Egypt country page (Source 5) and its three Egypt news items (Sources 1, 3, 4) — these document 2023-24 training workshops on dissemination, open data standards and CAADP indicator computation with MoALR and CAPMAS, but no policy instrument. Checked the GSARS 'Sustainable Statistical Systems' page (Source 6) for whether Egypt had adopted SPARS, the nearest sectoral governance/planning instrument; the adopters list names seven countries and Egypt is not among them. Then examined the national data-governance domain: Egypt's Open Data Policy 2025 issued by the National Council for AI (Source 9, T3) — the governing horizontal instrument, which covers all public institutions and flags a forthcoming Data Governance Law, but has no agricultural provisions. Then the national statistics domain: CAPMAS's own statement of mandate and strategic objectives to UNSD (Source 2, T1), which describes coordination gaps and duplication between CAPMAS, MoALR and IDSC but no agricultural data governance rules; and the PARIS21 NSS assessment of Egypt (Source 10, T5, not usable for a prerequisite row anyway). Finally checked the two agricultural-policy analyses: OECD's 2026 Policies for the Future of Farming and Food in Egypt (Source 7) — only front matter, foreword and acknowledgements were retrieved, with no text on data governance — and a 2001 World Bank export-strategy record (Source 8), which is a catalog page only. Dead ends: no MoALR decree, no national agricultural data strategy, and no agricultural data-sharing regulation surfaced in any retrieved page.
4.5.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. The quoted instrument is a whole-of-government open data policy issued by the National Council for Artificial Intelligence; it is sector-agnostic and contains no agriculture-specific provisions (no farm data, no agricultural registry, no MoALR-specific data governance rules). It is cited as evidence that the national data-governance domain was examined and that no agricultural data governance framework sits within it, not as a measure of the named construct. The adjacent sector instrument examined, FAO's GSARS country page for Egypt, lists only capacity-building activities and explicitly names the SPARS adopters as 'Angola, Madagascar, Mozambique, Tanzania, Togo, Liberia, Zimbabwe' — Egypt is not among them.

4.7.value: DATA GAP — 1) ID4D DataBank source landing page (Source 1) — variable pickers only, no data rendered. 2) ID4D global dataset page (Source 2) — global headlines (800 million without official ID; 2.8 billion without digital ID for online transactions; ~45 percent of countries offer a digital ID credential) but no country rows. 3) Data360 dataset page (Source 3) and Data Catalog entry (Source 4) — metadata and coverage descriptions only. 4) DataBank saved report (Source 5) — the only page with actual series values; contains the correct series names including 'Digital ID verification (1 = yes; 0 = no)' and 'ID ownership, total (% of population ages 15+)', but the rows are not labelled with a country and the panel has all 199 economies selected, so the 71.4/87.4 values cannot be assigned to Egypt; the 2017 female 48.4 / male 94.2 split argues against Egypt. 5) Findex 2025 Egypt microdata study description (Source 6) and its data dictionary (Source 7) — confirm the ID4D module variables (fin46-fin51) were added to the Egypt file, but publish no tabulated Egypt percentage. 6) ID4D 2021 Volume 1 document page (Source 8) — abstract and citation metadata only, no country table in the retrieved text. 7) Global Digital Identity Index Egypt page (Source 9) — Egypt-specific but T5 and a composite score, inadmissible for a UC:FIN prerequisite. Dead end: no Egypt-attributed digital-ID coverage percentage in any supplied page.
4.7.note: Next level not proposed: Not applicable — the level is withheld rather than set below 5. The specific missing item is an Egypt-row value from the ID4D digital-ID series (or a national/regulator publication of the share of Egyptians holding a digitally verifiable/online-authenticating credential) that can be copied verbatim from a fetched page. The indicator name is 'Digital ID coverage (%)'. Two distinct ID4D constructs are in play and the supplied pages confirm they are different things: (a) foundational ID ownership, published as 'ID ownership, total (% of population ages 15+)' — a card/credential ownership measure that is NOT a digital ID measure; and (b) digital ID, which ID4D describes as 'a government-recognized digital identity to securely transact online' and reports as country-level availability ('people in approximately 45 percent of countries can obtain at least one government-recognized digital identity credential'), plus binary supply-side flags such as 'Digital ID verification (1 = yes; 0 = no)'. Judged against the name as written, the correct series is the digital-ID one, and for Egypt no value of either series is present in the retrieved pages. Context, not evidence for this cell: the T5 Global Digital Identity Index page asserts for Egypt 'Online Digital Identity: No', i.e. no online-authentication digital credential — which, if it were admissible, would point to a very low digital-ID coverage rather than the high foundational-ID ownership figure the census flags as having been used. The census's observation therefore stands: the recorded Egypt series is on the wrong side of the naming question, and it is also on a different denominator (% of adults 15+) from the comparator country. An independent T1 series (World Bank WDI ID.OWN.TOTL.ZS (World Bank Identification for Development (ID4D))) reports 98.78 for 2024.

5.2.src: World Bank Open Data — Literacy rate, adult total (% of people ages 15 and above), Egypt, Arab Rep. (source: UNESCO Institute for Statistics)
5.2.note: Most recent available observation is 2022; UIS literacy figures for Egypt derive from census/survey self-reported literacy rather than direct assessment. Next level not proposed: Level 4 would require a published adult literacy rate above 80 percent. Egypt's most recent published figure is 79 percent (unrounded 79.45316 percent for 2022), which falls short of the 80 cut point. No admissible source in the retrieved pages publishes an Egyptian adult literacy figure at or above 80; the only above-80 figure available is the male-only subgroup rate (85.3%), which is a different construct and cannot be used to raise the national total. The World Bank/UIS series SE.ADT.LITR.ZS is exactly the adult literacy rate: percentage of people ages 15 and above who can, with understanding, read and write a short simple statement about their everyday life. National (not rural-specific) coverage, which matches the indicator as named. Cross-checks: FRED (T5, restating World Bank/WDI) reports 79.45316 for 2022, and the World Bank Gender Data Portal reports the same 2022 reference year disaggregated as 85.3% male / 73.3% female. Corroborated by an independent T1 series (World Bank WDI SE.ADT.LITR.ZS): 79.45 for 2022.
5.2.tier_detail: Most recent available observation is 2022; UIS literacy figures for Egypt derive from census/survey self-reported literacy rather than direct assessment

4.9.value: DATA GAP — Reviewed all six supplied pages in order. (1) World Bank project paper on Egypt's First NSDS (T1) — lists MOA only in the acronym table; describes CAPMAS-implemented statistical strategy components, no agricultural coordination body. (2) CAPMAS Economic Census 2017/2018 metadata (T1) — survey design only, no governance mechanism. (3) CAPMAS Arabic general publications catalog (T1) — list of statistical yearbooks, no relevant content. (4) CAPMAS Arabic methodology PDF extract (T1) — table of contents for public business sector accounts, irrelevant. (5) Ministry of Planning news item, 10 June 2024 (T3) — describes NSDS preparation 'in collaboration with 18 Egyptian ministries', i.e. multi-ministry consultation on statistics, not a standing agriculture coordination body. (6) Administrative Control Authority page on the National Coordination Committee (T3) — a genuine inter-ministerial standing committee constituted by PM Decree 2890/2010 as amended by 493/2014, but for anti-corruption; wrong construct. (7) PARIS21 NSS Assessment Egypt 2015 (domain tiered T5 here) — mentions a Consultancy Committee for Statistical Planning and Coordination (CCSPC) and weakening coordination mechanisms in the statistical system; again statistics, not agriculture, and not at an admissible tier for this prerequisite row. Dead ends: no MALR, Cabinet/IDSC, MCIT/Digital Egypt, or Sustainable Agricultural Development Strategy 2030 document was among the supplied pages, so the agriculture-side domain could not be searched. Recommend re-running retrieval against MALR, Egyptian Cabinet decrees (Al-Waqa'i al-Misriyya), and MCIT digital transformation governance documents before this cell is ratified.
4.9.note: Next level not proposed: No level is proposed.
