Announced/Adopted/Operating are all unsupported because no document naming an agricultural or digital-agriculture inter-ministerial mechanism was retrieved; Absent is also not recorded because the retrieved corpus does not cover the agriculture or digital-transformation policy domain at all, so a negative finding there would be an inference from silence in the wrong body of documents. The closest formally constituted inter-ministerial bodies in the retrieved pages are (a) the National Anti-Corruption Committee, established by Prime Minister's Decree No. 2890 of 2010 as amended by Decree No. 493 of 2014, chaired by the Prime Minister with ministerial membership (Administrative Control Authority page, T3) — an inter-ministerial mechanism, but for anti-corruption, with no agriculture or digital-agriculture mandate; and (b) the preparation of a national strategy for developing Egypt's statistical system described as developed 'in collaboration with 18 Egyptian ministries and government and research entities' (Ministry of Planning news item, T3) — a multi-ministry consultation process on statistics, not a standing coordination body for digital agriculture, and the Ministry of Agriculture appears only in an acronym list in the World Bank project paper. On the unratified definitional question (standing body vs. any documented recurring/project-based mechanism), the evidence retrieved fails on BOTH readings for the agriculture/digital domain: no standing body and no documented recurring project-based coordination in this domain appears in these pages.

4.6.value: DATA GAP — Started with MCIT (T3) publications register pages 3098, 10492 and 9283, which list the Egypt National AI Strategy (Jul 2021) and the National AI Strategy – Second Edition 2025-2030 (Jan 2025) with descriptions; none of these description texts mentions agriculture. Read the MCIT Artificial Intelligence landing page for institutional status (NCAI established 2019, mandate to issue and oversee the strategy; expanded Jan 2026) — again no agriculture reference. Checked MCIT's 'ICT Sector Achievements in 2025' press release for implementation evidence and agriculture-specific AI deployments: it confirms the second edition was unveiled but lists only health and speech-to-text AI solutions. Checked the OECD Artificial Intelligence Review of Egypt (T2) — the retrieved text is cover, foreword, acknowledgements and table of contents up to 'Egypt's National AI Strategy 14'; the substantive sector chapters were not in the retrieved text, so no OECD statement on an agriculture component could be quote-verified. Fell back to Daily News Egypt (T5), which reports the NCAI reviewing the national AI strategy and lists agriculture among the vital areas covered; recorded as context in construct_note rather than as the citation, since T5 supports existence facts only and the agriculture component could not be verified at T1-T3 in this retrieval set. Dead ends: no Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation page and no full text of either strategy edition was among the supplied pages.
4.6.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. Agriculture-sector content of the strategy is corroborated in the retrieved set only by a T5 news report; no retrieved official strategy text page names agriculture. The quoted T3 MCIT page establishes the first half of the construct — a national AI strategy that is officially published/issued by the NCAI (first edition Jul 2021; Second Edition 2025-2030, Jan 2025). It does not name agriculture. The agriculture component is attested only at T5: Daily News Egypt, reporting the NCAI's review of the national AI strategy, states 'This covers vital areas such as agriculture, water management and rationalisation, health, planning, culture, antiquities, industry, and infrastructure.' (https://www.dailynewsegypt.com/2020/12/05/egypts-national-ai-council-discusses-using-technology-in-agriculture-irrigation/). The OECD AI Review of Egypt (T2) text retrieved is front matter only; it lists an interview with 'Dr. Mohamed El Qersh (Ministry of Agriculture)' but no agriculture-component finding was retrievable. On the census's open question (publication vs. executive approval): the strategy is issued by the National Council for AI, chaired by the ICT Minister, whose listed responsibility is 'Issuing and overseeing the implementation of the National AI Strategy', so it clears both readings of 'Adopted'.

5.3.value: DATA GAP — Worked through all ten supplied pages in order of likely relevance. (1) World Bank Open Data SE.TER.ENRR country page for Egypt and (2) the all-countries table: both give Egypt, Arab Rep. 2025 = 38, but the series is total tertiary. (3) WDI Metadata Glossary for SE.TER.ENRR: confirmed the long definition covers tertiary education as a whole with no field-of-study restriction, which is what rules the figure out for this cell. (4) Gender Data Portal: female-disaggregated version of the same total series (Egypt 2025 = 38.6%) — a sex split, not a field split. (5) Human Capital Data Portal Egypt page: indicator index lists 'Gross school enrollment rate, tertiary (%)' but again no STEM breakdown, and no Egypt value is rendered in the retrieved text. (6) UNdata series 'Students in tertiary education enrolled in Engineering, Manufacturing and Construction programmes' — the correct family of series, Egypt is in the Reference Area list, but the retrieved records are page 1 of 50, alphabetical, running Afghanistan to Anguilla; no Egypt row to quote, and in any case the unit is 'Number', a headcount rather than a gross ratio. (7) UNdata 'Percentage of tertiary graduates from Science programmes' — same problem: Egypt listed as a selectable area, records shown stop at Anguilla, and the construct is graduates by field, not enrollment (% gross). (8) UNdata search results for 'TERTIARY education' — confirms UIS carries 'Gross enrollment ratio. Tertiary education' (total) and separate field-of-study headcount series, but no 'gross enrollment ratio, STEM' series is listed. (9) statisticsoftheworld.com and (10) indexmundi.com are T5 mirrors of the same total WDI/UIS series and are barred from carrying a statistic in any event. Dead end: nothing retrieved measures the STEM subset for Egypt, so the cell is held rather than filled with the total.
5.3.note: Next level not proposed: Level 1 is not proposed, let alone anything above it: the evidence does not establish that Egypt's STEM tertiary gross enrollment ratio is below 10 any more than it establishes that it is above it. Nothing in the retrieved pages states a STEM-specific numerator or ratio for Egypt at any year, so even the bottom rung is unevidenced for the construct as named. Judged against the indicator NAME ('Tertiary STEM enrollment (% gross)'), the best available evidence sits on the wrong side of the open definitional question flagged in the indicator census. The World Bank Open Data page for SE.TER.ENRR lists Egypt, Arab Rep. at 38 for 2025 (Gender Data Portal gives female 38.6% for 2025; IndexMundi's older UIS extract gives 38.90 for 2018). SE.TER.ENRR is explicitly defined by the WDI metadata glossary as 'the ratio of total enrollment, regardless of age, to the population of the age group that officially corresponds to the level of education shown' for tertiary education as a whole — all fields, not science, technology, engineering and mathematics. Scoring 38 against cut points calibrated for a STEM SHARE would place Egypt at level 4, whereas Egypt's actual STEM subset is necessarily a fraction of that 38 and would almost certainly fall in a much lower band. Recording the total as if it were STEM would convert a data gap into a confident high score, so it is withheld here as context only. An independent T1 series (World Bank WDI SE.TER.ENRR) reports 38.04 for 2025.

5.4.value: DATA GAP — 1) Checked national statistical sources first for a farmer digital-skills variable: CAPMAS Agricultural Property and Rein 2017 metadata (censusinfo.capmas.gov.eg) and the FAO microdata record for Egypt's Agricultural Census 2009-2010 — scope lists holdings characteristics, cultivated area, irrigation/drainage, employment, machinery, livestock; no ICT or digital-skills module, hence a dead end. 2) Searched the digital-agriculture literature for Egypt: IFPRI/CGSpace Policy Note (Sept 2024) and IFPRI Discussion Paper 02359 / Food Policy 2026 article on the Minya-Beni Suef RCT — these carry the only percentages, but they are baseline barrier self-reports (54/52/49/19/16/14 percent) and treatment effects in percentage points (uptake +20pp, utilization +18-26pp, trust +8-13pp), none of which is a digital-literacy rate. 3) FAO openknowledge 'Empowering small-scale farmers through digital innovation: NENA' (2026) — discusses digital literacy as a barrier qualitatively, regional scope, no Egypt figure on the landing page. 4) ICARDA 'Current Situation of Digital Agriculture in Egypt' (2023) — abstract cites 'knowledge levels of farmers' as a constraint, no statistic, and the item is Limited Access. 5) ScienceDirect version of the RCT paper returned a captcha page with no content. Conclusion: no published national digital-literacy figure for Egyptian farmers in the supplied pages.
5.4.note: Best available quantified evidence is a non-representative RCT baseline in two governorates among smartphone-owning members of donor-supported farmer organizations; the headline figure is self-reported digital ILliteracy as a barrier, i.e. the inverse of the indicator's direction. Next level not proposed: Withholding a level rather than proposing one: no admissible source states, for Egypt, the share of farmers who are digitally literate. The evidence does not show a nationally scoped measurement of farmer digital literacy at any value, so even level 1 (a value below 10) cannot be evidenced. Indicator name asserts a national percentage of farmers who are digitally literate. The retrieved evidence (IFPRI Policy Note, Sept 2024, baseline of ~4,000 GIZ-supported smallholders in Minya and Beni Suef) instead reports the share of sampled farmers naming barriers to mobile-app use: 54 percent cited unawareness of existing applications, 52 percent cited general digital literacy / farmer digital illiteracy as a key challenge, 49 percent cited lack of smartphone access, and about 65 percent recommended digital literacy training. These are perception/barrier shares from a two-governorate purposive sample, not a national literacy rate, and 52 runs in the opposite (lower-is-better) direction from the indicator's H direction. The related FAO NENA study and IFPRI/ICARDA notes discuss limited digital skills qualitatively but publish no percentage. Egypt's agricultural census (2009-2010) and CAPMAS agricultural property statistics cover holdings, land, irrigation, machinery and employment; they contain no digital-skills module.

5.5.value: DATA GAP — 1) FAO Egypt country office page and FAO e-Agriculture news (22 July 2019) — confirmed launch of a digital agricultural extension model with MoALR, thematic areas and planned ToT for extension personnel. 2) FAO Digital Services Portfolio Country Cases page — confirmed El Mufeed launched 2019, content expansion in 2019–2020, promotional campaign; checked for Egypt usage/reach numbers and found none (numbers given only for Senegal). 3) MCIT Digital Egypt and ICT 2030 Strategy pages (T3) — national digital strategy pillars, no agricultural extension component or extension performance data. 4) World Bank Climate Resilient Agri-Food Transformation Project PID (P180480) — mentions strengthening nation-wide agriculture information system and early warning services but no digital extension service figures. 5) IFC Country Private Sector Diagnostic — agribusiness/ICT constraints, no extension figures. 6) ICARDA/CGSpace working paper 'E-Extension and Digital Augmentation of the Egyptian Agricultural Sector' (T2) — study of readiness for e-extension, not an evaluation of an operating service; full text behind login (bitstream page returned only a login prompt). 7) IFPRI Egypt SSP blog on a randomized digital literacy intervention (T5) — reports uptake effects for two Egyptian apps, but is T5 and evaluates the training intervention, not the extension service, so not used for quality or scale.
5.5.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. Implementer's own (FAO) descriptive account; no independent evaluation or usage statistics for Egypt on the page. The evidence describes a national digital agricultural advisory/extension service delivered through a mobile application in partnership with the Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation, which is the named construct (digital extension capability). It does not quantify capability (e.g. number of extension agents equipped or farmers reached in Egypt).

5.12.value: DATA GAP — 1) FAO Country Gender Assessment of the Agriculture and Rural Sector – Egypt (T2, openknowledge.fao.org): checked contents and available body text; sections cover agricultural labor, extension access and rural finance, but the retrieved text contains no digital-ag or ICT workforce gender figure. Dead end for this construct. 2) CGIAR/ICARDA 'Social Equity (Women and Youth) Issues to Scale Digital Transformation of Egyptian Agriculture' (T2, cgspace) — exactly on topic by title, but the page is a metadata record with Access Rights 'Limited Access'; no figures retrievable. Most promising lead, unverifiable. 3) GFRAS Egypt country page (T5): contains the only sex-disaggregated ICT-in-agriculture numbers found (ICT Support Staff 16 F / 22 M within a 7,421-person ministry extension system, Worldwide Extension Study 2011) — recorded in construct_note as context only, not usable as a statistic under the T5 rule and not the named construct. 4) Journal of Agricultural Sciences Sri Lanka article on Egypt's extension system (T5): age and specialisation of extension workers, no gender share, no digital roles. 5) UNDP Digital Agribusiness Map for Egypt (T5): startup and regional agritech mapping, adoption percentages, no workforce gender data. 6) Alliance Bioversity/CIAT agri-food-climate-tech ecosystem page: blocked by Cloudflare verification, no text. 7) ERF/GIZ Green Jobs in Egypt (T5): abstract notes digitalization of agriculture is 'an untapped opportunity for green job creation' and discusses gendered transition qualitatively, but publishes no digital-ag workforce gender percentage. Not searched/unavailable here: CAPMAS labor force survey ICT-occupation tabulations by sex, ITU ICT gender statistics, MALR staffing returns — any of these, if they disaggregate agriculture-linked ICT roles, would be the route to closing this cell.
5.12.note: Next level not proposed: Level withheld rather than set below 5 because the prerequisite for any rung — a figure measuring the gender composition of a defined digital-ag workforce in Egypt from an admissible publisher — is absent. What is missing specifically: sex-disaggregated employment data for Egyptian agtech firms or for ICT-in-agriculture occupations, published by CAPMAS, ITU, ILO, a ministry, or a T2 analytical report. The closest evidence is the GFRAS/IFPRI-FAO-IICA Worldwide Extension Study (2011) staffing table for Egypt's ministry-based extension system, which reports an 'Information, Communications & Technology (ICT) Support Staff' category of 38 people, of whom 16 are female and 22 male (~42%), alongside overall extension-staff figures (19% female among subject matter specialists, under 4% female among field-level extension staff). This is (a) a 2011 headcount of one small ICT-support unit inside a public ministry, not the 'digital-ag workforce' in the sense of agtech-company employees or ICT-in-agriculture roles generally; (b) carried on a T5-tier domain, so it cannot be used as a statistic under the tiering rule. Recording ~42% would place the cell at level 3 on the 20/35/45/50 ladder on the strength of 38 civil-service posts — precisely the false precision this cell must avoid. The UNDP Digital Agribusiness Map (T5) and the ERF green-jobs report (T5) describe Egypt's agritech startup ecosystem and green/agricultural employment but publish no sex-disaggregated headcount for digital-ag or agritech roles. The FAO Country Gender Assessment (T2) covers women in agriculture and rural labor and access to extension, but the retrieved text contains no digital-ag or ICT workforce gender share.

5.8.value: DATA GAP — Order of examination: (1) MCIT Human Development pages for the Digital Egypt Pioneers Initiative (DEPI) — read the full track list for both DEPI and DEPI Industry, looking for an agriculture/agrifood/agtech track; none present. (2) MCIT press release on the DEG 2024 graduation — checked the description of DEPI's specialized tracks and trainee numbers; tracks are AI, data analysis, cybersecurity, programming, with no sectoral agriculture stream. (3) MCIT/NTI Digital Egypt Youth upskilling programmes — tracks are networks, cybersecurity, virtualization, embedded systems, AI and IoT, cloud, IT, fibre optics, 5G, career development; no agriculture. (4) FAO Egypt digital agriculture launch (2019) and the e-Agriculture mirror — Training of Trainers for MoALR extension personnel on app content, not data science. (5) FAO story on the digital skills course for extension agents in Damas, Dakahlia — confirmed the curriculum is basic digital tools plus the El Mufeed app. (6) FAO Egypt country office page — capacity development on information management systems mentioned in general terms, no training pipeline named. (7) FAO NERC/20/INF/21 Agriculture 4.0 regional paper — regional recommendations only, no Egyptian pipeline. (8) Global Affairs Canada project browser entry for the climate-smart agribusiness skills network — an agricultural TVET pipeline (Agribusiness Centre of Competence, 10 technical schools, 24,000 expected students) but with curricula described as climate-smart agribusiness and gender-responsive competency-based, with no data-science or agtech-analytics component, and school opening only prepared for 2026. Dead end: nothing in the retrieved set links the national data-science pipeline to agriculture, or the agricultural training programmes to data science.
5.8.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Canada, Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. Nearest-adjacent instrument cited is the implementing ministry's own press release; no independent evaluation of any agriculture-linked training pipeline was retrieved. The indicator names an "agtech/data-science training pipeline". The strongest Egyptian evidence in the retrieved pages sits on the data-science side only: DEPI/DEG is a generic national ICT and AI/data-science talent pipeline (7 tracks listed on the MCIT programme page: AI and Data Science, Infrastructure and Cybersecurity, Management and ERP, Digital Marketing and Arts, Software Development, Data Analytics, Digital Game Creation; DEPI Industry adds education, legal, finance, software, marketing and healthcare AI tracks) with no agriculture or agrifood track named, and 13,800 of 25,000 DEPI trainees reported for 2024 within a 220,000-trainee DEG cohort. On the agriculture side, the FAO/MALR digital-skills course for extension agents teaches basic tools ("Word, YouTube, e-mail, Facebook, WhatsApp, Zoom and the FAO app El Mufeed"), i.e. digital literacy rather than data science, and the Canada-funded "Egypt green skills for the climate-smart agribusiness network" builds an agribusiness TVET Centre of Competence with no data-science or agtech-analytics content described. Under a conjunctive reading of the slash (agtech data-science training), the named instrument is not evidenced; under a purely disjunctive reading, DEPI would qualify on the data-science half alone. This cell is recorded conjunctively, against the indicator name as written, because the "agtech" half is what distinguishes this row from a general ICT-skills indicator.

5.7.value: DATA GAP — 1) CGSpace/IFPRI planning-workshop deck (T2) — the only retrieved document that names a Digital Transformation Unit inside MALR and cites its founding decree; used as the primary citation. 2) moa.gov.eg Arabic news release of 6 Dec 2021 on the joint MALR–MCIT digital transformation launch (T3) — describes the Hodhod AI advisory app, AI crop-area mapping, farmer smart card and 20 e-services, but frames all of it as cooperation between the two ministries and does not name or describe a ministry digital/AI unit. 3) moa.gov.eg achievements page and Arabic/English e-services pages (T3) — searched for a unit, department or sector entry; the ministry-structure and achievements listings retrieved contain no digital/AI unit, only an AI training course for directorate managers. 4) moa.gov.eg English welcome message (T3) — refers only to 'a digital transformation programme in the agricultural sector', not a unit. 5) MCIT page on Managing Agriculture Knowledge (T3) — returned a 404, dead end. 6) sis.gov.eg Food Security and Agricultural Innovation Strategy (T3) — 404, dead end. 7) Egypt National AI Strategy PDF (ai.gov.eg, T3) — table of contents and executive summary retrieved; institutions named are the National Council for AI, MCIT and MHESR, with agriculture appearing as an application sector (7.1), not as a ministry-of-agriculture AI unit. 8) elwatannews (T5) — reports a MALR spokesperson saying a digital transformation unit was created for the first time in the agricultural sector; corroborating but T5, so not used as the citation for this prerequisite row.
5.7.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. Evidence is a workshop presentation delivered by a MALR official and archived by a CGIAR repository; the underlying decree text itself was not retrieved, and the presentation is largely forward-looking (action plan in future tense). The indicator names a standing digital/AI unit inside the ministry of agriculture. The evidence establishes a Digital Transformation Unit (AG-DTU) inside MALR created by MCIT ministerial decree 605/2020, with GIS, e-services and foresight functions — this is a digital unit inside the MoAg, so it sits on the right side of the open question. The 'AI' element, however, is not shown to reside in this unit: the AI work quoted on the ministry's own site (the 'Hodhod' AI advisory app and AI-based crop-area mapping) is described as a joint MALR–MCIT programme, not as output of the AG-DTU. So the AI half of the row name is matched only by an inter-ministerial programme, not by a named in-ministry AI unit.

6.3.value: DATA GAP — 1) B-READY 'Economy' data page (worldbank.org/en/businessready/economy) — the retrieved text is an unpopulated template (shows a placeholder 'South Asia / Lower middle income' and an 'Empty chart'); no Egypt data rendered in the fetched text. 2) B-READY 2024 publications page and the openknowledge 2024 publication record — describe 50 economies, no country figures. 3) 'Economies covered by B-READY' — checked the full 2024 list of 50: Egypt absent (MENA entries are Iraq, Morocco, West Bank and Gaza); the 2025 additions table in the retrieved text is cut off after 'Mali', so no confirmation either way for 2025, and no score in any case. 4) B-READY 2025 publications page and homepage — report-level messages only (101 economies), no per-economy scores in text. 5) Methodology page — describes scoring, no values. 6) World Bank Data Blog on B-READY in WDI — confirms 0-100 scale and 50-economy coverage, names top performers (Hungary, Estonia, Singapore, Greece, Slovak Republic, Georgia, Rwanda); Egypt not mentioned. 7) B-READY 2024 report PDF front matter/table of contents — no country tables in the retrieved extract. 8) GAFI (investinegypt.gov.eg) news, 23-07-2025 — Egypt preparing for B-READY 2026 participation; an announcement, not a score. Conclusion: no admissible published B-READY value for Egypt exists in the supplied pages; recording nothing found rather than importing a comparator or a national proxy.
6.3.note: Next level not proposed: The specific missing element for any level, including level 1, is a published Egypt-specific B-READY overall score. The B-READY 2024 economy-coverage table omits Egypt, and neither the 2025 report page, the B-READY data/economy page, the methodology page, the WDI B-READY blog, nor the openknowledge record contains an Egyptian figure. No B-READY score of any kind (overall, pillar, or topic) is published for Egypt, Arab Rep. in the supplied pages. The B-READY 2024 coverage table lists the 50 inaugural economies and Egypt is not among them; the Middle East & North Africa entries listed for 2024 are Iraq, Morocco and West Bank and Gaza. The B-READY 2025 additional-economies table in the same page is truncated mid-list (ends at 'Mali'), so it cannot be verified from the retrieved text whether Egypt is in the 2025 edition, and no Egyptian figure appears anywhere in the retrieved pages. The Egyptian investment authority (GAFI) page states Egypt is preparing to participate in B-READY 2026, which implies it was not yet scored at the time of that July 2025 notice.

6.1.value: DATA GAP — Started with the country-specific WIPO GII ranking pages: the 2025 PDF (edocs/gii-ranking/2025/eg.pdf) and the equivalent HTML economy page (wipo.int/gii-ranking/en/egypt) - both give rank 86/139, input/output ranks and the Innovation Tracker, but no composite score. Checked the 2024 Egypt PDF (edocs/gii-ranking/2024/eg.pdf): rank 86/133, pillar ranks only, again no score; its bubble chart axis is labelled 'GII Score' but no numeric value for Egypt is in the text. Checked the WIPO Benchmark section page for Egypt, which does carry numeric pillar scores for 2025 (Institutions 39.07 down to Knowledge and technology outputs 16.90) but no overall figure. Checked the 2023 Egypt profile (wipo-pub-2000-2023/eg.pdf), which carries 2023 pillar scores (e.g. Egypt | Score: 19.87) and strengths/weaknesses, again with no composite. Scanned the two full GII 2024 report PDFs and the GII 2024 results web chapter: only front matter, contents and narrative on leading economies were retrieved - the economy profile for Egypt (p.153) and the full ranking table with scores were not in the retrieved text. The Egyptian chamber news page (T5) contained no usable content. Conclusion: the composite GII score for Egypt exists in WIPO's ranking table but is not present in any supplied page, so it is not recorded as a number; a statement based on the published rank and pillar scores is recorded instead.
6.1.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. Composite GII score for Egypt is not printed in any of the retrieved pages; only the rank and the seven pillar scores are published, so the level is inferred from those published components rather than read off a headline figure. The sources are WIPO's own GII outputs for Egypt, i.e. exactly the named construct, but they express it as a rank (86th of 139 in 2025; 86th of 133 in 2024) and as seven pillar scores rather than as the single overall 0-100 GII score that this cell's cut points (25/35/45/55) presuppose. The 2023 profile likewise publishes only pillar scores (e.g. 'Egypt | Score: 19.87' for Knowledge and technology outputs). No retrieved page carries the composite figure, so no number is recorded.

6.4.value: DATA GAP — Started with the CGIAR/Alliance Bioversity-CIAT item "The state of the agri-, food-, and climate-tech innovation ecosystem in Egypt" (2024) as the highest-tier and best-scoped candidate; the retrieved page is a DSpace metadata record only, containing no figures or findings text, so nothing quotable on ecosystem size. Then checked AgFunder's Africa AgriFoodTech Investment Report landing pages for 2022, 2023 and 2024 — all are gated download forms with continent-level headline numbers only and no Egypt breakout. AgFunderNews' September 2023 data snapshot was the only page carrying Egypt-specific agrifoodtech deal and funding figures, and the May 2025 AgFunderNews piece corroborates Egypt's standing among the top three African ecosystems. MAGNiTT's FY2024 and H1 2024 Egypt country pages were checked for an agtech sector cut: they are paywalled summaries reporting all-sector Egyptian VC (FinTech $39m, IT Solutions, total $86m in H1 2024) with no agriculture sector line. Dead ends: no Egyptian government or T1 source (ITIDA, Ministry of Agriculture, CAPMAS) on agtech venture activity was among the retrieved pages, so no official count of agtech startups or public agtech fund could be verified.
6.4.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt, Kenya, Nigeria rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. Proprietary commercial deal database (AgFunder), reported through the publisher's own news arm; category definition is self-defined and not independently audited. The indicator names an AGTECH venture ecosystem. The only retrieved country-level evidence is AgFunder/AgFunderNews "agrifoodtech" deal flow, an explicitly broader denominator that folds in downstream food-tech, eGrocery, in-store retail tech and agri-fintech alongside farmer-facing agtech. The same AgFunder framework reports for Egypt figures such as $112m across 24 deals in 2022 and just $700k in H1 2023 (context only, not recorded as the value here, both because they are T5 statistics and because they count the wider agrifoodtech category). The CGIAR/Alliance Bioversity-CIAT report "The state of the agri-, food-, and climate-tech innovation ecosystem in Egypt" (T2, 2024) is the nearest correctly-scoped analytical source, but only its catalog metadata was retrieved, with no ecosystem figures in the supplied text. So the existence of an active venture ecosystem touching agriculture in Egypt is established; its magnitude as strictly agtech is not.

6.9.value: DATA GAP — Started with FAO Egypt sources (e-Agriculture 2019 digital extension launch; FAO Egypt Our Office; FAO Egypt Partners page) - these show government-UN cooperation and a partner list containing only ministries, UN agencies and bilateral donors, no private firms, so they evidence public-international, not public-private, digital-ag partnership. Checked the FAO 'Practical Farmers' Toolkit - Geodata for Climate Smart Agriculture in Egypt' link: 404, dead end. Checked the FAO/openknowledge rural advisory services policy brief for Egypt: it describes pluralism of public, private and civil-society advisory providers as a recommendation, with no named operating digital-ag PPP. Checked the IFC/World Bank Country Private Sector Diagnostic (both documents1.worldbank.org and ifc.org copies): the retrieved front matter lists an appendix on PPPs in Egypt and an agribusiness chapter, but the retrieved text carries no digital-agriculture PPP instrument or figure. The Alliance of Bioversity/CIAT story on the Cairo digitalization workshop (T5) shows an 80-participant public-private consultation and calls for 'strong public-private partnerships' - i.e. an aspiration, so it supports Announced at most. The CGIAR/IITA GeoAgro-MiSR Agronomy Solution Profile was the only retrieved source naming both public and private partners and reporting actual farmer reach, so it was used as the basis for the Operating rung and the scale field.
6.9.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. Implementer-adjacent profile prepared by the CGIAR initiative that supports the tool; several milestone dates and outcome figures are marked 'unspecified' in the document itself. The indicator name asserts operating public-private partnerships in digital agriculture. The GeoAgro-MiSR evidence does pair public bodies (Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation and Agricultural Research Centre-linked institutions) with genuinely private firms (GeoAgro, John Deere dealerships), so the 'private' half is not thin in the way the census flags for Egypt's ministry/state-owned-bank flagship. But the arrangement is a donor-funded (Government of Japan) CGIAR/ICARDA-brokered project partnership, not a PPP contracted under Egypt's PPP law; the IFC/World Bank Country Private Sector Diagnostic's PPP annex (Appendix B, 'The Role of Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs) in Egypt') covers PPPs generally and contains no digital-agriculture PPP in the retrieved text. The other retrieved items (FAO digital extension model 2019, FAO Egypt partner list, the Alliance/CIAT Cairo consultation workshop of Jan 2025) are government-UN or government-research collaborations and dialogue events, not private-sector partnerships in operation.

6.12.value: DATA GAP — 1) Checked the Digital Public Goods Alliance registry page (247 DPGs) for any Egypt-origin or Egypt-deployed product — visible listing runs alphabetically Aam Digital to caMicroscope and includes agriculture DPGs from FAO (AGRIS, AGROVOC, Agrontology, AgriTech Observatory) and Norway (Altinn), but no Egyptian entity; the country filter results were not rendered in the supplied text. 2) Checked the DPGA homepage for member/country statements — 55 members listed, no Egypt-specific text. 3) Checked MCIT's Digital Egypt strategy page, Cloud First Policy 2024 publication page, Artificial Intelligence page, 2021 ICT achievements release, and 2022 institutional-development feature for any reference to digital public goods, open-source national products, or DPG registration — none found; the vocabulary throughout is 'digital transformation', 'digital services', 'DPI'. 4) Checked the 2024 Global DPI Summit press release, the closest adjacent instrument, and the 2026 WSIS session outcome document (UNDP Egypt/MCIT) — both discuss DPI design principles and AI governance, not DPGs. 5) Checked the SIS release on 242/270 Digital Egypt services and the 'Karnak' large language model with agriculture applications — no statement that Karnak or any Digital Egypt component is open-source or a registered DPG. Dead end: no agriculture-ministry or FAO-Egypt page carrying a DPG deployment claim was retrieved.
6.12.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. Nearest-adjacent evidence is a government self-description; the DPG Alliance registry page retrieved was rendered only in part (alphabetical entries A through C), so absence of an Egyptian registry entry is inferred from the visible listing plus absence of any DPG reference in Egyptian government artifacts. The indicator names DIGITAL PUBLIC GOODS (open-source software, open data, open AI systems or open content meeting the DPG Standard). The best available Egyptian evidence concerns DIGITAL PUBLIC INFRASTRUCTURE (Digital Egypt platform with 242 services, national payment systems, digital ID, Cloud First Policy) — DPI is a delivery-layer concept and none of the cited Egyptian systems is stated to be an open-source or registered DPG. On the census's open question, the evidence sits on neither side cleanly: Egypt neither registers a national product in the DPG registry (no Egyptian entity appears in the retrieved registry text) nor articulates a DPG adoption policy; it articulates a DPI posture instead. No agriculture-sector DPG (e.g. FAO's AGROVOC, AGRIS, AgriTech Observatory, all listed in the registry) is stated to be deployed by Egypt in any retrieved page.

6.14.value: DATA GAP — 1) FAO STI Portal (T1) entry for Agri Cash [Egypt] — the only country-specific, admissible-tier record of an operating agri-fintech rail; quoted for the presence rung, but contains no user or disbursement figures and no smallholder disaggregation. 2) Central Bank of Egypt financial inclusion events page (T3) — confirms farmers are a named inclusion segment with card and wallet issuance drives, but reports no agricultural or smallholder statistic. 3) CBE news release on the Second Financial Inclusion Strategy 2026-2030 (T3) — gives national inclusion 77.6% and 54.7 million active accounts and names the Ministry of Agriculture as a partner, but nothing on agri-specific rails or smallholders; rejected under the construct rule. 4) CGAP publications on digitising value-chain finance and smallholder DFS (T4) — global or Zimbabwe/Senegal/Rwanda/Cambodia/Mozambique/Uganda/Tanzania/Côte d'Ivoire/Nigeria/Bangladesh evidence, no Egypt content; cross-border carry-over refused. 5) UNDP Egypt 'Rural Resilience in Egypt' qualitative study — Egypt-specific and rural-finance relevant but qualitative, with no agri-fintech rail figures in the retrieved text. 6) Daily News Egypt (T5) on the MALR/e-finance 'Agri Egypt' network and the Farmer Card's conversion to a Meeza payment card — recorded as context in construct_note only; T5 is inadmissible for this prerequisite row and the item is in any case about registered landholders generally. Dead end: no CBE, MALR, Agricultural Bank of Egypt or FRA document reporting smallholder-specific counts of agri-fintech accounts, cards or loans was among the retrieved pages.
6.14.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. FAO STI Portal entry is an AI-assisted extraction harvested from Digital Agri Hub; the page itself states 'Record status	Newly extracted from original record - Not checked, not enriched' and 'AI stamp	AI-assisted extraction of information', so the underlying claims are vendor-derived rather than independently verified. The indicator names rails FOR SMALLHOLDERS. The quoted evidence describes a fintech platform 'developed for Egyptian farmers' generally; the FAO record lists prospective users spanning medium-size farms, small-micro entrepreneurs, smallholder farms and SMEs, i.e. smallholders are one target segment among several, not the defining population, and no smallholder-disaggregated usage figure is published. The nearest state instrument, the Farmer Card converted into a Meeza payment card under the MALR/e-finance 'Agri Egypt' network, is issued to registered landholders generally (reported only in Daily News Egypt, T5, quoting a database 'representing 9.4 million feddan') and is likewise not smallholder-specific. The Central Bank of Egypt (T3) treats farmers as a financial-inclusion target segment ('"Farmers Financial Inclusion Day" in September') and reports 77.6% national financial inclusion and 54.7 million active accounts at end-2025, but those are whole-population figures, not smallholder or agricultural rails. Best available evidence therefore sits on the wrong side of the open definitional question flagged in the indicator census.

3.10.value: DATA GAP — Started with FAO's T1 STI/ATIO Portal innovation records for Egypt, which yielded three explicitly typed E-commerce/online marketplace entries (Agri Cash, Bashaier, Nile) — used Nile as the quoted anchor because it carries an operating-status sentence. Checked FAO Egypt country office page and FAO Digital Services Portfolio country cases for a government or FAO-run agricultural e-commerce platform in Egypt: the Egypt entry covers only the El Mufeed advisory app (the e-commerce platform Senlouma described there is Senegal, not Egypt, and was excluded under the no-cross-border rule). Checked the World Bank Egypt DECA 2020 for a digital-platforms chapter reference to agricultural marketplaces — only the table of contents and front matter were retrieved, no agri e-commerce figure. Checked the IFPRI/CGIAR policy note on digital agricultural technology in Egypt for evaluation or scale data — it names apps (Hodhod, Mahsooly, The Smart Farmer Guide) and characterises the ecosystem as pilot-stage, but gives no platform-level user or transaction figures. Checked IFC's e-commerce report (MaxAB) and the Cartona corporate site for scale numbers: both are downstream FMCG retail rather than farmer-facing, and Cartona is T5 vendor material from which statistics may not be recorded. The Alliance Bioversity-CIAT page on digitalization of Egypt's food crop value chains was blocked by a Cloudflare verification screen and could not be read. No published count or registry of Egyptian agricultural e-commerce platforms was found, so no numeric value is recorded.
3.10.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. FAO STI Portal innovation profiles are harvested from Digital Agri Hub and enriched by automated AI extraction; the record itself states "Newly extracted from original record - Not checked, not enriched", so the descriptive claims are not independently verified by FAO staff. The census asks whether the row counts only farmer-facing platforms or any agri-food value-chain commerce platform. The evidence quoted sits on the narrower, farmer-facing side of that question: Nile connects fresh-produce growers to commercial buyers, Bashaier connects small-scale horticulture farmers to buyers, and Agri Cash sells inputs to farmers and markets their crops. Downstream agri-food value-chain platforms also exist in Egypt but sit on the wider side and are weaker evidence: Cartona is an FMCG B2B retail marketplace serving mom-and-pop grocers (vendor page, T5, statistics not admissible), and IFC documents MaxAB, an FMCG B2B distribution platform for MSME retailers — neither transacts with farmers. If the definition is ratified as farmer-facing only, the FAO STI Portal entries still support the rung; if ratified as any agri-food commerce platform, the population is larger still.

3.9.value: DATA GAP — Started with FAO country and corporate sources: FAO Egypt 2019 launch news on the digital agricultural extension model with MALR (announcement-level, four thematic areas, ToT plans, no users); FAO e-Agriculture reprint of the same launch (duplicate, no figures); FAO Digital Services Portfolio 'About' page (confirms Egypt roll-out, no country figures); FAO Agro-informatics DSP project page (quoted — confirms Egypt-specific advisory services and farmer-to-farmer forum, status Ongoing, 'Impact' field blank, no user counts). Checked FAO STI Portal entry on GeoAgro-Misr (ICARDA/CGIAR harvested, AI-enriched record; its own adoption narrative states it cannot elaborate on usage, so no reach figure). AFRAS Egypt country brief on fao.org returned a Cloudflare bot-verification page, not content — a dead end. World Bank documents retrieved were a 1997 Egypt extension project information document and a 1991 MENA regional extension paper, both pre-digital and one not country-specific. GSMA AgriTech Accelerator report has scaling figures but its cohort and implementation countries are Ghana, Senegal, Nigeria, Kenya, Myanmar, Tunisia etc., not Egypt — not carried across the border. The IFPRI/WUR Food Policy RCT is the only Egypt-specific empirical piece; it concerns two Egyptian apps but reports treatment effects on uptake, not platform user totals, and states Egyptian uptake remains low. Conclusion: operation established, scale not published in any retrieved page.
3.9.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt, Jordan, Senegal rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. Implementer's own project page; no independent verification of live service status or usage. The evidence establishes existence and ongoing operation of digital advisory platforms in Egypt, but not the 'at scale' half of the indicator name, which the assessment's own census records as having no ratified threshold. None of the retrieved pages carries any user, subscriber or farmer-reached count for the FAO DSP in Egypt or for the two Egyptian advisory/marketing apps studied by IFPRI/WUR. The one substantive performance statement available — the peer-reviewed RCT (Abdelaziz & Abay) — points the other way, stating that 'In Egypt, the focus of this study, uptake of these technologies remains low despite the increasing and considerable investment and availability of digital agricultural tools', i.e. availability without demonstrated scale. That paper evaluates a digital-literacy training intervention, not the platforms' own performance, so it is recorded here as context rather than as quality evidence for the platform.

6.13.value: DATA GAP — Checked, in order: (1) World Bank Enterprise Survey 2025 Egypt study page and data dictionary — confirms national coverage but universe is the non-agricultural formal private economy, and no digital-adoption headline figure appears on the retrieved pages; (2) enterprisesurveys.org Egypt 2025 economy profile — 'Innovation and Technology' topic listed but the retrieved table shows only Regulations/Compliance Time indicators, no digital-adoption value; (3) WBES 2008 Egypt variable q52b (website use in client interactions) — 36.4% of 1156 cases, but pre-dates the period, excludes agriculture, and is explicitly not a population statistic; (4) ERF Survey of Enterprises' Digitization in Egypt 2022 (SEDE) — variable list only, no tabulated percentages and no agriculture breakdown on the retrieved pages; (5) OECD 'SME Digitalisation in Egypt' chapter — retrieved text is introductory/conceptual, contains no Egypt adoption percentage in the supplied page; (6) ICARDA 'Current Situation of Digital Agriculture in Egypt' — the only construct-matched statement about SME adoption of digital agriculture tools, quoted here; (7) IFPRI/CGIAR policy note on app developers and (8) Food Policy RCT on digital literacy training — both corroborate low, pilot-stage uptake but measure farmers/developers, not firm adoption rates. No percentage for the named construct exists in the supplied pages.
6.13.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. Qualitative finding only; no quantified adoption share published, and the ICARDA item itself is listed as 'Limited Access' (only the abstract text is available on the fetched page). Level inferred from qualitative descriptions rather than a measured percentage. The ICARDA finding is about adoption of digital agriculture tools by SMEs in Egypt's agri-sector, i.e. the agribusiness side of the indicator's undefined 'SME/agribusiness' population, but it is qualitative, not a percentage. Evidence sitting on the other side of the slash (economy-wide SMEs) exists but is a different construct and excludes agriculture: the World Bank Enterprise Surveys universe is explicitly the 'non-agricultural formal private economy' (2025 round, 1024 firms, national coverage), and the ERF Survey of Enterprises' Digitization in Egypt 2022 (806 firms) carries firm-level digital variables (own website, online selling, internet use) but no agriculture-specific tabulation was retrieved. A retrieved WBES 2008 microdata variable shows 36.4% of 1156 sampled Egyptian firms answering 'Yes' to regularly using a website in interactions with clients, but that page itself warns these 'cannot be interpreted as summary statistics of the population of interest', it is 2008, and it excludes agriculture — so it is not an answer to this cell. The IFPRI/CGIAR policy note and the Food Policy RCT describe low uptake among Egyptian smallholder farmers, which is a household rather than a firm population.

8.2.src: World Bank Open Data (World Development Indicators / Global Findex): Account ownership at a financial institution or with a mobile-money-service provider, female (% of population ages 15+) — Egypt, Arab Rep.
8.2.note: Nationally representative demand-side survey (Gallup World Poll sample of ~1,000 adults per economy); Findex Egypt sampling excludes the frontier governorates (<2% of population), and sub-group estimates such as the female series carry wider sampling error than the national figure. Next level not proposed: Level 4 would require female account ownership above 60 percent. The published 2024 figure of 40.21 is barely over the 40 cut and roughly 20 percentage points short of 60; no source in the retrieved pages reports any Egyptian female account-ownership figure at or above 60. Note also that the margin over the 40 threshold is thin (0.21 points) and rests on a single survey round, so the level-3 placement is itself near the boundary with level 2. The quoted series is female-specific (women ages 15+), matching the indicator name. Two caveats bearing on the unratified definition: (a) the WDI series FX.OWN.TOTL.FE.ZS defines "account" as an account at a financial institution OR with a mobile-money-service provider, so mobile money is counted inside this total and is scored again at 8.4 — on the wrong side of the open definitional question flagged in the indicator census; (b) the figure is national (all women), not rural women, so it is not a rural-female measure. For context, the older Findex 2021 round in the World Bank DataBank shows "Account, women (% age 15+)" for Egypt at 9.3 (2014), 27.0 (2017) and 24.2 (2021); the 40.21 value is the 2024/Findex 2025 round and represents a sharp increase over 2021. Corroborated by an independent T1 series (World Bank WDI FX.OWN.TOTL.FE.ZS (Global Findex wave)): 40.21 for 2024.
8.2.tier_detail: Nationally representative demand-side survey (Gallup World Poll sample of ~1,000 adults per economy); Findex Egypt sampling excludes the frontier governorates (<2% of population), and sub-group estimates such as the female series carry wider sampling error than the national figure.

7.12.value: DATA GAP — Started with the MCIT press release announcing the Egyptian Charter for Responsible AI (April 2023) as the most directly on-point national instrument; confirmed launch, issuing body and content structure. Cross-checked the MCIT Artificial Intelligence landing page for institutional standing (NCAI, its 2026 expansion, ECRAI activity, adoption of an AI Governance Framework). Checked the MCIT Publications index, which lists the Guide to Egypt National AI Governance Framework, National Generative AI Guidelines and National Guidelines for Trustworthy and Responsible AI (all March 2026) — searched their descriptions for any agriculture or farmer scope and found none. Opened the ai.gov.eg Guide PDF text to verify status ('Approved for Publication'), authorisation date and legislative base (Constitution, Personal Data Protection Law, Cybercrime Law); the supplied extract stops at the executive summary and contains no consent clause text to quote. Checked the OECD AI Review of Egypt for an independent evaluation of safeguard implementation — the supplied text is title page, foreword, acknowledgements and table of contents only, with no quotable finding, so it could not support quality_evidence. Checked the UNESCO RAM country page and UNESDOC record; both are T5-tiered navigation/landing pages here and carry no quotable safeguard evaluation. Dead end: no agriculture-sector data-consent or farmer-rights instrument surfaced in any of the nine pages, and the Ministry of Agriculture appears only as an interviewee in the OECD acknowledgements.
7.12.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. Government self-description of its own instruments; no independent evaluation of implementation was retrievable in the supplied pages. The indicator name as written does not restrict the safeguards to agriculture, so the cross-sector Egyptian regime is taken to answer it. It must be recorded, however, that the evidence sits on the cross-sector side of the census's open question: nothing in the Charter, the National AI Governance Framework (March 2026), the National Guidelines for Trustworthy and Responsible AI, or the Generative AI Guidelines is agriculture- or farmer-specific, and no farm-data consent instrument was found. 'Consent' as such is also not named among the Charter's five values; consent obligations sit in the Personal Data Protection Law (2020), referenced as part of the Framework's legislative base but not quotable in detail from the retrieved pages.

7.2.value: DATA GAP — Order of examination: (1) MCIT AI portal (mcit.gov.eg/en/Artificial_Intelligence) — confirms NCAI, National AI Strategy, AI governance framework, but the retrieved text names no agricultural AI deployment. (2) MCIT news item on GreenHack Ismailia — the only Egypt-specific, government-published item naming AI applied to agriculture; establishes prototype-stage AI pest detection, quoted here. (3) ICARDA 'Current Situation of Digital Agriculture in Egypt' (CGSpace, 2023) — abstract only (item is Limited Access); reports sensors and mobile apps as the tools 'fairly widely used' and government apps 'under development'; no AI deployment claim. (4) FAO Digital Services Portfolio country case for Egypt and FAO Egypt El Mufeed page — El Mufeed is a participatory content app, no AI; note that the same FAO page attributes 'satellite imagery and artificial intelligence-driven advice' to E-Tolbi in SENEGAL, which is not evidence for Egypt and is not carried across. (5) FAO e-Agriculture AMAN app page — GPS/SMS/GIS early warning, explicitly not AI. (6) World Bank PID P180480 Climate Resilient Agri-Food Transformation Project — concept stage, agriculture information system and early warning, no AI component in retrieved text. (7) UNDP Digital Agribusiness Map (2025) — lists agri-tech startups and adoption percentages (e.g. 'Precision Irrigation Adoption 15%') but does not label these as AI, so it cannot be used as AI scale evidence. Dead end: no retrieved page carries a user count, hectare count or beneficiary figure for any AI-enabled agricultural solution in Egypt.
7.2.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. Government press release describing a prototype competition; no independent verification of any fielded AI agricultural solution. The indicator names DEPLOYED AI-enabled agricultural solutions. The strongest Egypt-specific AI-in-agriculture evidence retrieved is a government-sponsored hackathon in which teams built AI-powered pest-detection prototypes (first prize EGP 20,000; second EGP 15,000; fourteen teams) — prototypes and intent, not deployment with users. The adjacent digital-agriculture artifacts for Egypt in the retrieved pages are not AI: FAO's El Mufeed is a content-based extension app; AMAN is a GPS/SMS poultry disease reporting platform ('A GPS and Google Map are used for locating 2.5 Million farms'); ICARDA's 2023 stocktake reports that 'only sensors and mobile apps are fairly widely used in Egypt' and that government apps 'Al Mufeed, Hudhud (extension services tools), and DAIRS (climate early warning) are also under development'. The UNDP Digital Agribusiness Map lists agri-tech startups (NileBot, Mozare3, Baramoda, Agrimatic Farms, FreshSource) but the retrieved text does not characterise any of them as AI-enabled and gives no deployment figures for AI. So the best available evidence sits on the 'announced/prototype' side of the deployment question, not the deployed side.

8.6.value: DATA GAP — 1) UN SDG Country Profile for Egypt, goal 5 (T1) — found SDG 5.b.1 female mobile ownership series (79.0% 2014 to 96.2% 2022) and a chart captioned 'Proportion of individuals who own a mobile telephone, by sex (%)', but the male series values are not present in the retrieved text, so no pp gap could be verified. 2) GSMA Mobile Gender Gap Reports 2022, 2023, 2024 (T4 PDFs) — retrieved text covers front matter, contents and introduction only; LMIC aggregates present (83% of women in LMICs own a mobile phone, 2023), no Egypt country table in the supplied text; also the GSMA gap is relative, not pp. 3) GSMA Gender Gap 2025 landing page (T4) — LMIC-level gaps only (8% mobile ownership gap, 14% smartphone gap in 2024), no Egypt figure. 4) Global Findex 2021 Egypt microdata catalog page and G20 Financial Inclusion Indicators Egypt page (T1) — the G20 page lists 'Access to a mobile phone, female (% age 15+)' and 'Access to a mobile phone, male (% age 15+)' as available indicators but returns N/A / no values in the retrieved text for Egypt; Findex Gender Brief covers account ownership gaps (4 pp world, 13 pp MENA), a different construct. 5) Egypt MICS 2013-14 data dictionary (T1) — shows variable MT4A 'Own a mobile phone' in the women's file but no published tabulation and no male counterpart file value. 6) Egypt Human Development Report 2021 — retrieved text is front matter only, no phone-ownership-by-sex figure. Dead end: no supplied page carries a quotable Egypt percentage-point gender gap in phone ownership.
8.6.note: Next level not proposed: Even the lowest cut (a value below 20 pp giving level 1) cannot be certified, because no source in the supplied pages states any percentage-point gap for Egypt; the male ownership rate needed to compute one is not quotable from the retrieved text. Level withheld pending retrieval of the ITU/UN SDG 5.b.1 sex-disaggregated series with both male and female values for Egypt, or an Egypt row from a GSMA methodology annex with the underlying ownership percentages. Nearest evidence is the UN SDG Country Profile for Egypt (SDG 5.b.1, proportion of individuals who own a mobile telephone, by sex), which in the retrieved text reports only the female figure — 96.2% of women owning a mobile telephone in 2022, up from 79.0% in 2014 — without a quotable male counterpart. That is a level, not a gap, so it measures a different construct from 'gender gap in phone ownership (pp)'. Separately, the GSMA Mobile Gender Gap series is the widely quoted source for this construct but publishes a RELATIVE gap on a male-ownership base (a percentage of male ownership, e.g. 8% for LMICs in 2024), not percentage points, which is precisely the basis ambiguity flagged in the indicator census; and no Egypt row from GSMA appears in the supplied pages. The indicator name's sign convention (male minus female vs absolute difference) is also unresolved, so even a derived number could not be scored unambiguously.

8.4.value: DATA GAP — 1) Checked the two Findex Egypt microdata catalog entries (2021, catalog/4638; 2025, catalog/7897) — study description, coverage, sampling, and data-dictionary variable lists only; account_mob is listed as a variable but no Egypt value is reported. 2) Checked the Global Findex 2021 Microdata Codebook PDF — gives the definition of account_mob but no country figures. 3) Checked the Findex 2021 Glossary PDF — defines 'Account (%)' and mobile-money-related indicators, no Egypt figures. 4) Checked the Findex collection landing page — narrative only. 5) Checked the IHSN mirror of the 2021 Egypt data dictionary — variable list only. 6) Checked the NTRA (tra.gov.eg) Q2 2025 mobile wallet press release — this is the only Egypt-specific quantitative page, but it reports active wallet counts, transaction volumes/values and operator market shares, not a share of adults. Dead ends: no Findex country-level indicator table, no WDI series page (FX.OWN.TOTL.MO.ZS), no CBE financial inclusion report, and no GSMA State of the Industry page was among the supplied sources. Concluded found=false with abstain=true rather than deriving 46.3m wallets over an adult population.
8.4.note: Only supply-side operator-reported wallet counts available in supplied pages; no demand-side survey percentage for Egypt present. Next level not proposed: Even the lowest rung cannot be evidenced: no supplied source states any percentage of Egyptian adults with a mobile money account. The Findex Egypt catalog pages carry only metadata (sample sizes, sampling procedure, variable lists) and the Findex glossary page carries only definitions; the country-level indicator table containing Egypt's account_mob value was not among the retrieved pages. The named construct is the Global Findex 'Mobile money account (%)' — the percentage of adults (15+) who report personally using a mobile money service in the past year. The Findex glossary and codebook pages supplied define this construct ('account_mob Has a mobile money account = 1 if the respondent used mobile money services to pay bills or to send or receive money in the past year') but contain no Egypt value. The only Egypt quantitative evidence supplied is the NTRA regulator's Q2 2025 report stating that the total number of active mobile wallets reached 46.3 million nationwide, up from 35.8 million in Q2 2024. That is a count of wallets registered/active with telecom operators, not a survey-measured share of adults; one person may hold multiple wallets across Vodafone Cash, e& Cash, Orange Cash and WE Pay, and no adult-population denominator is given on the page. It is therefore context, not an answer to this cell.

8.11.value: DATA GAP — 1) UN DESA e-Government Survey 2024 landing page and LOSI methodology/city data pages — LOSI includes content/technology criteria and Cairo is assessed, but the retrieved pages contain no per-indicator language result for Cairo or Egypt and no national local-language service share. 2) CAPMAS censusinfo metadata catalog (DDI-EGY-CAPMAS-BEIMIS-2011) variable V232 on website language — closest quantified language item found, but wrong construct (enterprise websites, multilingual flag, n=6, 2011). 3) MCIT indicators page and publications list (ICT Indicators in Brief, Quarterly Bulletin, Measuring the Digital Society) — titles only in the retrieved text, no language-of-service statistic. 4) MCIT 2025 ICT sector achievements press release — 210 Digital Egypt services, 10.7m users, no language breakdown. 5) MCIT Digital Transformation and Digital Egypt strategy pages — narrative only. 6) UNESCO-hosted Egypt report on multilingualism and universal access to cyberspace — qualitative project descriptions (Eternal Egypt trilingual portal, Arabic e-Content Initiative, the 0.3% global-Arabic-e-content figure) but no measure of local-language service availability. Dead ends: no FAO/GSMA/extension-service source in the supplied set, and nothing agriculture-specific at all.
8.11.note: Next level not proposed: Not applicable in the usual sense because no level is proposed; the specific missing item is any published count or share of Egyptian public/agricultural advisory services available in Arabic or other local languages, with a stated denominator. Context only, not recorded as the value: (a) CAPMAS 'Basic Electronic Indicators for Measuring the Information Society – Internet companies (A&B) 2011', variable V232 (اللغة المستخدمة على الموقع الإلكتروني للمنشأة اكثر من لغة) reports 4 of 6 valid records = 66.7% with mean 0.7 — but this is the share of surveyed internet-service firms whose own website uses more than one language, based on 6 unweighted records, and the page itself warns the figures cannot be interpreted as representative of the population. It is neither a service-delivery measure, nor rural/agricultural, nor a measure of Arabic-language availability specifically (multilingual ≠ local language). (b) MCIT's 2025 achievements page reports 210 government services on the Digital Egypt platform, but publishes no breakdown by language, so no numerator/denominator for local-language service delivery exists. (c) The UNESCO report on Egypt's implementation of the Multilingualism Recommendation documents Arabic e-content and trilingual portal projects, i.e. existence of local-language content initiatives, but states no share. On the census's open question: the best available evidence sits on the wrong side of a %-share framing — nothing in these pages supplies a denominator, which supports converting 8.11 to a qualitative/ladder construct rather than a percentage.

8.9.value: DATA GAP — Order of inspection: (1) FAO Egypt news on the FAO-MALR digital agriculture initiative (2019) — describes a digital extension model, ToT and awareness sessions, no user or coverage figures. (2) FAO microdata catalog, Egypt Agricultural Census 2009-2010 — gives the holdings universe and complete enumeration method but no digital-service variables, so no denominator-plus-numerator pairing is possible. (3) CAPMAS Central Data Catalog and its Agriculture-Quarter collection — 629 studies listed, agriculture bulletins on income, production movement and property, nothing on digital service use by farmers. (4) FAO GSARS Egypt country page — statistical capacity work only, no indicator values. (5) ICARDA 'Current Situation of Digital Agriculture in Egypt' (CGSpace) — Limited Access; the abstract notes only sensors and mobile apps are 'fairly widely used' and that government apps are under development, but publishes no percentage. (6) FAO 'Empowering small-scale farmers through digital innovation: NENA' — regional synopsis page, no Egypt-specific reach figure on the retrieved page. (7) IFPRI/CGSpace policy note on Egyptian app developers — the quoted qualitative finding on pilot-stage and non-national scale. (8) Abdelaziz & Abay, Food Policy (WUR repository) — RCT treatment effects in percentage points, explicitly localised; recorded in construct_note as context, not used as the value. Dead end: no Egyptian source in these pages publishes a smallholder reach share, and 'reached' is undefined in all of them.
8.9.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. qualitative characterisation only; no national denominator, no count of smallholders reached, and no published definition of 'reached' (registered vs active vs benefiting). The indicator names a national percentage of SMALLHOLDERS reached by digital services. Nothing in the retrieved pages states such a percentage for Egypt. The closest quantified evidence is the Abdelaziz & Abay randomized intervention (Food Policy, WUR repository copy), which reports treatment effects — 'the standard digital training alone increased uptake by 20 percentage points and utilization by 18 percentage points' — but these are experimental impacts in a localised trial, not a national share of smallholders reached, and the paper's own framing is that 'In Egypt, the focus of this study, uptake of these technologies remains low'. The FAO NENA report (openknowledge.fao.org) is regional and its landing page carries no Egypt-specific reach figure. The ICARDA report is Limited Access and its abstract carries no percentage. So the evidence sits on the wrong side of the unratified definition question: it speaks to the magnitude of reach qualitatively, but no source measures a national smallholder share, and 'reached' is nowhere operationalised.

8.12.value: DATA GAP — 1) Checked IFPRI Egypt country publication list (Source 9) for any impact evaluation of digital agriculture — found the Abdelaziz & Abay randomized intervention, whose stated outcomes are knowledge, utilization, trust and uptake, i.e. adoption/diffusion, not yield or income. 2) Checked IFPRI Egypt SSP overview (Source 7) and the IFPRI/USAID workshop page on digital tools in Egypt (Source 8) — the latter explicitly says the livelihood impact of these tools remains largely understudied. 3) Checked the EIBC Phase 2 project page (Source 10, egyptssp.ifpri.info, T5) — digital agriculture component described as landscape exploration plus a price-monitoring tool with Mahsoly; no yield/income outcome measurement reported. 4) Checked FAO Digital Services Portfolio country cases (Source 2) and the DSP project page (Source 4) — the Impact field on the DSP project page is empty apart from a design statement; the Egypt case describes promotion and content, with no yield or income figures. 5) Checked FAO Egypt office page (Source 3) — programme descriptions only. 6) Checked the FAO story on digital education for women (Source 5) — contains a single farmer's testimonial about increased income from app use plus Facebook marketing; anecdotal, unquantified, and confounded with digital marketing, so not documented impact evidence. 7) Checked the World Bank 2021 Egypt value-chain report (Source 6) — modeled economy-wide GDP, welfare, employment and water impacts of investment scenarios, with a digital technologies section, but no measured yield or income impact of digital tools. Dead end: Source 1 is a BRAC extension phase-out RCT in Uganda and is not evidence about Egypt.
8.12.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. The indicator names yield or income as the documented outcome. The strongest Egyptian evidence retrieved — the IFPRI randomized intervention — states its outcomes as "knowledge, utilization, trust, and uptake" of mobile apps, i.e. diffusion and adoption. That sits on the wrong side of the census's open question. The only yield/income-flavoured material found is anecdotal: an FAO story in which one poultry farmer in Damas village says "The increase in income did not only result because of what I have learnt and applied from the El Mufeed app, but also because of digital marketing" — a single unmeasured testimonial, not documented impact evidence. The World Bank 2021 value-chain report models economy-wide GDP and welfare impacts of agri-food investment scenarios, not measured yield or income effects of digital tools.

8.17.value: DATA GAP — Worked through the ten supplied pages in order. Source 1 (FAO geodata toolkit for CSA in Egypt) resolved to a 404 error page — dead end, no content. Source 2 (FAO AFRAS Egypt country brief) returned a Cloudflare bot-verification interstitial, no substantive text — dead end. Source 3 (FAO e-Agriculture, 2019) gave supply-side narrative on the FAO/MALR digital extension model and the Central Laboratory for Agricultural Climate, but no reach figures. Source 4 (FAO/WMO agrometeorological services) is global/thematic and names Cambodia, the Philippines and the Greater Horn of Africa, not Egypt — cross-border figures excluded under the one-country rule. Source 5 (FAO SCALA Egypt) gave NDC/NAP context and noted an early warning system for smallholder farmers at roadmap stage; no reach percentage. Source 6 (ICARDA/CGSpace, Current Situation of Digital Agriculture in Egypt) is abstract-only, limited access, and lists DAIRS climate early warning as under development with no user numbers. Source 7 (MDPI Sustainability 2019) supplied the nearest farmer-level quantity, 51.9% with no climate-change knowledge across 792 farmers in two Nile Delta governorates — awareness, sub-national, wrong construct. Source 8 (WMO 2024 State of Climate Services) gives only global NMHS capacity shares, no Egypt row on the page. Source 9 (EMA/WMO workshop PDF) describes early-warning and forecasting activity under the NAP with no coverage statistic. Source 10 (Information Development, T5 mirror, abstract only) gives 382 farmers in Dakhalia, weather forecasts among most-received information, 47% low information behavior — one governorate, behavioural clustering, not reach. No page in the set contains a national percentage for climate advisory reach in Egypt, so found=false and a ratification hold is recorded.
8.17.note: Next level not proposed: Even the lowest rung is not supported: nothing in the evidence quantifies, at national scale, the proportion of Egyptian farmers who receive climate or agrometeorological advisories. The supply-side artifacts (DAIRS, CALR agrometeorological data, NAP early-warning work) are described as existing or under development with no coverage figure attached, so no cut point can be tested. Indicator names farmer-side REACH of climate advisories (% of farmers receiving them), nationally. Available Egypt evidence sits on the wrong side of that question in two ways. (a) Demand-side proxies that are not reach: Kassem et al. (MDPI, Sustainability 2019) report that 51.9% of 792 surveyed farmers in two Nile Delta governorates had no knowledge of the climate change phenomenon — climate-change awareness, not receipt of an advisory, and sub-national. Kassem et al. (Information Development, abstract only) surveyed 382 farmers in Dakhalia governorate and found weather forecasts among the most frequently received information types and that 47% had 'low information behavior' — again a single governorate and a behavioural typology, not a reach percentage. (b) Supply-side existence facts: FAO/e-Agriculture describes a digital extension model and the Central Laboratory for Agricultural Climate issuing agrometeorological data; ICARDA's abstract lists DAIRS (climate early warning) and extension apps Al Mufeed and Hudhud as 'under development'; the EMA/WMO workshop note describes climate early-warning support under the NAP. These establish that advisory issuance platforms exist or are being built, but none states how many or what share of farmers actually receive advisories.

A1-CAND-IRR.value: DATA GAP — 1) FAO AQUASTAT Egypt country tables PDF (Source 1) — Table 4 carries the exact line 'Total area equipped for irrigation (1+2+3) 2002 3 422 178 ha / • as % of cultivated area 2002 100 %', and Table 1 confirms cultivated area 3 422 178 ha (2002). This is the quoted source. 2) AQUASTAT global map of irrigated areas, Egypt page (Source 2) — confirms 3 422 178 ha equipped for 2002 and that all of it was actually irrigated, but does not restate the percentage. 3) AQUASTAT country profile landing pages (Sources 3 and 4, 2016 vintage) — navigation shells only, no numeric content. 4) AQUASTAT Country Profile – Egypt 2016 full text (Source 8, T2 FAO repository) — gives 2013 cultivated area 3 761 000 ha but the supplied excerpt stops before the irrigation section, so no updated equipped-area share could be quote-verified; a newer figure may exist in the unretrieved portion. 5) World Bank agricultural land and agricultural value-added pages (Sources 6, 7) — different constructs, not used. 6) FAO country profile fact sheet (Source 5) shows an 'Arable Land 02 / 99% Irrigated' pie chart label but the fragmentary chart text is not a reliable equipped-for-irrigation statistic and was not used. 7) Siebert et al. Global Map of Irrigation Areas v4 (Source 9) — methodology document, no Egypt-specific percentage in the supplied text.
A1-CAND-IRR.note: EVIDENCE REJECTED — the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep. Figure is from the AQUASTAT 2005 survey round with reference year 2002; the underlying area figure originates from Egypt's Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation agricultural statistics. A more recent AQUASTAT country profile (2016) reports cultivated area of 3 761 000 ha for 2013 but the supplied pages do not carry an updated equipped-share percentage. AQUASTAT's 'total area equipped for irrigation as % of cultivated area' is the named construct exactly. Note that in Egypt essentially all cultivation is irrigated (Nile Valley/Delta and reclaimed desert), hence the 100% value; the same page also reports total water-managed area as 100% of cultivated area.

A1-CAND-IMP.value: DATA GAP — 1) Source 1 (data.un.org, FAOSTAT item 21035) — exact construct and unit; scanned the record table but the fetched text stops within the Albania rows on page 1 of 81, so no Egypt row available to quote. 2) Source 6 (fao.org Food_Security_Indicators.xlsx text) — contains an Egypt series (146 147 147 145 144 ...), but the surrounding header and the >100 values identify it as 'Average dietary energy supply adequacy (percent)', not the cereal import dependency ratio; the workbook's index lists 'Cereal import dependency ratio' under STABILITY (I_3.1) but that table's Egypt row is not in the fetched text. 3) Source 5 (GIEWS Egypt Country Brief) — cereal import requirements in tonnes only, no ratio. 4) Source 7 (World Bank PID P178926) — wheat-specific import share of use (62 percent), different construct. 5) Sources 2, 3, 4 (FAOSTAT home, dataset catalog, country profile tool) — metadata/landing pages, no Egypt figure. 6) Source 8 (OECD Egypt agriculture review) — qualitative statements on import concentration, no ratio value. 7) Source 9 (Food Systems Dashboard) — definition page only, no Egypt value, and T5 in any case. Conclusion: the figure almost certainly exists in FAOSTAT for Egypt, but it is not present in the supplied page text and will not be reconstructed here.
A1-CAND-IMP.note: The correct construct and series exist at T1 (FAOSTAT Suite of Food Security Indicators, item 21035, 3-year averages 2000-2002 through 2018-2020), and Egypt is listed among the 226 countries in the filter list, but the Egypt value itself is not in the retrieved text. Nearby context that is NOT the named construct: FAO GIEWS Egypt Country Brief states cereal import requirements for 2026/27 forecast at 29 million tonnes (a volume, not a dependency ratio); the World Bank PID states 'Wheat imports account for nearly 62 percent of total wheat use in the country' — wheat only, not all cereals, and computed on use rather than the FAO (imports - exports)/(production + imports - exports) formula. Neither substitutes for the cereal import dependency ratio.
