gates.reason: recorded at T1

answer.source_title: World Bank, World Development Indicators — Employment in agriculture (% of total employment) (modeled ILO estimate), Egypt, Arab Rep.
answer.quote: Egypt, Arab Rep.	2025	18
answer.data_quality_flag: ILO modelled estimate (ILOEST) rather than a direct survey observation; the 2025 figure is a model nowcast, and the World Bank country page displays it rounded to an integer
answer.construct_note: The indicator name 'Employment in agriculture (%)' omits the denominator; the quoted series is explicitly '% of total employment', which is the standard reading and is what is recorded here. The series covers ISIC-A (agriculture, hunting, forestry and fishing), i.e. slightly broader than crop-and-livestock agriculture alone, so the figure is a mild upper bound on agriculture-only employment share. It is also a modelled ILO nowcast for 2025, not an observed CAPMAS survey result. National corroboration sits on the same side: the CAPMAS 2024 Labour Force Survey, as reported by Egypt's State Information Service (T3), states 'Agriculture and fishing remained the largest employment sectors, engaging 5.594 million workers, representing 18.7 percent of the workforce.' A T5 aggregator (statisticsoftheworld.com) shows the unrounded WDI value as 17.5% for 2025, but T5 cannot carry a statistic, so the rounded T1 value of 18 is recorded.
answer.quality_evidence: Source is the World Bank WDI country page for Egypt, Arab Rep., drawing on the ILO Modelled Estimates database (ILOEST), accessed January 2026, licensed CC BY-4.0. The same value is independently supported in direction and magnitude by CAPMAS's own 2024 Labour Force Survey (18.7% of employment in agriculture and fishing), which reduces the risk that the modelled nowcast is materially off.
answer.scale_evidence: National-level figure covering total employment in Egypt; CAPMAS 2024 LFS reports 29.928 million employed persons in total, of whom 5.594 million in agriculture and fishing.
answer.rung_argument: Level 1 would apply to a value at or above 45% of total employment in agriculture; Egypt's 2025 WDI/ILO figure of 18 is far below that, so the 45 cut is passed (level 2). The 30 cut is also passed: 18 is well below 30, and the trajectory in the same series is monotonically downward (the WDI chart axis for Egypt runs from roughly 40% in the early 1990s to under 20% by 2025), with the national CAPMAS survey independently placing agriculture and fishing at 18.7% of the workforce in 2024. That establishes level 3. The value itself is the ratified quantity here; the construct match is direct on the denominator (% of total employment) and only marginally broad on the numerator (ISIC-A includes forestry and fishing), which if anything inflates rather than deflates the figure and therefore cannot push the score down a rung.
answer.negative_finding: Level 4 requires the share to fall below 15% of total employment. It does not: the T1 published value is 18 for 2025, and the closest national survey evidence (CAPMAS LFS 2024, 18.7%) is higher still. No admissible source in the retrieved pages shows Egypt's agricultural employment share under 15%; even the unrounded aggregator series (17.5%, T5, not admissible for a statistic) would remain above the cut.
answer.search_trail: 1) World Bank WDI indicator page SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS filtered to Egypt (Source 1) — carries the country row 'Egypt, Arab Rep. 2025 18' from ILOEST; used as the value of record. 2) Global WDI page for the same series (Source 2) — same value, no country-specific added detail. 3) DataBank report for EGY (Source 3) — returned a server error, no data. 4) ILOSTAT data portal, Egypt country profile, ILO Modelled Estimates methodology page and employment topic page (Sources 4-7) — all blocked by Cloudflare bot verification, no figures retrievable, so the unrounded ILOSTAT value could not be quote-verified. 5) CAPMAS microdata catalogue entry for the 2020 Annual Labour Force Survey bulletin (Source 8) — metadata only, no employment-by-sector figure on the page. 6) Egypt State Information Service report of CAPMAS's 2024 annual LFS (Source 9, T3) — gives 18.7% of the workforce in agriculture and fishing for 2024; used as corroboration, not as the recorded value, since the T1 WDI series is the named construct's standard source. 7) statisticsoftheworld.com (Source 10, T5) — shows 17.5% for 2025 and a full back series, but T5 material is admissible for existence facts only, never a statistic, so it was not used for the value.

1.2.name: Cereal yield (kg/ha)

gates.reason: recorded at T1

answer.source_title: World Bank, World Development Indicators — Cereal yield (kg per hectare) - Egypt, Arab Rep. (AG.YLD.CREL.KG)
answer.quote: Egypt, Arab Rep.	2023	7,402
answer.data_quality_flag: FAO-compiled from national questionnaire returns; WDI notes complete cross-country consistency is not possible
answer.construct_note: The WDI series AG.YLD.CREL.KG is exactly the named construct: cereal yield in kilograms per hectare of harvested land, covering wheat, rice, maize, barley, oats, rye, millet, sorghum, buckwheat and mixed grains harvested for dry grain (per the WDI metadata glossary page retrieved as Source 2). The figure is national for Egypt, Arab Rep., which is the unit the indicator names.
answer.quality_evidence: T1 publisher (World Bank WDI, sourced from FAO/FAOSTAT QCL). Indicator code, long definition, unit of measure (kg per hectare) and reference period 1961-2024 are documented on the WDI Metadata Glossary page. The country page and the all-countries table both carry the same value for Egypt, Arab Rep., most recent year 2023.
answer.scale_evidence: National annual figure for Egypt, Arab Rep.: 7,402 kg/ha, most recent year 2023. A T5 aggregator (statisticsoftheworld.com) reproduces the same WDI series and shows a stable 2000-2023 band of roughly 6,044-7,556 kg/ha, consistent with the quoted T1 value but not relied on for the recorded number.
answer.rung_argument: The recorded value is taken verbatim from a T1 source that publishes a single headline figure for the named construct for the named country: Egypt, Arab Rep., 2023, 7,402 kg per hectare. Construct match is exact — the WDI metadata defines the series as cereal yield in kg per hectare of harvested land, which is the indicator as named, and no unit conversion or derivation was applied. The value is national, which is the correct geography for this indicator. Against the threshold ladder, 7,402 clears 1500, 3000, 4500 and 6000, so all four cut points are passed and the level is 5. Egypt's cereal yield is dominated by irrigated Nile Valley rice, maize and wheat, which is consistent with a value in the 7,000 kg/ha range and with the long run of the series (6,044-7,556 kg/ha since 2000).
answer.negative_finding: Not required: level 5 is the top of the ladder and the value 7,402 kg/ha exceeds the highest cut point of 6000. gates.reason: the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep.

answer.value: No national all-crop post-harvest loss rate is published for Egypt in the retrieved sources; FAO's Egypt factsheet reports commodity-specific losses of 10 to 20 percent for wheat in traditional shona storage, preliminary estimates of 25 to 35 percent for grapes, and more than half of tomatoes fully spoilt or quality-damaged by the time they reach consumers, while a peer-reviewed grape study reports node-level post-harvest losses of 10.06, 5.82, 6.53 and 7.06 percent for growers, rural traders, wholesalers and retailers.
answer.unit: percent (commodity-specific ranges, not a single national rate)
answer.source_title: FAO, Food loss and waste in Egypt (country factsheet, FAO Representation in Egypt)
answer.quote: Wheat losses in traditional storage shona are estimated to be 10 to 20 percent, with further losses
answer.data_quality_flag: Commodity-specific and partly described by the source as 'preliminary' estimates; the wheat figure covers one stage (traditional shona storage) rather than the whole chain, and no weighting to a national all-crop rate is published
answer.construct_note: The indicator name asserts an all-crop NATIONAL post-harvest loss rate for Egypt. Nothing in the retrieved pages publishes such a national figure. What exists is (a) FAO commodity-level estimates for Egypt (wheat 10-20 percent in traditional shona storage; grapes 25-35 percent 'preliminary'; tomatoes 'more than half' spoilt or quality-damaged) and (b) a peer-reviewed grapes-only supply-chain study with node averages of 10.06/5.82/6.53/7.06 percent. These are partial, commodity- and stage-specific measures, some of which mix quantity loss with quality/economic loss (the tomato and grape statements explicitly include 'quality loss and damage'), which sits on the wrong side of the census's open question. The FAO SDG 12.3.1a portal pages retrieved give only global and regional food-loss percentages (world 13.3 percent in 2023; sub-Saharan Africa 23.0 percent) with no Egypt value, and those are not this country's figure.
answer.quality_evidence: Source 6 is an FAO country factsheet published on openknowledge.fao.org (T2 by the supplied domain tiering); its Egypt loss numbers are drawn from FAO project assessments and are labelled 'estimated' or 'preliminary'. Source 9 is a peer-reviewed article in Journal of Environmental Management based on primary data from 343 grape farmers and middlemen in Egypt, using LCA and the Category Method - methodologically strong but single-commodity. No nationally representative loss survey for Egypt appears in any retrieved page; the FAO introduction deck (Source 7) itself notes 'Reliable nationally representative data on losses are generally not available'.
answer.scale_evidence: Coverage is limited to four value chains named for Egypt (wheat, grapes, tomatoes, fish) plus one commodity-specific academic study. No aggregation across the ten-commodity SDG basket, no national weighting, and no year attached to the factsheet estimates.
answer.rung_argument: Reading the cut points for a lower-is-better threshold (>30 percent = level 1; at or below 30 = 2; at or below 20 = 3; at or below 12 = 4; at or below 5 = 5): Level 1 would require evidence that Egypt's post-harvest losses exceed 30 percent across the board - not supported, since the staple crop (wheat, by far the largest single food chain) is put at 10-20 percent at the storage stage and the grape value-chain study finds node losses in the 6-10 percent band. Level 2 is supported: taken together, the evidence indicates that typical Egyptian post-harvest losses for the major measured chains fall below 30 percent, with the compounded grape chain (10.06 + 5.82 + 6.53 + 7.06) and the FAO grape range of 25-35 percent straddling but not systematically exceeding that line, and cereals clearly under it. The value recorded is deliberately a statement, not a number, because no publisher has produced a single national all-crop rate for Egypt and averaging these heterogeneous, differently-scoped figures would manufacture a precision the sources do not have.
answer.negative_finding: Level 3 was not proposed because nothing in the evidence shows Egyptian post-harvest losses at or below 20 percent on any national or all-crop basis. The only figure fully under 20 percent is a single-stage wheat storage range whose own source says there are 'further losses all along the value chain'; the two horticultural chains measured (grapes 25-35 percent preliminary; tomatoes 'more than half' spoilt or quality-damaged) sit well above 20 percent. 8.5.name: Women who own land (% holders)

gates.reason: the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep.

answer.unit: % of agricultural landholders who are female
answer.source_title: The Social Research Center, American University in Cairo — Research on the Economic Participation of Women in Agriculture (citing Abdel Aal, Mohammed (2002), Women in Agriculture, unpublished background paper)
answer.quote: Overall female holders represent only 5.72% of the total number of landholders in Egypt .
answer.data_quality_flag: Figure published on a university research-centre web page citing an unpublished background paper; no reference year is stated on the page and the figure is roughly two decades old. No percentage from the 2009/2010 agricultural census surfaced in the retrieved pages.
answer.construct_note: The indicator's name says women who OWN land, but its own parenthetical unit is '% holders', and every figure available for Egypt in the retrieved pages counts female agricultural HOLDERS/landholders (operators of a holding, who may rent rather than own) rather than registered landowners. The quoted 5.72% is a share of landholders, not of documented owners. Corroborating holder counts from FAO's T1 census summaries: the 1999/2000 Agricultural Census reports 'Total (Civil persons) 4 537 319', 'Male 4 300 687', 'Female 236 632'; the 1990 census reports holders 'Total 3 470 813', male '3 185 060', female '285 753'. Both are counts, not published percentages, so they are used only as corroboration and not as the recorded value. Separately, the same AUC page reports women hold 6.1% of the cultivated area in Lower Egypt and 4.1% in border governorates — an area-based, not holder-based, measure. No sex-disaggregated statistic on legal land OWNERSHIP (e.g. FAO Gender and Land Rights Database Indicator 2, 'Distribution of agricultural landowners by sex') was retrievable for Egypt: the GLRD country page returned a 404 error, and the FAO/PIM technical note in the retrieved pages lists the indicators but its Egypt tables were not in the supplied text.
answer.quality_evidence: The recorded percentage comes from an academic research-centre publication summarising Egyptian agricultural-holding data; it is directionally consistent with two independent T1 FAO census summaries (1990: 285 753 female of 3 470 813 holders; 1999/2000: 236 632 female of 4 537 319 civil-person holders), which place the female share of holders in the same single-digit range. No source in the retrieved set disaggregates land OWNERSHIP by sex for Egypt, so the ownership-versus-operation question flagged in the indicator census cannot be resolved from this evidence.
answer.scale_evidence: National coverage: the 1999/2000 and 1990 agricultural censuses were complete enumerations covering the entire country and all sectors of agriculture; the AUC figure is stated as an overall national share with regional breakdowns (Lower Egypt 7.28%, Upper Egypt 3.87%, border governorates 4.56%). All regional shares are also below 10%.
answer.rung_argument: The scoring is a threshold on the published value. The only published percentage for the named construct in the retrieved pages is 5.72% of landholders being female, which falls below the first cut point of 10, placing the cell at level 1. The value is credible in magnitude because two T1 FAO census summaries independently report female holders as a small minority of all holders (236 632 of 4 537 319 in 1999/2000; 285 753 of 3 470 813 in 1990). The construct sits on the 'holder/operator' side rather than the 'owner' side of the unratified definition, which is recorded rather than scored around, since the indicator's own unit is '% holders'.
answer.negative_finding: Level 2 would require a published figure above 10% of holders (or owners) being women. Nothing in the retrieved pages shows that: the highest regional female-holder share published is 7.28% (Lower Egypt), the national figure is 5.72%, and the underlying FAO census counts imply a share in the same single-digit range. No more recent Egyptian figure (e.g. from the 2009/2010 census) was retrievable to test whether the share has since crossed 10%.

Dead ends: no World Bank/WDI 'female share of agricultural holders' page and no SDG 5.a.1 (ownership/secure tenure rights over agricultural land, by sex) value for Egypt appeared in the supplied pages.

3.3.name: National farmer registry

gates.reason: the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep.

answer.value: Egypt has no separately constituted national farmer registry in the retrieved record; the nearest instrument is the Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation's farmer smart-card subsidy scheme, which the government describes as building a database of farmers and cultivated land from each cardholder's name, identity information and agricultural landholding numbers.
answer.source_title: Egypt State Information Service — "Agriculture ministry spokesman: State beefs up efforts to serve farmers in villages nationwide"
answer.quote: Each card bears the farmer's name, identity information and agricultural landholding numbers, thus building a vast database for farmers and cultivated land.
answer.data_quality_flag: Government communiqué rather than a programme document or legal instrument; the unit of record is ambiguous (cardholder vs. landholding), and no official enumeration of registrants was found in an admissible-tier source
answer.construct_note: The indicator names a register of FARMERS (individuals). The only Egyptian instrument found is a subsidy smart-card scheme whose database is built from landholding records — the card is issued against agricultural landholding numbers, and Al-Ahram (T5) reports that the card must go to the owner rather than the tenant and that heirs of one plot must nominate a single cardholder. That means the unit of record is effectively the holding, not the farmer, and cultivating tenants can be excluded. The evidence therefore sits on the holding-registry side of the open definitional question flagged in the indicator census. No FAO farmer-registry assessment covering Egypt was retrievable: the FAO NENA regional dialogue page names Morocco, Jordan and Lebanon only, and the FAO situation-analysis page was blocked by a bot check.
answer.rung_argument: Absent is exceeded: a national instrument holding farmer-level records demonstrably exists — the Ministry of Agriculture's smart-card scheme, described by the government's own information service as building a database of farmers and cultivated land. Announced is exceeded: the scheme is not a statement of intent but an operating ministerial programme with a named project director, an inter-ministerial contract (agriculture and military production) and card manufacture under way. Adopted is exceeded: the T3 page states the ministry 'has embarked upon launching a farmer subsidy program; issuing farmers electronic smart cards', i.e. cards are actually being issued and used to channel subsidised fertiliser, seed and pesticide quotas, and delivery is supervised by the ministry, the agricultural associations and the Agricultural Bank of Egypt. That is live service delivery, so Operating (base level 3).
answer.negative_finding: Level 4 was not proposed because no independent or official evaluation, audit, performance report or service standard for the registry/card database was found — the only descriptive material is the implementer's own communiqué, which is design and intent, not measured quality. answer.value: Egypt publishes government agricultural data through the CAPMAS Central Data Catalog (an Agriculture collection of 47 studies) and the Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation's Economic Affairs Sector database pages, but neither constitutes open, machine-readable, AI-ready agricultural data: the CAPMAS agriculture entries are catalogued with access filters of 'Licensed data files' or 'Data not available' and the downloadable artefacts are PDF bulletins, while the MALR databases are Arabic-only HTML query screens with no open licence, no bulk download and no API, so the named instrument is absent.

answer.construct_note: The named construct is a conjunction — open AND machine-readable AND AI-ready agricultural data. The quoted CAPMAS page is offered as evidence that the right place was searched: it is Egypt's national statistical microdata catalogue and it does hold an Agriculture collection (47 studies), but its data-access filters offer only 'Licensed data files' and 'Data not available', the study pages (e.g. Annual Bulletin of Fish Production 2022, catalog/788) expose only a PDF 'Other Materials' download, and the access-policy page states 'The site does not publish individual data about individuals'. answer.value: Egypt's National Authority for Remote Sensing and Space Sciences (NARSS), acting for the Ministry of Higher Education and coordinating with the Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation, produced and presented remote-sensing/AI-based crop inventory and classification maps for the winter 2023-2024 and summer 2024 seasons covering strategic crops (wheat, clover, sugar beet) in the governorates; no official government or T1 statistical document retrieved confirms that these EO products are routinely integrated into national agricultural statistics or administrative decision systems.

answer.quote: The National Authority for Remote Sensing and Space Sciences (NARSS) and the Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation presented a map of crops for the winter agricultural season 2023-2024.
answer.data_quality_flag: Operational claim rests on a single T5 news report (existence fact only); no NARSS or MALR primary document, budget line or service description was retrieved, and the news item describes the work in project language ('the project's principal researcher'), leaving routine institutionalisation unverified.

The retrieved evidence establishes production of EO-derived crop maps by the national space agency in coordination with the agriculture ministry — i.e. EO products reaching the agricultural administration. It does NOT establish 'integration' in the stronger sense of EO layers embedded in a national agricultural information system, statistical production, or a formal institutional data-sharing arrangement: the CAPMAS agricultural bulletins in the T1 microdata catalogue (cultivated area, land reclamation, irrigation) show no EO-derived input. Announced is exceeded: the activity is not merely declared — outputs were produced and presented. Adopted is exceeded in the weak sense that the ministry is a named counterpart and the work spans two consecutive seasons (winter 2023-2024 and summer 2024). Operating is proposed because concrete outputs exist and were delivered: a geographic database and digital and paper maps of field verification points for wheat, clover and sugar beet in the governorates. 3.11.name: Agricultural data interoperability standards

gates.reason: the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep.

answer.value: Egypt has cross-government data-openness instruments — a 2025 national Open Data Policy issued by the National Council for Artificial Intelligence (which includes an Annex on metadata standards for open data and anticipates a forthcoming Data Governance Law), an Egyptian Data Governance Authority, a national Open Data Portal used by MoALR/CAPMAS staff in FAO GSARS dissemination training, and Ministry of Agriculture sectoral databases — but no agriculture-specific data interoperability or data-exchange standard (no national agri-data schema, ontology, API specification or harmonisation instrument) is published or named among them; the only agricultural semantic-interoperability work located is a university research project, not a national standard.
answer.source_title: National Council for Artificial Intelligence, Arab Republic of Egypt — Open Data Policy (2025)
answer.quote: This policy sets out the overarching framework for data openness across Egyptian public institutions during the transitional period prior to the enactment of the Data Governance Law and its accompanying data classification framework.
answer.construct_note: The quoted instrument is Egypt's horizontal, cross-government Open Data Policy (2025), not an agricultural data interoperability standard. It is cited only as the nearest adjacent instrument examined — evidence that the right domain was searched — not as a measure of the named construct. 3.8.name: National soil map/database

gates.reason: the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep.

answer.value: Egypt has national soil map/database assets: a national soil map of Egypt (Hammad, 1975) held in the EUDASM national soil map archive, scanned FAO legacy paper maps for Egypt (non-georeferenced JPEG), and a GIS-based national soil database operated since 1997 by the Executive Authority for Land Improvement Projects (EALIP) that produced whole-country soil information maps at 1:100 000, plus digital soil and terrain data produced by NARSS with FAO and the European Soil Bureau; no evidence was found in the retrieved sources of a currently operating national soil information service (Egypt is not among the national soil information systems listed by FAO's Global Soil Partnership/GLOSIS).
answer.source_title: FAO, Land Resources Information Systems in the Near East — Country report: Land and water resources information system in Egypt
answer.quote: A Geographic Information System (GIS) has been in use at EALIP since 1997, and a GIS-based soil database was used for production of maps and other related materials on soil salinity, sodicity and water table level, and on gypsum and subsoiling requirements.
answer.data_quality_flag: Primary evidence is 2001-vintage (FAO workshop country report); no post-2010 official documentation of the national soil database's current status was retrieved
answer.construct_note: The indicator census asks whether a digitised legacy paper map satisfies the row or whether an operating digital soil information service is required. The Egyptian evidence sits on BOTH sides but strongest on the weaker side: the clearest artifacts are legacy products (Soil Map of Egypt, Hammad 1975, in EUDASM; ~scanned, non-georeferenced FAO legacy paper maps listing Egypt). The stronger, database-side evidence — EALIP's GIS-based national soil database with nationwide 1:100 000 salinity/sodicity/water-table maps — is documented only as of 1997-2001. If the ratified definition requires an operating, current digital soil information service, this cell would drop toward Announced/Absent, because Egypt does not appear among the regional and national soil information systems listed on FAO's GLOSIS page (CamSIS, MaSIS, SISLAC).
answer.scale_evidence: EALIP's GIS-based soil database yielded national coverage: "EALIP produced information maps for subsoiling, gypsum requirement, watertable depth and salinity for the whole country at the district level (1:100 000), for one governorate at the village level (1:25 000) and for three governorates at the basin level (scale 1:2 500)" (FAO, y4357e07). A parallel FAO page records EALIP coverage of 12 million feddans studied and 11 million feddans improved.
answer.rung_argument: Absent is ruled out: a national soil map of Egypt exists (EUDASM entry, Hammad 1975) and FAO's legacy map catalogue explicitly lists Egypt among countries with archived/scanned soil maps. Announced is exceeded: the instrument is not merely proposed — a GIS-based soil database was actually stood up at EALIP in 1997 and NARSS produced digital soil and terrain data of Egypt in cooperation with FAO and the European Soil Bureau. Adopted is supported: an institutionally mandated body (EALIP, established 1971 under the Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation) held and used a national soil database, and nationwide derived maps were produced from it. 4.1.name: Data protection/privacy law

gates.reason: the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep.

answer.value: Egypt has an enacted general data protection statute: Law No. 151 of 2020 promulgating the Personal Data Protection Law, issued by the President on 13 July 2020, which applies to personal data processed electronically by any holder, controller or processor and entered into force three months after publication in the Official Gazette; the law itself provides that the Minister of Communications and Information Technology must issue its Executive Regulations within six months, and no evidence of those regulations or of an operating supervisory authority appears in the pages retrieved.
answer.source_title: Arab Republic of Egypt, Law No. 151 of 2020 Promulgating the Personal Data Protection Law (English text hosted on ILO NATLEX)
answer.quote: This law shall be published in the Official Gazette and shall come into force after three (3) months from the following day of its publication.
answer.data_quality_flag: Unofficial English translation of the Arabic text; the crawler labelled the natlex.ilo.org domain T5, but the document quoted is the national legal instrument itself, reproduced in the ILO's NATLEX national legislation database, hence tiered T3 as a government legal artifact.
answer.construct_note: The indicator names a data protection/privacy law; the quoted artifact is Egypt's economy-wide personal data protection statute (Law 151/2020). It is general-purpose, not agriculture-specific, and by its Article 3 excludes data held by national security authorities, the Central Bank, and data processed for official statistical purposes.
answer.rung_argument: Absent is ruled out: a named instrument exists and its text is retrievable (Law No. 151 of 2020, signed 13 July 2020). Announced is exceeded: this is not a draft or a stated intention but a law passed by the House of Representatives and promulgated by the President, published in the Official Gazette and in force three months later, with defined scope, definitions of controller/processor/data subject, and jurisdiction assigned to the economic courts. Adopted is therefore established on the face of the instrument. Level = 3 for Adopted; quality_evidence and scale_evidence are both empty, so no increment applies.
answer.negative_finding: Operating was not proposed. Nothing in the retrieved pages evidences implementation: Article 4 of Law 151/2020 makes the annexed law's operation contingent on Executive Regulations to be issued by the Minister of Communications and Information Technology, and Article 6 gives addressees one year from the issuance of those Regulations to comply — no retrieved source shows that those Executive Regulations have been issued, that the Personal Data Protection Center referred to in Article 3 is constituted and staffed, or that any registration, licensing, complaint-handling or enforcement activity has occurred. No evaluation, audit or performance report was retrieved (hence quality_evidence empty), and no figures on registrations, complaints, or enforcement actions were retrieved (hence scale_evidence empty).
answer.search_trail: Started with the World Bank GovTech pages supplied (GTMI main page, GTMI 2025 update, 2025 GTMI survey guidance note, GovTech data page, 2025 GTMI Brief): all describe the index and its 'laws and regulations' enabler component but none of the retrieved text contains any Egypt-specific data protection value or statement, so none could be quoted for this cell. Then went to the primary legal artifact: the full English text of Law No. 151 of 2020 on ILO NATLEX (Source 7), corroborated by identical text on acc.com (Source 9) and a law-firm translation (Source 10, T5, not used for the quote). 3.4.name: Digital land/plot registration

gates.reason: the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep.

answer.value: Egypt operates a digitised property registration system under the Ministry of Justice's Real Estate Publicity and Notarization Authority — handwritten entry was eliminated in all branches nationwide by end-2021, offices use electronic ledgers and the Digital Egypt platform, and in July 2025 a paperless G2G-integrated property registration system was launched in 16 new-urban-community registry offices — while the agricultural real-property register (al-sijil al-'ayni al-zira'i) is reported only as having had its 'first phase' developed.
answer.source_title: Egyptian Cabinet (Presidency of the Council of Ministers), news item on the Prime Minister's inspection of the Real Estate Publicity and Notarization Authority headquarters in Ramses, Cairo
answer.quote: وتطوير عدد من مكاتب السجل العيني، وإدارات السجل العيني بالمكاتب الرئيسية للشهر العقاري ومأموريات الشهر العقاري، وافتتاح مأموريات شهر عقاري في كل تجمع عمراني جديد، وربط مكاتب الشهر العقاري بالجهات الحكومية، وتطوير المرحلة الأولى من السجل العيني الزراعي
answer.data_quality_flag: Operating and coverage statements come from government/implementer press releases (Cabinet, MCIT); no independent audit or evaluation of registry performance was retrieved, and no published coverage figures exist for the agricultural cadastre specifically
answer.construct_note: The indicator name reads generically as 'Digital land/plot registration', and the operating evidence is for Egypt's economy-wide real-estate registration and notarisation system (Shahr Aqari / sijil ayni), which is dominated by urban and new-urban-community property: the July 2025 G2G paperless launch covers 16 registry offices in new cities (Alamein, New Administrative Capital, 6th of October, etc.), and the 2021 World Bank project (P177720) frames the objective as scaling up registration 'in selected new urban communities'. The specifically agricultural register — al-sijil al-'ayni al-zira'i — appears in the same government sources only as a geographic database linked to the notarisation system (MCIT 2012) and as 'first phase' development (Cabinet). So the evidence sits on the all-property/urban side of the unresolved definitional question; if this row is later ratified to mean digital registration of agricultural holdings or usufruct specifically, the rung would need to be re-scored downward, as no operating national agricultural digital cadastre with published coverage was found in these pages.
answer.scale_evidence: Cabinet (2022): 110 notarisation branches opened inside post offices and 103 outside them; phases 1 and 2 completed for 230 of 250 targeted notarisation premises; 1,102 staff transferred of whom 975 took up posts; handwritten entry eliminated in all branches nationwide by end-2021. Cabinet (17 July 2025): the Ministry of Justice–NUCA G2G integrated registration system launched simultaneously in 16 new-urban-community registry offices listed by city across the country. MCIT (2012): 100 of 350 notarisation offices mechanised, main information centre operating, project database containing more than 3.5 million mechanised transactions and about 100,000 mechanised powers of attorney issued monthly.
answer.rung_argument: Absent is ruled out: a national land/plot registration register exists and is being digitised — the Ministry of Justice's own sector page names supervision of 'the digital transformation strategy and mechanisation of all services provided to citizens at notarisation, real estate publicity and sijil ayni offices' as a standing function. Announced is exceeded: the digitisation is not a plan but a funded, legislated programme (Law 27/2018 as amended by Law 177/2022 on real estate registration in new urban communities, and the 2022 amendment of Law 114/1946). Adopted is exceeded: the system is not merely adopted on paper — Cabinet reports that handwritten entry was eliminated in all branches nationwide by end-2021, that electronic ledgers have replaced paper registers in upgraded offices, that services are delivered through the Digital Egypt platform, and MCIT reports a live central information centre linked to the national ID and to the agricultural sijil ayni geographic databases. Operating is therefore established. Scale evidence is filled with published reach figures (numbers of mechanised/upgraded offices, 16 G2G-integrated new-city registry offices, 3.5 million mechanised transactions), giving 3 + 1 = 4.
answer.negative_finding: Level 5 was not proposed because quality_evidence is empty: nothing retrieved is an independent or official evaluation, audit or performance report on how well the digital registry works. The only performance-flavoured statements (transactions completed within ten minutes, improved accuracy) are the implementers' own descriptions in MCIT and Cabinet press releases, which are design/self-report, not evaluation. On the contrary, the World Bank's 2021 concept-stage PID for the Modernization of Egyptian Property Registration Project states the objective is 'to establish the foundations of a modern and efficient land administration and management system at national level', implying those foundations were not yet in place, which argues against crediting quality.

Checked the 2007 IFC SmartLessons brief on property registration reform (fee reform, deeds per month) — that is a pre-digital fee reform, not digital registration, so not used as the anchor. Discarded the Bosnia and Herzegovina Real Estate Registration Project PID as another country. Then went to Egyptian government artifacts: Ministry of Justice sector page (digital transformation and mechanisation mandate), MCIT press release of 30 Jan 2012 (mechanisation programme scale figures, link to the agricultural sijil ayni geographic databases), Cabinet news 24902 (nationwide elimination of handwriting, branch counts, first phase of the agricultural sijil ayni), and Cabinet news 82685 of 17 July 2025 (paperless G2G registration launched in 16 new-city registry offices under Law 27/2018 as amended by Law 177/2022). Dead end: no source in the set gives a figure for the share of agricultural plots or holdings digitally registered, and no independent evaluation or audit of registry performance was retrieved.

gates.reason: the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep.

answer.value: Egypt is placed in Tier 1, the top tier of the ITU Global Cybersecurity Index 2024, with a perfect score, as stated by Egypt's Ministry of Communications and Information Technology.
answer.unit: GCI 2024 tier classification (five-tier model; score reported on a 0-100 scale)
answer.source_title: Arab Republic of Egypt, Ministry of Communications and Information Technology - Telecommunications / Industry / Cyber Security
answer.quote: Tier 1 ranking with a perfect score in the ITU
answer.data_quality_flag: Government self-report of an ITU classification; the ITU GCI 2024 report page carrying Egypt's own country profile/score was not among the retrieved sources, so the figure could not be quote-verified from ITU itself. A second government source (NTRA, tra.gov.eg) carries the same Tier 1 claim in its page title but the retrieved body text was empty.
answer.construct_note: The indicator is named 'Cybersecurity framework (ITU GCI)'. The evidence is the GCI 2024 result for Egypt. Note the census question flagged for this row: ITU's GCI 2024 moved to a tier-based model and does not publish a single overall 0-1 index score per country; scores in that edition are expressed out of 100 (and the register's Egypt entry of '100' is on that 0-100 scale, not the 0-1 scale implied by the cut points, while Nigeria's 0.824 is on a 0-1 scale). The two register entries are therefore indeed incommensurable. The evidence here sits on the 0-100 / tier side of that question. Normalised (100/100 = 1.0), Egypt still clears the top cut point of 0.8, so the ambiguity does not change the level for this country, but it does mean the recorded 'value' is a tier/statement rather than an ITU-published 0-1 overall score.
answer.quality_evidence: The GCI is described by ITU as measuring 'the commitment of countries to cybersecurity' across five pillars - Legal, Technical, Organizational, Capacity Development and Cooperation - aggregated into an overall score (ITU GCI landing page, T1). ITU states the 5th edition was built on review of over 30,000 URLs and more than 1,000 PDFs, with each country submission independently verified. The specific Egypt result, however, is quoted here from the Egyptian ICT ministry rather than from an ITU page carrying Egypt's profile.
answer.scale_evidence: Tier 1 in GCI 2024 is the highest of the five tiers (role-modelling countries). The same MCIT page evidences the underlying institutional apparatus consistent with a top-tier score: the Egyptian Supreme Cybersecurity Council as highest national authority, EG-CERT as national technical authority and executive arm, a first National Cybersecurity Strategy (2017-2021) and a current strategy (2023-2027) in force. ITU's own page separately records Egypt's earlier GCI history (ranked in 2014 edition).
answer.rung_argument: Level 1 (below 0.2): ruled out - Egypt has a legally constituted national cybersecurity authority (ESCC), an operating national CERT (EG-CERT) and successive national strategies, far beyond a near-zero commitment score. Level 2 (0.2-0.4) and level 3 (0.4-0.6): ruled out - all five GCI pillars are evidenced (legal instruments including accession to the UN Convention against Cybercrime, technical measures via EG-CERT incident response and forensics, organisational measures via ESCC and the 2023-2027 strategy, capacity development via training/cyberdrills/awareness academies, and cooperation via Arab and ITU cyberdrill participation). Level 4 (0.6-0.8): ruled out - a Tier 1 placement in GCI 2024 corresponds to the highest band of the index, which on any normalisation exceeds 0.8. Level 5: the government source states a 'perfect score' and Tier 1 placement, i.e. the maximum attainable on the published scale (100/100, equivalently 1.0 on a 0-1 basis), which is above the top cut point of 0.8. The argument here is about the VALUE and its construct match, not arithmetic: the value is a tier plus a reported perfect score rather than an ITU-published 0-1 figure, and that is the correct characterisation of what GCI 2024 actually publishes.
answer.negative_finding: Level 5 is proposed, so no higher rung exists. The residual weakness to record instead: the ITU pages retrieved do not themselves carry Egypt's GCI 2024 score or tier, so the top-of-scale placement rests on a T3 national-government statement rather than a T1 quote from the ITU report; and no ITU-published single 0-1 overall score for Egypt exists to place directly against these cut points.
answer.search_trail: Started with the ITU GCI publication landing pages (itu.int/pub and itu.int/epublications) - both carry front matter, acknowledgements, foreword and disclaimers only; neither retrieved page contains any country score table, so Egypt's 2024 figure could not be quoted from ITU. Checked the ITU news item 'Egypt Ranked Ninth at Global Cybersecurity Index' - this is the 2014 first edition (rank 27th of 193 per that page's own text) and is a decade out of date, so not used as the value. Checked the Belgian CCB mirror of the GCI 2024 PDF - the retrieved extract stops at the foreword and contains no country tables. Checked Egypt's NTRA (tra.gov.eg) page - title asserts Tier 1 but the retrieved body was 'undefined', so not quotable. Settled on the MCIT (Egyptian ICT ministry) Cyber Security page, a T3 government artifact, which states the Tier 1 / perfect score GCI 2024 result verbatim. Recorded as a statement rather than a number because ITU GCI 2024 publishes tiers and 0-100 pillar scores, not a 0-1 overall index score of the kind the register's cut points assume.

answer.source_title: National Council for Artificial Intelligence, Arab Republic of Egypt — Open Data Policy (2025)
answer.quote: This policy outlines Egypt’s roadmap to promote and expand open data practices throughout the public sector during the transitional period preceding the enactment of the forthcoming Data Governance Law, its executive regulations, and the accompanying data classification framework.
answer.construct_note: The quoted instrument is a whole-of-government open data policy issued by the National Council for Artificial Intelligence; it is sector-agnostic and contains no agriculture-specific provisions (no farm data, no agricultural registry, no MoALR-specific data governance rules). It is cited as evidence that the national data-governance domain was examined and that no agricultural data governance framework sits within it, not as a measure of the named construct. The adjacent sector instrument examined, FAO's GSARS country page for Egypt, lists only capacity-building activities and explicitly names the SPARS adopters as 'Angola, Madagascar, Mozambique, Tanzania, Togo, Liberia, Zimbabwe' — Egypt is not among them.

Rung 'Announced' would require a government or ministry statement of intent to create such a framework; the only announced forthcoming instrument is the general Data Governance Law referenced in the Open Data Policy, which is not agricultural. Rung 'Adopted' would require an issued agricultural data policy, decree or strategy; the FAO GSARS country page for Egypt lists only training packages (basic training, HR policies, master sampling frame, CAPI, dissemination, CAADP indicators) and shows Egypt is not among the countries that adopted SPARS, which is the standard sectoral planning/governance instrument for agricultural statistics. Rung 'Operating' would additionally require evidence of the framework functioning; none exists because no framework exists. answer.construct_note: Judged against the indicator NAME ('Tertiary STEM enrollment (% gross)'), the best available evidence sits on the wrong side of the open definitional question flagged in the indicator census. The World Bank Open Data page for SE.TER.ENRR lists Egypt, Arab Rep. at 38 for 2025 (Gender Data Portal gives female 38.6% for 2025; IndexMundi's older UIS extract gives 38.90 for 2018). Scoring 38 against cut points calibrated for a STEM SHARE would place Egypt at level 4, whereas Egypt's actual STEM subset is necessarily a fraction of that 38 and would almost certainly fall in a much lower band. 5.4.name: Digital literacy among farmers (%)

gates.reason: no value asserted

answer.abstain_reason: No source in the retrieved set publishes a digital-literacy rate among farmers for Egypt. The only quantified evidence (IFPRI/GIZ policy note and discussion paper) comes from a purposively selected RCT baseline of smartphone-owning smallholders in two governorates (Minya and Beni Suef) who are members of GIZ-supported farmer organizations, and it reports the share of farmers who CITED digital illiteracy as a barrier to app use — a self-reported obstacle in the inverse direction of the indicator, not a measured literacy rate, and not nationally representative. Recording it as a national digital-literacy percentage would convert a data gap into a confident score.
answer.source_title: IFPRI (CGSpace), Abdelaziz, F. & Abay, K.A., 'Digital Literacy Training to Promote Diffusion of Digital Agricultural Tools to Smallholder Farmers', Policy Note, September 2024
answer.data_quality_flag: Best available quantified evidence is a non-representative RCT baseline in two governorates among smartphone-owning members of donor-supported farmer organizations; the headline figure is self-reported digital ILliteracy as a barrier, i.e. the inverse of the indicator's direction.
answer.construct_note: Indicator name asserts a national percentage of farmers who are digitally literate. The retrieved evidence (IFPRI Policy Note, Sept 2024, baseline of ~4,000 GIZ-supported smallholders in Minya and Beni Suef) instead reports the share of sampled farmers naming barriers to mobile-app use: 54 percent cited unawareness of existing applications, 52 percent cited general digital literacy / farmer digital illiteracy as a key challenge, 49 percent cited lack of smartphone access, and about 65 percent recommended digital literacy training. These are perception/barrier shares from a two-governorate purposive sample, not a national literacy rate, and 52 runs in the opposite (lower-is-better) direction from the indicator's H direction. The related FAO NENA study and IFPRI/ICARDA notes discuss limited digital skills qualitatively but publish no percentage. Egypt's agricultural census (2009-2010) and CAPMAS agricultural property statistics cover holdings, land, irrigation, machinery and employment; they contain no digital-skills module.
answer.quality_evidence: Peer-reviewed and IFPRI discussion-paper evidence (Food Policy 2026; IFPRI DP 02359) is methodologically strong for the RCT's own purpose (registered trial AEARCTR-0012723) but was never designed to estimate a population digital-literacy rate; the 52 percent figure is a baseline self-report of a perceived barrier among a screened sub-population.
answer.scale_evidence: Sample confined to about 4,000 farmers across roughly 30 farmer organizations in two Upper Egypt governorates (Minya and Beni Suef), of whom only the 2,400 smartphone owners were eligible for intervention. No national or governorate-representative sampling frame; no coverage of the Delta or reclaimed lands.
answer.rung_argument: No level is proposed. A threshold score here would require a published percentage of farmers assessed as digitally literate in Egypt. Nothing in the retrieved pages provides one: the census sources carry no digital-skills variable, the FAO NENA report treats digital literacy only narratively, and the IFPRI RCT provides a barrier-perception share from a non-representative two-governorate sample framed as illiteracy. Scoring 52 as if it were a literacy rate would simultaneously invert the direction and generalise a purposive Upper Egypt sample to the nation.
answer.negative_finding: Withholding a level rather than proposing one: no admissible source states, for Egypt, the share of farmers who are digitally literate. The evidence does not show a nationally scoped measurement of farmer digital literacy at any value, so even level 1 (a value below 10) cannot be evidenced.
answer.search_trail: 1) Checked national statistical sources first for a farmer digital-skills variable: CAPMAS Agricultural Property and Rein 2017 metadata (censusinfo.capmas.gov.eg) and the FAO microdata record for Egypt's Agricultural Census 2009-2010 — scope lists holdings characteristics, cultivated area, irrigation/drainage, employment, machinery, livestock; no ICT or digital-skills module, hence a dead end. 2) Searched the digital-agriculture literature for Egypt: IFPRI/CGSpace Policy Note (Sept 2024) and IFPRI Discussion Paper 02359 / Food Policy 2026 article on the Minya-Beni Suef RCT — these carry the only percentages, but they are baseline barrier self-reports (54/52/49/19/16/14 percent) and treatment effects in percentage points (uptake +20pp, utilization +18-26pp, trust +8-13pp), none of which is a digital-literacy rate. 3) FAO openknowledge 'Empowering small-scale farmers through digital innovation: NENA' (2026) — discusses digital literacy as a barrier qualitatively, regional scope, no Egypt figure on the landing page. 4) ICARDA 'Current Situation of Digital Agriculture in Egypt' (2023) — abstract cites 'knowledge levels of farmers' as a constraint, no statistic, and the item is Limited Access. 5) ScienceDirect version of the RCT paper returned a captcha page with no content. Conclusion: no published national digital-literacy figure for Egyptian farmers in the supplied pages.

gates.reason: the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep.

answer.value: Egypt has an operating digital agricultural extension service: the FAO/Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation mobile app "El Mufeed" (Digital Services Portfolio), launched in 2019 with content on Citrus Production, Date Palm Production, Healthy Nutrition and Household Poultry Production and a COVID-19 food safety theme added in 2020, with training of trainers delivered to MoALR extension personnel; however, no published evaluation of its performance or figures on its user reach for Egypt were found.
answer.source_title: FAO, Digital Services Portfolio — Country Cases (Egypt)
answer.quote: The FAO app El Mufeed, launched in 2019, has been built through a participatory approach, with inputs from farmers and rural women that took part in an inception workshop that was divided into five thematic groups.
answer.data_quality_flag: Implementer's own (FAO) descriptive account; no independent evaluation or usage statistics for Egypt on the page.
answer.construct_note: The evidence describes a national digital agricultural advisory/extension service delivered through a mobile application in partnership with the Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation, which is the named construct (digital extension capability). It does not quantify capability (e.g. number of extension agents equipped or farmers reached in Egypt).
answer.rung_argument: Absent is ruled out: a named digital extension instrument exists — FAO/MoALR's El Mufeed app. Announced is exceeded: it was not merely proposed; FAO 'has launched in Egypt a digital model of agricultural extension' (e-Agriculture news, 22 July 2019) under a 2018–2022 FAO–Government programme. Adopted is exceeded: content was developed with the Agriculture Research Centre, Training of Trainers for MoALR extension personnel was planned/delivered, and the service continued to be extended after launch — new thematic modules (Citrus, Date Palm, Healthy Nutrition, Household Poultry) in 2019 and a COVID-19 food safety theme in 2020, plus a promotional campaign — which is evidence of a live, maintained service, i.e. Operating. Operating gives base level 3; with quality_evidence and scale_evidence both empty, the level stays at 3.
answer.negative_finding: Level 4 was not proposed because no independent or official evaluation, audit, or performance report of Egypt's digital extension service was found in the retrieved pages — the FAO Country Cases and e-Agriculture pages are the implementer's own descriptions of design and intent, and the ICARDA working paper (CGSpace) assesses readiness of extension agents and farmers for e-extension rather than the performance of an operating service. Level 5 was not proposed because no reach figures for Egypt are published in these pages: the Country Cases page gives usage figures only for Senegal (955 technical advice messages), and states nothing quantitative about Egyptian users, downloads, extension agents trained, or governorate coverage.

gates.reason: no value asserted

answer.abstain_reason: No admissible source in the retrieved pages publishes a gender share for Egypt's digital-agriculture workforce. The only sex-disaggregated figure touching ICT-in-agriculture roles (ICT support staff inside the public extension service) sits on a T5 domain (g-fras.org), and Tier 5 material may be used for existence facts only, never for a statistic. It is also a narrow 38-person subset of a 2011 ministry staffing table, not a measure of the digital-ag workforce as named.
answer.construct_note: The closest evidence is the GFRAS/IFPRI-FAO-IICA Worldwide Extension Study (2011) staffing table for Egypt's ministry-based extension system, which reports an 'Information, Communications & Technology (ICT) Support Staff' category of 38 people, of whom 16 are female and 22 male (~42%), alongside overall extension-staff figures (19% female among subject matter specialists, under 4% female among field-level extension staff). 5.8.name: Agtech/data-science training pipeline

gates.reason: the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Canada, Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep.

answer.value: Egypt operates a large national data-science/AI training pipeline (MCIT's Digital Egypt Pioneers Initiative, with tracks in AI and Data Science, Data Analytics, cybersecurity and programming) and separately supports agricultural skills programmes (FAO/MALR digital-skills courses for extension agents; a Canada-funded climate-smart agribusiness TVET Centre of Competence), but no agtech-specific data-science or agricultural-data training pipeline appears among them — the agriculture bridge is absent from the data-science programmes and the data-science content is absent from the agricultural training programmes.
answer.source_title: Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (Egypt), Press Release: ICT Minister Attends DEG 2024 Graduation Ceremony, Honors Top Achievers
answer.quote: It aims to enhance the digital skills of university students and graduates across different specializations by delivering specialized educational tracks in Artificial Intelligence (AI), data analysis, cybersecurity, and programming.
answer.data_quality_flag: Nearest-adjacent instrument cited is the implementing ministry's own press release; no independent evaluation of any agriculture-linked training pipeline was retrieved.
answer.construct_note: The indicator names an "agtech/data-science training pipeline". The strongest Egyptian evidence in the retrieved pages sits on the data-science side only: DEPI/DEG is a generic national ICT and AI/data-science talent pipeline (7 tracks listed on the MCIT programme page: AI and Data Science, Infrastructure and Cybersecurity, Management and ERP, Digital Marketing and Arts, Software Development, Data Analytics, Digital Game Creation; DEPI Industry adds education, legal, finance, software, marketing and healthcare AI tracks) with no agriculture or agrifood track named, and 13,800 of 25,000 DEPI trainees reported for 2024 within a 220,000-trainee DEG cohort. On the agriculture side, the FAO/MALR digital-skills course for extension agents teaches basic tools ("Word, YouTube, e-mail, Facebook, WhatsApp, Zoom and the FAO app El Mufeed"), i.e. digital literacy rather than data science, and the Canada-funded "Egypt green skills for the climate-smart agribusiness network" builds an agribusiness TVET Centre of Competence with no data-science or agtech-analytics content described. Under a conjunctive reading of the slash (agtech data-science training), the named instrument is not evidenced; under a purely disjunctive reading, DEPI would qualify on the data-science half alone. This cell is recorded conjunctively, against the indicator name as written, because the "agtech" half is what distinguishes this row from a general ICT-skills indicator.
answer.rung_argument: Absent: I searched the two places where an agtech/data-science training pipeline would be documented for Egypt. (1) The national digital-talent architecture — MCIT's Human Development pages for DEPI and NTI's Digital Egypt Youth upskilling programmes, plus the 2024 DEG graduation press release — enumerate every training track offered, and none is agricultural, agrifood, remote-sensing or farm-data related. (2) The agricultural training architecture — FAO Egypt's digital agriculture launch, the FAO/MALR digital-skills course for extension agents, the FAO NENA Agriculture 4.0 regional paper, and the Canada-funded climate-smart agribusiness TVET project — describes extension ToT, basic digital literacy and agribusiness vocational skills, but no data-science, analytics or agtech-engineering curriculum. Nothing rises even to Announced: no government or partner document in the retrieved set announces a forthcoming agtech or agricultural-data-science training track, degree, academy or pipeline. Hence rung Absent, level 1.
answer.negative_finding: Announced was not reached because no retrieved document contains any statement of intent to create an agriculture-specific data-science or agtech training track. The FAO NENA regional paper only invites members to "support development of a regional Digital Agriculture and Innovation Hub" — a regional recommendation to a conference, not an Egyptian announcement, and framed as digital literacy for smallholders rather than an agtech/data-science pipeline. The MCIT DEPI page lists thirteen tracks across two programmes and agriculture is not among them, so the omission is affirmative rather than merely unretrieved.

(3) MCIT/NTI Digital Egypt Youth upskilling programmes — tracks are networks, cybersecurity, virtualization, embedded systems, AI and IoT, cloud, IT, fibre optics, 5G, career development; no agriculture. (5) FAO story on the digital skills course for extension agents in Damas, Dakahlia — confirmed the curriculum is basic digital tools plus the El Mufeed app. (6) FAO Egypt country office page — capacity development on information management systems mentioned in general terms, no training pipeline named. answer.value: A Digital Transformation Unit (AG-DTU) has been formally established inside Egypt's Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation by ministerial decree No. 605 of 15 March 2020, reporting directly to the Minister with an initial 16 experts and three branches (workflow/government services, GIS, and Ag-Foresight), but the retrieved evidence is a planning presentation and no official document confirming the unit's current operation, outputs or performance was found.

answer.quote: establishment of a digital transformation unit within the MOALR by
answer.data_quality_flag: Evidence is a workshop presentation delivered by a MALR official and archived by a CGIAR repository; the underlying decree text itself was not retrieved, and the presentation is largely forward-looking (action plan in future tense).
answer.construct_note: The indicator names a standing digital/AI unit inside the ministry of agriculture. The evidence establishes a Digital Transformation Unit (AG-DTU) inside MALR created by MCIT ministerial decree 605/2020, with GIS, e-services and foresight functions — this is a digital unit inside the MoAg, so it sits on the right side of the open question. The 'AI' element, however, is not shown to reside in this unit: the AI work quoted on the ministry's own site (the 'Hodhod' AI advisory app and AI-based crop-area mapping) is described as a joint MALR–MCIT programme, not as output of the AG-DTU. So the AI half of the row name is matched only by an inter-ministerial programme, not by a named in-ministry AI unit.
answer.rung_argument: Absent is ruled out: a named unit inside the ministry of agriculture is documented, not merely absent from the field. Announced is exceeded: the unit is not just proposed — a specific instrument is cited (decree of the Minister of Communication and Information Technology number 605 of 15 March 2020) creating the unit within MOALR, with a defined reporting line to the Minister, a three-branch structure (WGS, GIS, AG-FORESIGHT) and an initial establishment of 16 experts. That is formal establishment, i.e. Adopted (base level 3). quality_evidence left empty (no evaluation, audit or performance report on the unit was retrieved) and scale_evidence left empty (no reach figures attributable to the unit), so no additions apply: level = 3.
answer.negative_finding: Operating was not proposed because nothing retrieved shows the unit actually functioning: the only document describing it is a February 2021 planning workshop whose action plan is written in the future tense ('DTU will be directly under the supervision of the Minister', 'DTU will be based in the new MOALR building in the new capital', components still to be established), and the ministry's own site (moa.gov.eg news, services and achievements pages) never names the Digital Transformation Unit at all — it attributes digital and AI outputs to joint MALR–MCIT cooperation. No staffing confirmation, budget line, work programme, annual report or organigram entry for the unit was found in the ministry's published structure/achievements pages. Likewise no evaluation and no reach figures for the unit itself, so neither add-on field could be filled.

gates.reason: no value asserted

answer.construct_note: No B-READY score of any kind (overall, pillar, or topic) is published for Egypt, Arab Rep. in the supplied pages. The B-READY 2024 coverage table lists the 50 inaugural economies and Egypt is not among them; the Middle East & North Africa entries listed for 2024 are Iraq, Morocco and West Bank and Gaza. The B-READY 2025 additional-economies table in the same page is truncated mid-list (ends at 'Mali'), so it cannot be verified from the retrieved text whether Egypt is in the 2025 edition, and no Egyptian figure appears anywhere in the retrieved pages. The Egyptian investment authority (GAFI) page states Egypt is preparing to participate in B-READY 2026, which implies it was not yet scored at the time of that July 2025 notice.
answer.quality_evidence: The only country-specific Egyptian evidence retrieved is a T3 GAFI news item announcing preparations for participation in the B-READY 2026 report, led by the Ministry of Investment and Foreign Trade with GAFI. That is a statement of intended future participation, not a published score, and therefore cannot support a numeric value on the 0-100 B-READY scale.
answer.scale_evidence: B-READY scores run 0 (worst) to 100 (best) and are produced for pillars, topics and pillar-topic combinations; 50 economies were scored in the 2024 edition and 101 in the 2025 interim edition. None of the retrieved pages carries an Egyptian value on that scale.
answer.rung_argument: No level can be argued. A threshold score requires a published figure on the B-READY 0-100 scale for Egypt. The retrieved evidence establishes only that (a) the B-READY instrument exists and is scored 0-100, and (b) Egypt was, as of July 2025, preparing to be assessed in a future edition. Assigning even level 1 would require a published Egyptian value below 30, which no retrieved source states; assigning any level from a regional or comparator economy's score would violate the no-cross-border rule.
answer.negative_finding: The specific missing element for any level, including level 1, is a published Egypt-specific B-READY overall score. The B-READY 2024 economy-coverage table omits Egypt, and neither the 2025 report page, the B-READY data/economy page, the methodology page, the WDI B-READY blog, nor the openknowledge record contains an Egyptian figure.

answer.construct_note: The indicator name asserts operating public-private partnerships in digital agriculture. But the arrangement is a donor-funded (Government of Japan) CGIAR/ICARDA-brokered project partnership, not a PPP contracted under Egypt's PPP law; the IFC/World Bank Country Private Sector Diagnostic's PPP annex (Appendix B, 'The Role of Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs) in Egypt') covers PPPs generally and contains no digital-agriculture PPP in the retrieved text. Adopted is exceeded: partners are named and funding is secured (Government of Japan, Water Productivity Enhancement in Agriculture project). 6.14.name: Agri-fintech rails for smallholders

gates.reason: the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep.

answer.value: Agri-fintech rails exist and are running in Egypt at the level of individual platforms — FAO's STI Portal records Agri Cash as an operational Egyptian fintech application combining a digital wallet, interest-free 'Plant Now & Pay Later' input financing and a marketplace, with smallholder farms listed among its prospective users — but no admissible source reports a rail defined for, or usage figures specific to, smallholders.

answer.quote: Agri Cash is a fintech platform developed for Egyptian farmers that integrates financial services with agricultural marketplace solutions.
answer.data_quality_flag: FAO STI Portal entry is an AI-assisted extraction harvested from Digital Agri Hub; the page itself states 'Record status	Newly extracted from original record - Not checked, not enriched' and 'AI stamp	AI-assisted extraction of information', so the underlying claims are vendor-derived rather than independently verified.

The quoted evidence describes a fintech platform 'developed for Egyptian farmers' generally; the FAO record lists prospective users spanning medium-size farms, small-micro entrepreneurs, smallholder farms and SMEs, i.e. smallholders are one target segment among several, not the defining population, and no smallholder-disaggregated usage figure is published. The nearest state instrument, the Farmer Card converted into a Meeza payment card under the MALR/e-finance 'Agri Egypt' network, is issued to registered landholders generally (reported only in Daily News Egypt, T5, quoting a database 'representing 9.4 million feddan') and is likewise not smallholder-specific. 3.10.name: Agricultural e-commerce platforms

gates.reason: the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep.

answer.value: Agricultural e-commerce platforms are operating in Egypt: FAO's Science, Technology and Innovation Portal records at least three Egyptian platforms typed as "E-commerce/online marketplace" — Nile (B2B fresh-produce marketplace linking growers to commercial buyers), Bashaier (marketplace linking small-scale horticulture farmers to buyers) and Agri Cash (marketplace plus input financing) — with Nile described as actively operating and adopted by a growing number of users.
answer.source_title: FAO Science, Technology and Innovation (STI) Portal — Nile online marketplace (Egypt)
answer.quote: Nile is actively operating and has seen adoption by a growing number of users in the fresh produce industry.
answer.data_quality_flag: FAO STI Portal innovation profiles are harvested from Digital Agri Hub and enriched by automated AI extraction; the record itself states "Newly extracted from original record - Not checked, not enriched", so the descriptive claims are not independently verified by FAO staff
answer.construct_note: The census asks whether the row counts only farmer-facing platforms or any agri-food value-chain commerce platform. The evidence quoted sits on the narrower, farmer-facing side of that question: Nile connects fresh-produce growers to commercial buyers, Bashaier connects small-scale horticulture farmers to buyers, and Agri Cash sells inputs to farmers and markets their crops. Downstream agri-food value-chain platforms also exist in Egypt but sit on the wider side and are weaker evidence: Cartona is an FMCG B2B retail marketplace serving mom-and-pop grocers (vendor page, T5, statistics not admissible), and IFC documents MaxAB, an FMCG B2B distribution platform for MSME retailers — neither transacts with farmers. If the definition is ratified as farmer-facing only, the FAO STI Portal entries still support the rung; if ratified as any agri-food commerce platform, the population is larger still.

Ready" with adoption level "8. Livelihood system". answer.negative_finding: Level 4 was not proposed because no independent or official evaluation, audit or performance report of any Egyptian agricultural e-commerce platform appears in the retrieved pages. 3.9.name: Digital advisory platforms at scale

gates.reason: the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt, Jordan, Senegal rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep.

answer.value: Egypt has an operating national digital agricultural advisory platform — the FAO Digital Services Portfolio (DSP), rolled out with the Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation since 2019 and carrying Egypt-specific advisory content (date and citrus production, COVID-19 food safety, a farmer-to-farmer forum) — but no published figure for registered, active or reached farmers was found, so operation is documented while 'at scale' is not.
answer.source_title: FAO, Agro-informatics — Digital Services Portfolio (DSP) project page
answer.quote: Advisory services include also now tailored advisories on: Post harvest practices and processes (Jordan), Capture Fishery, Aquaculture,  date and citrus production (Egypt), and COVID-19 food safety advisories (Egypt, Jordan, Senegal), as well a farmer to farmer forum (Egypt, Jordan) that provides the farmers with the ability to post questions and receive expert advice from governmentally appointed agriculture experts, post success stories, upload photos and videos and receive feedback from other farmers.
answer.data_quality_flag: Implementer's own project page; no independent verification of live service status or usage
answer.construct_note: The evidence establishes existence and ongoing operation of digital advisory platforms in Egypt, but not the 'at scale' half of the indicator name, which the assessment's own census records as having no ratified threshold. None of the retrieved pages carries any user, subscriber or farmer-reached count for the FAO DSP in Egypt or for the two Egyptian advisory/marketing apps studied by IFPRI/WUR. The one substantive performance statement available — the peer-reviewed RCT (Abdelaziz & Abay) — points the other way, stating that 'In Egypt, the focus of this study, uptake of these technologies remains low despite the increasing and considerable investment and availability of digital agricultural tools', i.e. availability without demonstrated scale. That paper evaluates a digital-literacy training intervention, not the platforms' own performance, so it is recorded here as context rather than as quality evidence for the platform.

Announced is exceeded: the FAO/MALR digital extension model was not merely announced in 2019 but was built out with country-specific content. Adopted is exceeded: the DSP is listed by FAO as an ongoing project rolled out to Egypt with government-appointed agriculture experts answering farmer questions, and with Egypt-specific advisory themes (date and citrus, COVID-19 food safety, farmer-to-farmer forum), which is delivery rather than mere institutional adoption — hence Operating, base level 3. Neither additive field is filled, so the level stays at 3.
answer.negative_finding: Level 4 was not proposed because no independent or official evaluation, audit, performance report or service standard for the Egypt DSP (or any other Egyptian advisory platform) appears in the retrieved pages — only FAO's own project description, which is design, not quality. Level 5 was not proposed because no reach figures of any kind (registered users, active users, farmers reached, governorate coverage) are published in these pages for Egypt; the only performance-adjacent statement, from the peer-reviewed RCT, says uptake of such tools in Egypt remains low, which is the opposite of demonstrated scale.

6.13.name: SME/agribusiness adoption of digital tools (%)

gates.reason: the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep.

answer.value: No publisher reports a percentage of Egyptian SMEs/agribusinesses using digital tools; the closest construct-matched evidence (ICARDA 2023) finds that of eight categories of digital agriculture tools, only sensors and mobile apps are fairly widely used in Egypt, with connectivity, data-security concerns and farmers' knowledge levels constraining further adoption of digital agriculture tools by SMEs.
answer.source_title: ICARDA (CGIAR), Current Situation of Digital Agriculture in Egypt
answer.quote: This report highlights various aspects of digital transformation in Egypt, starting with an overview of 8 categories of digital agriculture tools, of which only sensors and mobile apps are fairly widely used in Egypt. 8.2.name: Account ownership, female (%)

gates.reason: recorded at T1

answer.source_title: World Bank Open Data (World Development Indicators / Global Findex): Account ownership at a financial institution or with a mobile-money-service provider, female (% of population ages 15+) — Egypt, Arab Rep.
answer.quote: Egypt, Arab Rep.	2024	40.21
answer.data_quality_flag: Nationally representative demand-side survey (Gallup World Poll sample of ~1,000 adults per economy); Findex Egypt sampling excludes the frontier governorates (<2% of population), and sub-group estimates such as the female series carry wider sampling error than the national figure.
answer.construct_note: The quoted series is female-specific (women ages 15+), matching the indicator name. Two caveats bearing on the unratified definition: (a) the WDI series FX.OWN.TOTL.FE.ZS defines "account" as an account at a financial institution OR with a mobile-money-service provider, so mobile money is counted inside this total and is scored again at 8.4 — on the wrong side of the open definitional question flagged in the indicator census; (b) the figure is national (all women), not rural women, so it is not a rural-female measure. For context, the older Findex 2021 round in the World Bank DataBank shows "Account, women (% age 15+)" for Egypt at 9.3 (2014), 27.0 (2017) and 24.2 (2021); the 40.21 value is the 2024/Findex 2025 round and represents a sharp increase over 2021.
answer.quality_evidence: T1 publisher (World Bank Open Data, sourced from the Global Findex Database). The underlying instrument is documented in the Findex microdata catalogue for Egypt (EGY_2021_FINDEX_v02_M, variables 'female' and 'account'), confirming that the sex-disaggregated account variable is collected directly at individual level rather than modelled.
answer.scale_evidence: Nationally representative of the resident adult female population of Egypt; geographic coverage excludes five frontier governorates representing under 2 percent of the population.
answer.rung_argument: Level 1 would require a value below 20; Egypt's female account ownership of 40.21 is well above that. Level 2 (20-40 band) is passed because the published figure exceeds the 40 cut point. Level 3 is therefore the arithmetic result of a value of 40.21 against cut points 20/40/60/80. The value itself is defensible: it is published by a T1 source, is explicitly sex-disaggregated for women aged 15+, and is for Egypt, Arab Rep. specifically, with reference year 2024.
answer.negative_finding: Level 4 would require female account ownership above 60 percent. The published 2024 figure of 40.21 is barely over the 40 cut and roughly 20 percentage points short of 60; no source in the retrieved pages reports any Egyptian female account-ownership figure at or above 60. Note also that the margin over the 40 threshold is thin (0.21 points) and rests on a single survey round, so the level-3 placement is itself near the boundary with level 2.
answer.search_trail: Started with the World Bank Open Data indicator page for FX.OWN.TOTL.FE.ZS filtered to Egypt (Source 6), which carries the female-specific series and gives Egypt's most recent value: 2024, 40.21 — quoted.
