7.12.name: Responsible-AI safeguards (consent, rights)

gates.reason: the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep.

answer.value: Egypt has an adopted cross-sector responsible-AI regime — the Egyptian Charter for Responsible AI (launched by the National Council for AI in April 2023, built on five values including Human-Centeredness, Transparency and Explainability, Fairness and Accountability), supplemented by the Personal Data Protection Law (2020) and, from March 2026, a Guide to Egypt's National AI Governance Framework and National Guidelines for Trustworthy and Responsible AI issued by the Egyptian Center for Responsible AI — but none of the retrieved instruments contains agriculture- or farmer-specific consent and rights safeguards.
answer.source_title: Egypt, Ministry of Communications and Information Technology — Press Release: Egyptian Charter for Responsible AI Launched
answer.quote: The Egyptian Charter for Responsible AI serves five main values: Human-Centeredness, Transparency and Explainability, Fairness, Accountability, and Security and Safety. Values are fostered by following 13 General Guidelines, which are overarching rules applicable to all members of the AI ecosystem, and 16 Implementation Guidelines, which are technical considerations, mainly applicable to any entity developing, deploying, or managing an AI system.
answer.data_quality_flag: Government self-description of its own instruments; no independent evaluation of implementation was retrievable in the supplied pages.
answer.construct_note: The indicator name as written does not restrict the safeguards to agriculture, so the cross-sector Egyptian regime is taken to answer it. It must be recorded, however, that the evidence sits on the cross-sector side of the census's open question: nothing in the Charter, the National AI Governance Framework (March 2026), the National Guidelines for Trustworthy and Responsible AI, or the Generative AI Guidelines is agriculture- or farmer-specific, and no farm-data consent instrument was found. 'Consent' as such is also not named among the Charter's five values; consent obligations sit in the Personal Data Protection Law (2020), referenced as part of the Framework's legislative base but not quotable in detail from the retrieved pages.
answer.rung_argument: Absent is ruled out: named responsible-AI safeguard instruments demonstrably exist for Egypt. Announced is exceeded: the Charter was not merely trailed but launched by the National Council for AI at its seventh meeting in April 2023, and the Guide to Egypt's National AI Governance Framework carries the status 'Approved for Publication', Edition 2.0, authorised by the Minister of Communications and Information Technology on 15 March 2026. That formal issuance of a governing instrument with values, 13 general guidelines and 16 implementation guidelines, sitting on the Personal Data Protection Law and Cybercrime Law, establishes Adopted (level 3). Neither quality_evidence nor scale_evidence could be filled from admissible quotable material, so no increment applies.
answer.negative_finding: Operating was not proposed because the retrieved pages describe supervision prospectively rather than evidentially — the Charter states that government AI projects 'should be supervised' by MCIT and that MCIT 'presents periodically a report', but no compliance report, audit result, register of impact assessments, or enforcement action was retrievable. Level 4 was not proposed because quality_evidence is empty: the only potentially independent assessments in the retrieved set are the OECD AI Review of Egypt, whose supplied text is front matter only and carries no quotable finding on safeguard performance, and the UNESCO RAM report, whose supplied pages are a catalogue record and a country landing page (tiered T5 here), neither containing an evaluative statement about how the safeguards work in practice. Level 5 was not proposed because scale_evidence is empty: no figures on entities covered, assessments conducted, complaints handled, or sectoral reach of the Charter or Framework appear in any supplied page.
answer.search_trail: Started with the MCIT press release announcing the Egyptian Charter for Responsible AI (April 2023) as the most directly on-point national instrument; confirmed launch, issuing body and content structure. Cross-checked the MCIT Artificial Intelligence landing page for institutional standing (NCAI, its 2026 expansion, ECRAI activity, adoption of an AI Governance Framework). Checked the MCIT Publications index, which lists the Guide to Egypt National AI Governance Framework, National Generative AI Guidelines and National Guidelines for Trustworthy and Responsible AI (all March 2026) — searched their descriptions for any agriculture or farmer scope and found none. Opened the ai.gov.eg Guide PDF text to verify status ('Approved for Publication'), authorisation date and legislative base (Constitution, Personal Data Protection Law, Cybercrime Law); the supplied extract stops at the executive summary and contains no consent clause text to quote. Checked the OECD AI Review of Egypt for an independent evaluation of safeguard implementation — the supplied text is title page, foreword, acknowledgements and table of contents only, with no quotable finding, so it could not support quality_evidence. Checked the UNESCO RAM country page and UNESDOC record; both are T5-tiered navigation/landing pages here and carry no quotable safeguard evaluation. Dead end: no agriculture-sector data-consent or farmer-rights instrument surfaced in any of the nine pages, and the Ministry of Agriculture appears only as an interviewee in the OECD acknowledgements.

7.2.name: AI-enabled agricultural solutions deployed

gates.reason: the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep.

answer.value: Egypt has national AI governance machinery (National Council for AI, established 2019) and government-run innovation activity aimed at AI in agriculture — MCIT/ITIDA/TIEC's GreenHack hackathon (June 2025, Ismailia) awarded prizes to AI-powered pest-detection prototypes for citrus farms — but none of the retrieved sources documents an AI-enabled agricultural solution actually deployed to farmers in Egypt; the digital agriculture tools evidenced for Egypt (FAO's El Mufeed extension app, the AMAN poultry disease early-warning app, government apps Hudhud and DAIRS) are described as mobile/sensor/extension tools under development, not as AI-enabled solutions in deployment.
answer.source_title: Egypt, Ministry of Communications and Information Technology — 'Creativa Innovation Hubs Announce Winners of GreenHack Hackathon in Ismailia'
answer.quote: The program featured hands-on workshops and advisory sessions focused on designing and developing cutting-edge solutions using Artificial Intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), and robotics to serve the smart agriculture sector.
answer.data_quality_flag: Government press release describing a prototype competition; no independent verification of any fielded AI agricultural solution
answer.construct_note: The indicator names DEPLOYED AI-enabled agricultural solutions. The strongest Egypt-specific AI-in-agriculture evidence retrieved is a government-sponsored hackathon in which teams built AI-powered pest-detection prototypes (first prize EGP 20,000; second EGP 15,000; fourteen teams) — prototypes and intent, not deployment with users. The adjacent digital-agriculture artefacts for Egypt in the retrieved pages are not AI: FAO's El Mufeed is a content-based extension app; AMAN is a GPS/SMS poultry disease reporting platform ('A GPS and Google Map are used for locating 2.5 Million farms'); ICARDA's 2023 stocktake reports that 'only sensors and mobile apps are fairly widely used in Egypt' and that government apps 'Al Mufeed, Hudhud (extension services tools), and DAIRS (climate early warning) are also under development'. The UNDP Digital Agribusiness Map lists agri-tech startups (NileBot, Mozare3, Baramoda, Agrimatic Farms, FreshSource) but the retrieved text does not characterise any of them as AI-enabled and gives no deployment figures for AI. So the best available evidence sits on the 'announced/prototype' side of the deployment question, not the deployed side.
answer.rung_argument: Absent is exceeded: the domain is not empty — Egypt has a National Council for Artificial Intelligence and a National AI Strategy, and the ICT ministry is explicitly running programmes to apply AI, IoT and robotics to 'the smart agriculture sector', with named AI pest-detection prototypes emerging from a state-backed hackathon in 2025. Announced is met: the state has publicly committed to and funded work on AI-enabled agricultural solutions, and specific AI agricultural applications have been named and prize-funded. Adopted is not met: no retrieved source shows an AI agricultural solution formally procured, licensed, institutionalised in a ministry programme, or made available to farmers. Level therefore = 2 (Announced), with no quality and no scale evidence to add.
answer.negative_finding: Adopted was not proposed because nothing in the retrieved pages shows an AI-enabled agricultural solution moving past prototype into institutional adoption or field release. The hackathon report describes winning teams and prize money, not procurement or rollout; the World Bank Climate Resilient Agri-Food Transformation Project PID (Apr 2024) is at concept stage and its objective text ('strengthen the nation-wide agriculture information system and early warning services') does not name AI; and the ICARDA stocktake places Egypt's government digital-agriculture apps 'under development'. Operating was likewise not proposed: no user, coverage or beneficiary figures for any AI agricultural solution appear in any source, so scale_evidence is left empty, and no evaluation, audit or performance report exists, so quality_evidence is left empty.
answer.search_trail: Order of examination: (1) MCIT AI portal (mcit.gov.eg/en/Artificial_Intelligence) — confirms NCAI, National AI Strategy, AI governance framework, but the retrieved text names no agricultural AI deployment. (2) MCIT news item on GreenHack Ismailia — the only Egypt-specific, government-published item naming AI applied to agriculture; establishes prototype-stage AI pest detection, quoted here. (3) ICARDA 'Current Situation of Digital Agriculture in Egypt' (CGSpace, 2023) — abstract only (item is Limited Access); reports sensors and mobile apps as the tools 'fairly widely used' and government apps 'under development'; no AI deployment claim. (4) FAO Digital Services Portfolio country case for Egypt and FAO Egypt El Mufeed page — El Mufeed is a participatory content app, no AI; note that the same FAO page attributes 'satellite imagery and artificial intelligence-driven advice' to E-Tolbi in SENEGAL, which is not evidence for Egypt and is not carried across. (5) FAO e-Agriculture AMAN app page — GPS/SMS/GIS early warning, explicitly not AI. (6) World Bank PID P180480 Climate Resilient Agri-Food Transformation Project — concept stage, agriculture information system and early warning, no AI component in retrieved text. (7) UNDP Digital Agribusiness Map (2025) — lists agri-tech startups and adoption percentages (e.g. 'Precision Irrigation Adoption 15%') but does not label these as AI, so it cannot be used as AI scale evidence. Dead end: no retrieved page carries a user count, hectare count or beneficiary figure for any AI-enabled agricultural solution in Egypt.

gates.reason: the recorded evidence attributes its facts to Egypt rather than to Egypt, Arab Rep.

answer.value: No publisher states a national share of Egyptian smallholders reached by digital agricultural services; the available T2 analyses find that uptake of digital tools among Egyptian smallholders remains low and that most Egyptian digital agriculture tools are pilot-stage or region-specific, with very few achieving national scale.
answer.source_title: IFPRI / CGSpace, Policy Note: Digital Agricultural Technology in Egypt: Insights from App Developers (Abdallah, Abdelhadi & Karachiwalla, December 2025)
answer.quote: highlights that many Egyptian digital tools remain pilot-stage or region-specific, with very few achieving
answer.data_quality_flag: qualitative characterisation only; no national denominator, no count of smallholders reached, and no published definition of 'reached' (registered vs active vs benefiting)
answer.construct_note: The indicator names a national percentage of SMALLHOLDERS reached by digital services. Nothing in the retrieved pages states such a percentage for Egypt. The closest quantified evidence is the Abdelaziz & Abay randomized intervention (Food Policy, WUR repository copy), which reports treatment effects — 'the standard digital training alone increased uptake by 20 percentage points and utilization by 18 percentage points' — but these are experimental impacts in a localised trial, not a national share of smallholders reached, and the paper's own framing is that 'In Egypt, the focus of this study, uptake of these technologies remains low'. The FAO NENA report (openknowledge.fao.org) is regional and its landing page carries no Egypt-specific reach figure. The ICARDA report is Limited Access and its abstract carries no percentage. So the evidence sits on the wrong side of the unratified definition question: it speaks to the magnitude of reach qualitatively, but no source measures a national smallholder share, and 'reached' is nowhere operationalised.
answer.quality_evidence: Two T2 sources bear on the construct: an IFPRI policy note synthesising interviews with Egyptian digital-agriculture app developers, and a peer-reviewed Food Policy article (Abdelaziz & Abay) based on a randomized controlled trial with Egyptian smallholders. Both are analytically credible on direction and barriers (digital illiteracy, connectivity, trust, gender gaps) but neither is designed to estimate national coverage; neither reports a population-level denominator of smallholder holdings against which 'reached' could be computed. The 2009-2010 Agricultural Census (FAO microdata) provides a holdings universe but contains no digital-service variables.
answer.scale_evidence: Scale evidence is negative rather than positive: the IFPRI note states Egyptian digital tools remain pilot-stage or region-specific with very few achieving national scale, and the Food Policy paper states uptake remains low despite considerable investment and availability of digital agricultural tools. FAO's 2019 MALR digital extension initiative is described as a model/pilot with training-of-trainers and awareness sessions, with no user counts reported. No source reports numbers of smallholder users of any Egyptian platform (Hodhod, Mahsooly, Al Mufeed, DAIRS).
answer.rung_argument: Level 1 (below the 10% cut) is what the evidence supports. The construct is real and evidenced in Egypt — multiple named platforms exist and smallholders are their target — but every source that characterises magnitude does so downward: the IFPRI policy note says Egyptian digital tools 'remain pilot-stage or region-specific, with very few achieving national scale', and the peer-reviewed RCT states that in Egypt 'uptake of these technologies remains low' despite investment and availability, with the trial itself designed to overcome near-baseline non-use (training raised uptake by 20 percentage points from a low base). There is therefore evidence of existence and of low reach, which places the cell at the floor rung, but no measured share at all — so the value is recorded as a statement, not a number, and the level is argued rather than computed.
answer.negative_finding: Level 2 would require published evidence that at least 10% of Egyptian smallholders are reached by digital services. No retrieved source reports any share, any user count, or any platform registration total for Egypt, and the only quantified figures are within-trial treatment effects from a localised randomized intervention with no national provenance. The affirmative statements that exist ('very few achieving national scale', 'uptake remains low') point away from, not toward, the 10% cut, but they are qualitative — so the 10% threshold is unrefuted as well as unmet, and the level 1 record should be read as a floor pending a national measurement.
answer.search_trail: Order of inspection: (1) FAO Egypt news on the FAO-MALR digital agriculture initiative (2019) — describes a digital extension model, ToT and awareness sessions, no user or coverage figures. (2) FAO microdata catalogue, Egypt Agricultural Census 2009-2010 — gives the holdings universe and complete enumeration method but no digital-service variables, so no denominator-plus-numerator pairing is possible. (3) CAPMAS Central Data Catalog and its Agriculture-Quarter collection — 629 studies listed, agriculture bulletins on income, production movement and property, nothing on digital service use by farmers. gates.reason: no value asserted

answer.abstain_reason: None of the retrieved pages publishes a figure for the share (%) of Egyptian farmers reached by climate/agrometeorological advisory services. The closest Egypt-specific quantities in the supplied pages measure adjacent but different constructs (climate-change awareness among farmers in two Nile Delta governorates; information behaviour of 382 farmers in Dakhalia toward mobile advisory services), and neither is a national reach rate. The WMO State of Climate Services page gives only a global count of NMHS capacity levels, with no Egypt figure. Since the construct cannot be quote-verified for Egypt at any tier, a ratification hold is set rather than a substituted number.
answer.construct_note: Indicator names farmer-side REACH of climate advisories (% of farmers receiving them), nationally. Available Egypt evidence sits on the wrong side of that question in two ways. (a) Demand-side proxies that are not reach: Kassem et al. (MDPI, Sustainability 2019) report that 51.9% of 792 surveyed farmers in two Nile Delta governorates had no knowledge of the climate change phenomenon — climate-change awareness, not receipt of an advisory, and sub-national. Kassem et al. (Information Development, abstract only) surveyed 382 farmers in Dakhalia governorate and found weather forecasts among the most frequently received information types and that 47% had 'low information behavior' — again a single governorate and a behavioural typology, not a reach percentage. (b) Supply-side existence facts: FAO/e-Agriculture describes a digital extension model and the Central Laboratory for Agricultural Climate issuing agrometeorological data; ICARDA's abstract lists DAIRS (climate early warning) and extension apps Al Mufeed and Hudhud as 'under development'; the EMA/WMO workshop note describes climate early-warning support under the NAP. These establish that advisory issuance platforms exist or are being built, but none states how many or what share of farmers actually receive advisories.
answer.quality_evidence: The only farmer-level survey figures in the supplied pages are peer-reviewed (T2, MDPI Sustainability 2019, n=792, two governorates) and a restricted-access journal abstract (Information Development, n=382, one governorate). Neither is a national statistic, neither was published as an advisory-reach rate, and no T1 official statistic (CAPMAS, MALR, EMA) reporting advisory reach appears in the retrieved set.
answer.scale_evidence: Supply-side scale is only qualitatively evidenced: FAO's 2019 digital extension model covered four thematic areas (citrus, date palm, household poultry, human nutrition) with no user counts; ICARDA records government apps including DAIRS climate early warning as under development; SCALA records that an early warning system for smallholder farmers is at roadmap stage ('for which a roadmap has been developed'). No user, subscriber or coverage numbers are published in any supplied page.
answer.rung_argument: No level is proposed. The threshold scale (20/40/60/80) requires a published percentage measuring farmer receipt of climate advisories in Egypt. No supplied page carries such a percentage. Assigning even level 1 would imply an evidenced value below 20%, which the sources do not establish; assigning a higher level from the 51.9%-unaware or 47%-low-information-behaviour figures would be a construct substitution (awareness/information behaviour in one or two governorates for national advisory reach) of exactly the kind that converts a data gap into a confident score. The level is therefore withheld pending a definition ruling on whether this row scores farmer receipt or supply-side issuance.
answer.negative_finding: Even the lowest rung is not supported: nothing in the evidence quantifies, at national scale, the proportion of Egyptian farmers who receive climate or agrometeorological advisories.
